title: Math for Computer Science
text:
These are the lecture notes for CSCI 201, math for computer science (discrete mathematics), at Western Washington University. General mathematics that several courses share, such as logic, sets and functions, is kept in the mathematics prerequisites site. These notes include its definitions, from the mds submodule, so each definition is written once and reads the same in both places.
The notes are available in multiple formats:

HTML Website: Navigate using the navbar for easy access to all pages
RevealJS Slides: Each chapter can generate a presentation format with -slides.html suffix
PDF Handouts: Each chapter can generate a PDF handout with -handout.pdf suffix
DOCX Documents: Each chapter can generate a Microsoft Word document with .docx extension



The notes are released under the MIT License; see the LICENSE file.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Course Description
This course is a rigorous introduction to the mathematical structures and reasoning techniques underlying computer science. Topics include sets, functions, relations, graphs, trees, and finite automata, with an emphasis on formal definitions and logical precision. You will learn to write mathematical proofs using direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction. Functional programming is introduced as a way to express computation and recursion within a mathematically grounded framework.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Course Outcomes
Homework, labs, and exams test and measure the outcomes below. On completion of CSCI 201, students will demonstrate:

A thorough understanding of the mathematical definitions of concepts important to computer science, including sets, tuples, functions, and relations.
A basic understanding of graphs, trees, and their traversals.
A basic understanding of the mathematical definition of finite automata.
A basic understanding of asymptotic notation.
A basic understanding of recurrence relations and loop invariants.
The ability to prove basic theorems involving these concepts using direct proof, contradiction, contrapositive, and mathematical induction.
The ability to use functional style effectively in a functional programming language.

Discrete Mathematics with Applications (5th ed.), by Susanna Epp.

Other useful references:

Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, by Kenneth Rosen; any recent edition.
Building Blocks for Theoretical Computer Science, by Margaret Fleck, which can be read at no cost on the author’s webpage.

Communication
Outbound. I will send official class announcements through Canvas Announcements. Please set Canvas to notify you of them right away, so you do not miss important information: in the course’s Canvas notification settings, set the Announcement row’s Email column to Notify immediately.
Inbound. All course-related correspondence goes through Canvas. Post nearly all questions and comments for me or the TAs on the class discussion forum, Canvas Discussions (link TBD). Anything that should not be posted there, such as a grading question or objection, goes in a Canvas message to me.
Confidential matters, such as information about your health, also go in a Canvas message to me, not to my email.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Questions and Corrections
If something in the course materials seems wrong, ask. The course materials include the notes, worksheets, assignments, and anything I say or show in class, including my slides. I will make mistakes, and so will the other authors of the materials.
Do not assume that you are the confused one when the material might be wrong. Ask your question first, in class or outside it, and we can talk through your reasoning together. If you are right, we all learn something and I fix the material. If you are not, we can jointly find out where the confusion started.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Health Precautions
If you are sick with something that could be communicable, let me know ahead of time and I will try to arrange a way for you to keep up, so you can stay home and not expose others needlessly. Please contact me if you have questions, concerns, or suggestions.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Software
The labs and the programming parts of homework use Racket, a functional programming language. Racket is free, and it comes with the DrRacket editor. For any software that comes pre-installed in the department labs, please use the default installed version.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Active Learning
Class time is for working on problems, not only for listening. You will be asked to think about questions on your own, write down answers, discuss them in small groups, and share your answers with the class. Sometimes you may be asked to write on the board. I will give you time to think things through before you are put on the spot. Please give me feedback about the structure of the class, the activities, or group dynamics.

ABCD Cards
On the first day of class, I will give each student an ABCD card, which you will use to vote on answers to questions in class. They work like electronic clickers, but they are free and need no batteries. They let both you and me quickly see how well you understand the material, so that I can adjust what I emphasize in class and you can adjust what you study outside it. Please bring this card to class each day. If you lose your card, print a new, landscape-mode color copy of the ABCD card.


Worksheets
Most classes include a worksheet: guided practice that reinforces the day’s concepts and prepares you for the exams. Please keep your worksheets organized and bring them to later classes. You are encouraged to work on worksheet problems with classmates, but each student submits their own work and should be able to explain it. I will post selected worksheet solutions after the submission deadline, and review common mistakes at the start of the next class. Most midterm and final exam questions will be adapted from worksheet problems.

Thresholds for plus and minus grades are at my discretion. The overall grade Canvas displays may be inaccurate; the weights above are the ones that count.

Homework and Worksheets
Homework assignments combine written work and programming. Homework and worksheets are graded on completion, meaning whether you made a solid effort to solve each problem:

Complete: 100%
Substantial effort: 80%
Minimal effort: 40%
Missing: 0%

The lowest worksheet score is dropped.
Quiz 0 is a short quiz in the first week that checks the CSCI 145 and precalculus material this course assumes. It is graded on completion and counts as one worksheet, and its main purpose is to show you (and me) what to review.
When writing up your work:

Type all written work. You do not need to use LaTeX, but I recommend it.
Hand-drawn diagrams are welcome when they help illustrate a concept, as long as they are legible.
Format code and pseudocode in a fixed-width font. Do not submit screenshots of your editor or terminal.
Show your work. An answer alone will not get full credit, on homework or on exams.



Labs
Weekly labs give hands-on programming practice, with a TA available to answer questions during the lab period. To get full credit, you must both attend lab and submit the deliverable by its deadline, which will typically be 10pm on the Monday after the lab (or the next class day, when that Monday is a holiday).

If you do not attend lab but submit the deliverable on time, your score is multiplied by 0.5. This penalty is waived automatically for one lab; if you have a legitimate reason to miss more, contact me and the TA ahead of time.
Attending a lab section other than your own requires permission from both me and the TA(s).
Late lab submissions are not accepted.



Exams
The course has two in-class midterm exams, tentatively on Wednesday, January 27 (week 4) and Wednesday, February 17 (week 7), and a cumulative final exam during finals week, in our classroom at the time WWU’s finals schedule assigns, which is set by the lecture time: Tuesday, March 16 for the 11:00 sections (CRNs 13745 and 13746) and Thursday, March 18 for the 9:00 sections (CRNs 13747 and 13748), both 10:30am–12:30pm.

Each midterm lasts 50 minutes, and you may bring one page of notes (front and back).
The final exam lasts 120 minutes, and you may bring two pages of notes (front and back).

If you know in advance that you will be unable to take an exam at the scheduled time, let me know at least one week before the exam, and we may be able to reschedule it.


Grading Questions
If you have a question about a grade, send it to me in writing, as a Canvas message (see Communication), within 48 hours of the graded work being returned. You will never lose points for asking.

Deadlines and Late Work
Canvas lists every due date.

Homework is due Friday at 10pm, with no-penalty extensions until Sunday at 10pm. I will not be available for help on weekends.
The last homework, Homework 6, is due before finals week and has no extension.
Lab deliverables are due as described under Labs.

Please talk to me in advance if you need an accommodation or an extension; the day an assignment is due is too late. If you miss a deadline or an exam because of a medical emergency, contact me as soon as possible to discuss arrangements.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Collaboration and AI Tools
Collaboration. You may work together on homework and worksheets unless an assignment or problem says it is individual. A group of about three works best, since it is hard for everyone to contribute in a large group. You may discuss the steps of an algorithm or proof on a whiteboard, but write your own math and code, and submit your own answers. Do not copy from classmates, the internet, a chatbot, or a forum.
AI tools. AI tools such as large language model chatbots are allowed on homework and worksheets only. Use them like a collaborator, not as a source of answers: you must still write your answer in your own words, and you are responsible for understanding it. Say whether you used an AI tool, and name it, on each assignment. Students who rely heavily on AI tools often struggle on exams, where the tools are not available. AI tools are not allowed on lab work, including lab work you finish after the lab period.
Exams are solo: work alone, without help from anyone else and without AI tools; the only aid allowed is your page(s) of notes, as described under Exams.

title: Proofs with Sets
text:
NoteSource





Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Proofs Involving Sets”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. These come from those notes:

what to show to prove that an element is in a set given in set-builder notation;
the direct and contrapositive outlines of a subset proof;
proving set equality by proving that each set is a subset of the other;
the theorem that a nonempty factor cancels from both sides of an equation between Cartesian products, with the proof of its first half.

Everything else is new: the exercises, the other examples and theorems, the second half of that proof, the membership test for a set built with an expression, and the section on disproving a claim about sets.




1 Proving membership







Exercise 1 (In or out) Let \(T = {\mathopen{}\left\{3k + 2 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition: Set-builder notation with an expression). Prove that \(17 \in T\) and that \(19 \notin T\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. \(17 \in T\). An element of \(T\) is a number of the form \(3k + 2\) with \(k\) an integer. Take \(k = 5\), which is an integer. Then \(3k + 2 = 3 \cdot 5 + 2 = 17\), so \(17 \in T\).
\(19 \notin T\). Suppose, for contradiction, that \(19 \in T\) (Definition: Proof by contradiction). Then \(19 = 3k + 2\) for some integer \(k\). Subtracting 2 from both sides gives \(3k = 17\), so \(k = 17/3\). But \(17/3\) is not an integer, since \(3 \cdot 5 = 15 < 17 < 18 = 3 \cdot 6\). This contradicts that \(k\) is an integer, so \(19 \notin T\).











Remark 1 (What to show for membership). To prove that \(a\) is an element of a set, show that \(a\) passes the set’s test:

for \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{x \in A : P(x)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition: Set-builder notation), show that \(a \in A\) and that \(P(a)\) is true;
for \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{x : P(x)\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the same notation with no set \(A\) named, show that \(P(a)\) is true;
for \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{f(k) : k \in A\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition: Set-builder notation with an expression), find some \(k \in A\) with \(f(k) = a\).

The last case is an existence proof, so it usually names the \(k\) (Definition: Constructive proof). To prove that \(a \notin S\), prove the negation of the test, often by contradiction, as in Solution 1.











Example 1 (A root of a polynomial) Let \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: 2x^2 - x = 0\right\}\mathclose{}}\). Then \(\frac{1}{2} \in S\).
The set has the form \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in A : P(x)\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so there are two things to show (Remark 1). First, \(\frac{1}{2}\) is a real number. Second,
\[
\begin{aligned}
2 \mathopen{}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\mathclose{}^2 - \frac{1}{2}
&= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2}
\\&= \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}
\\&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]






2 Proving a subset







Exercise 2 (A disk inside a square) Let \(D = {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x^2 + y^2 \le 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the points of the plane at distance at most 1 from the origin. Prove that \(D \subseteq [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\), where \([-1, 1] = {\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: -1 \le x \le 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition: Subset, Definition: Cartesian product, Definition: Closed interval).










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Let \((a, b) \in D\), so \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers with \(a^2 + b^2 \le 1\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a^2
&\le a^2 + b^2
&& \text{(} b^2 \ge 0 \text{)}
\\&\le 1.
&& \text{(} (a, b) \in D \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(a > 1\), then \(a^2 = a \cdot a > 1 \cdot 1 = 1\), and if \(a < -1\), then \(a^2 = (-a)^2 > 1\). Neither is possible, so \(-1 \le a \le 1\), that is, \(a \in [-1, 1]\). The same steps with \(a\) and \(b\) swapped give \(b \in [-1, 1]\). So \((a, b) \in [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\). Every element of \(D\) is in \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\), so \(D \subseteq [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\).











Remark 2 (The shape of a subset proof). By Definition: Subset, \(A \subseteq B\) means the conditional “if \(a \in A\), then \(a \in B\)” is true for every \(a\). So a proof of \(A \subseteq B\) is a proof of that conditional, either directly (Definition: Direct proof):

Suppose \(a \in A\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(a \in B\).
So \(A \subseteq B\).

or by contrapositive (Definition: Proof by contrapositive):

Suppose \(a \notin B\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(a \notin A\).
So \(A \subseteq B\).

The element \(a\) is arbitrary: the proof may use only that \(a \in A\) (or that \(a \notin B\)), nothing else about it.











Example 2 (A subset proof by contrapositive) Claim: \({\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x + y > 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x > 1 \text{ or } y > 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\). If two numbers add up to more than 2, at least one of them is more than 1.
We use the contrapositive outline of Remark 2. Suppose \(p \notin {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x > 1 \text{ or } y > 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\). If \(p\) is not a pair of real numbers, then \(p\) is not in the left-hand set either, since every element of that set is a pair of real numbers. Otherwise \(p = (a, b)\) with \(a\) and \(b\) real, and “\(a > 1\) or \(b > 1\)” is false. By De Morgan’s laws (Theorem: De Morgan’s laws), \(a > 1\) is false and \(b > 1\) is false, that is, \(a \le 1\) and \(b \le 1\), so \(a + b \le 1 + 1 = 2\). So \(p \notin {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x + y > 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\). So the left-hand set is a subset of the right-hand set.
The contrapositive turns the conclusion “\(x > 1\) or \(y > 1\)”, which does not say which number is large, into the hypothesis “\(a \le 1\) and \(b \le 1\)”, which says something about both.











Theorem 1 (Subsets of subsets) Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be sets. If \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq C\), then \(A \subseteq C\).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq C\), and let \(a \in A\). Since \(A \subseteq B\), \(a \in B\) (Definition: Subset). Since \(B \subseteq C\), \(a \in C\). So every element of \(A\) is in \(C\), and \(A \subseteq C\).











Example 3 (A chain of subsets) Let \(D\) be the disk of Exercise 2, and let \(H = {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x + y \le 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\). Solution 2 shows that \(D \subseteq [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\). Every point \((x, y)\) of \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\) has \(x \le 1\) and \(y \le 1\), so \(x + y \le 2\), and so \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1] \subseteq H\). By Theorem 1, \(D \subseteq H\).






3 Proving set equality







Exercise 3 (Absorbing an intersection) Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Prove that \(A \cup (A \cap B) = A\) (Definition: Union, Definition: Intersection).
Hint: prove that each side is a subset of the other.










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. \(A \cup (A \cap B) \subseteq A\). Let \(x \in A \cup (A \cap B)\). Then \(x \in A\) or \(x \in A \cap B\). In the first case, \(x \in A\). In the second case, \(x \in A\) and \(x \in B\), so again \(x \in A\). Either way, \(x \in A\) (Definition: Proof by cases).
\(A \subseteq A \cup (A \cap B)\). Let \(x \in A\). Then “\(x \in A\) or \(x \in A \cap B\)” is true, since its first part is true (Definition: Or), so \(x \in A \cup (A \cap B)\).
Each side is a subset of the other, so an element is in one side exactly when it is in the other, and the two sets are equal (Definition: Set).











Theorem 2 (Equal sets are subsets of each other) Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Then \(A = B\) if and only if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq A\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition: Set, \(A = B\) means that every \(x\) has \(x \in A \Leftrightarrow x \in B\). By Theorem: A biconditional is two conditionals, that biconditional is the same as “\(x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B\), and \(x \in B \Rightarrow x \in A\)”. A conjunction is true for every \(x\) exactly when each of its two parts is true for every \(x\). The first conditional, for every \(x\), is \(A \subseteq B\) (Definition: Subset), and the second, for every \(x\), is \(B \subseteq A\).











Remark 3 (The shape of a set equality proof). By Theorem 2, a proof of \(A = B\) has two parts, each a subset proof (Remark 2):

(\(\subseteq\)) Suppose \(a \in A\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(a \in B\).

(\(\supseteq\)) Suppose \(a \in B\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(a \in A\).

So \(A = B\).

This is the “if and only if” outline of Remark: The shape of an “if and only if” proof, applied to \(a \in A\) and \(a \in B\).











Example 4 (Two kinds of odd number) Claim: \({\mathopen{}\left\{4k + 1 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}} \cup {\mathopen{}\left\{4k + 3 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{2m + 1 : m \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
(\(\subseteq\)) Let \(x\) be in the left-hand side. If \(x = 4k + 1\) for some integer \(k\), then \(x = 2(2k) + 1\). If \(x = 4k + 3\) for some integer \(k\), then \(x = 2(2k + 1) + 1\). Both \(2k\) and \(2k + 1\) are integers (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so either way \(x\) is in the right-hand side.
(\(\supseteq\)) Let \(x = 2m + 1\) for some integer \(m\). The integer \(m\) is even or odd (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof).

If \(m\) is even, then \(m = 2j\) for some integer \(j\) (Definition: Even integer), so \(x = 2(2j) + 1 = 4j + 1\), and \(x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{4k + 1 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
If \(m\) is odd, then \(m = 2j + 1\) for some integer \(j\) (Definition: Odd integer), so \(x = 2(2j + 1) + 1 = 4j + 3\), and \(x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{4k + 3 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).

Either way, \(x\) is in the left-hand side. So the two sets are equal (Theorem 2).











Theorem 3 (A subset is its own intersection) Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Then \(A \subseteq B\) if and only if \(A \cap B = A\).










ProofProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose \(A \subseteq B\). We show \(A \cap B = A\) with Theorem 2. If \(x \in A \cap B\), then \(x \in A\) (Definition: Intersection). If \(x \in A\), then \(x \in B\), since \(A \subseteq B\), so \(x \in A \cap B\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Suppose \(A \cap B = A\), and let \(x \in A\). Then \(x \in A \cap B\), since the two sets are equal, so \(x \in B\). So \(A \subseteq B\).











Example 5 (Intersecting with a larger set) Let \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\).

\({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq B\), and \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\), as Theorem 3 says.
\({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 5\right\}\mathclose{}} \not\subseteq B\), since \(5 \notin B\), and \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 5\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), which is not \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\).












Theorem 4 (Cancelling a factor of a Cartesian product) Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be sets with \(C \ne \emptyset\). If \(A \times C = B \times C\), then \(A = B\) (Definition: Cartesian product).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose \(A \times C = B \times C\). Since \(C \ne \emptyset\), there is some \(c \in C\) (Definition: Empty set).
(\(\subseteq\)) Let \(a \in A\). Then \((a, c) \in A \times C\). Since \(A \times C = B \times C\), also \((a, c) \in B \times C\), so \((a, c) = (b, c')\) for some \(b \in B\) and \(c' \in C\) (Definition: Cartesian product). Two ordered pairs are equal only when their first entries are equal (Definition: Ordered pair), so \(a = b\), and \(a \in B\).
(\(\supseteq\)) Let \(b \in B\). Then \((b, c) \in B \times C = A \times C\), so \(b \in A\), by the same steps with \(A\) and \(B\) swapped.
So \(A = B\) (Theorem 2).











Example 6 (Why \(C\) must not be empty) The condition \(C \ne \emptyset\) in Theorem 4 is needed. Let \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(C = \emptyset\). A pair in \(A \times C\) would need a second entry in \(C\), and \(C\) has none, so \(A \times C = \emptyset\), and likewise \(B \times C = \emptyset\). So \(A \times C = B \times C\), but \(A \ne B\).
The proof uses the condition in its first step, to find an element \(c \in C\).






4 Disproving a claim about sets







Exercise 4 (Regrouping differences) Show that the claim “for all sets \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\), \(A - (B - C) = (A - B) - C\)” is false (Definition: Set difference).










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. A counterexample (Definition: Counterexample) is one choice of \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) for which the two sides differ. Let \(A = B = C = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
A - (B - C)
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} - ({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}})
\\&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} - \emptyset
\\&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}},
\end{aligned}
\]
while
\[
\begin{aligned}
(A - B) - C
&= ({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}) - {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}
\\&= \emptyset - {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}
\\&= \emptyset.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two sides differ, so the claim is false.











Remark 4 (Disproving a claim about all sets). A claim of the form “for all sets \(A\), \(B\), …, some equation holds” is disproved by one choice of sets for which it fails (Definition: Disproof). Small sets, such as \(\emptyset\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), are a good place to look. A Venn diagram (Definition: Venn diagram) can suggest where to look: shade each side, find a region shaded on one side only, and put an element in that region.











Example 7 (A union does not cancel) Claim to disprove: for all sets \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\), if \(A \cup B = A \cup C\), then \(B = C\).
Let \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(C = \emptyset\). Then \(A \cup B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(A \cup C = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so \(A \cup B = A \cup C\), but \(B \ne C\). So the claim is false.






References

title: Recursion
text:
NoteSource





The topics of this chapter follow Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes on recursion and recursive functions. These come from those notes:

the two parts of a recursive definition, a base case and a recursive rule;
the recursive definitions of the natural numbers and of the strings over an alphabet;
the three questions to ask when writing a recursive function: the base case, the recursive call and the combination;
the definition of a recursive algorithm.

Everything else is new: the exercises, the other examples, the Racket functions, the algorithm, the theorems and their proofs.




1 Recursive definitions







Exercise 1 (Double and subtract one) A sequence (Definition: Sequence) starts with \(a_0 = 2\), and each later term is twice the term before it, minus 1. Find \(a_1\), \(a_2\), \(a_3\), \(a_4\) and \(a_5\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. Each term comes from the one before it:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_1 &= 2 \cdot 2 - 1 = 3,
\\ a_2 &= 2 \cdot 3 - 1 = 5,
\\ a_3 &= 2 \cdot 5 - 1 = 9,
\\ a_4 &= 2 \cdot 9 - 1 = 17,
\\ a_5 &= 2 \cdot 17 - 1 = 33.
\end{aligned}
\]
To find \(a_5\) this way, we had to find \(a_1\) through \(a_4\) first.











Definition 1 (Recursive definition) Let \(n_0\) be an integer (Definition: Integers). A recursive definition (Wikipedia contributors 2026e) of a function (Definition: Function (map, mapping, transformation)) \(f\) on the integers \(n \ge n_0\) has two parts:

Base case: the value of \(f\) is given directly at \(n_0\), and possibly at a few more of the smallest inputs.
Recursive rule: \(f(n)\) at every other input \(n\) is given in terms of the values of \(f\) at inputs that are smaller than \(n\) and at least \(n_0\).












Example 1 (The double-minus-one sequence, defined recursively) The sequence of Exercise 1 has a recursive definition (Definition 1) with \(n_0 = 0\). Its base case is
\[
a_0 = 2,
\]
and its recursive rule is
\[
a_n = 2 a_{n-1} - 1
\quad\text{for every integer } n \ge 1.
\]
The recursive rule gives \(a_n\) from the single value \(a_{n-1}\) just before it, so this is a recursively defined sequence (Definition: Recursively defined sequence) with \(m = 1\).











Example 2 (Removing the last digit) For a natural number (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) \(n\), the floor (Definition: Floor) \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is \(n\) with its last decimal digit removed, such as \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor 2026 / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor 202.6\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = 202\).











Example 3 (Counting digits) Define a function \(d\) on the natural numbers (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) by
\[
d(n) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } n \le 9,
\\ 1 + d\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{} & \text{if } n \ge 10,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is the floor (Definition: Floor) of \(n / 10\), which is \(n\) with its last decimal digit removed. The first line is the base case and the second is the recursive rule (Definition 1). For \(n \ge 10\), the input \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is at least 1 and at most \(n / 10\), which is less than \(n\), so the recursive rule uses a smaller input, but usually not \(n - 1\). For example,
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(2026)
&= 1 + d(202)
\\&= 1 + 1 + d(20)
\\&= 1 + 1 + 1 + d(2)
\\&= 1 + 1 + 1 + 1
\\&= 4,
\end{aligned}
\]
and 2026 has 4 digits.






2 Recursively defined sets







Exercise 2 (Building a set of integers) A set (Definition: Set) \(S\) of integers is built by two rules:

\(1 \in S\);
if \(x \in S\), then \(x + 2 \in S\) and \(3x \in S\).

Every element of \(S\) comes from these two rules. Find every element of \(S\) that is less than 12.










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Starting from 1 and adding 2 again and again gives \(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11\), so all six are in \(S\). Tripling gives nothing new below 12: \(3 \cdot 1 = 3\) and \(3 \cdot 3 = 9\) are already in the list, and tripling 5 or more gives at least 15. Both rules turn an odd number into an odd number, so no even number is in \(S\). So the elements of \(S\) less than 12 are \(1, 3, 5, 7, 9\) and \(11\).











Definition 2 (Recursively defined set) A recursively defined set (Wikipedia contributors 2026e) is a set (Definition: Set) given by two parts, named as in Definition 1:

a base case, which names some elements of the set directly;
a recursive rule, which says how to build new elements of the set from elements already in it.

The set has no other elements: each of its elements comes from the base case by applying the recursive rule a finite number of times.











Example 4 (The natural numbers, defined recursively) The natural numbers (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) are a recursively defined set (Definition 2). The base case is \(1 \in \mathbb{N}\), and the recursive rule is that if \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), then \(n + 1 \in \mathbb{N}\). The base case gives 1, one application of the rule gives \(1 + 1 = 2\), a second gives \(2 + 1 = 3\), and so on. The non-negative integers (Definition: Non-negative integers) have the same recursive rule, with the base case \(0 \in \mathbb{N}_0\).











Definition 3 (Alphabet) An alphabet (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) is a finite, non-empty set (Definition: Set), whose elements are called its symbols. An alphabet is often written \(\Sigma\), the capital Greek letter sigma.











Example 5 (Three alphabets) Each of these sets is an alphabet (Definition 3):

\(\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1\right\}\mathclose{}\), the two binary digits;
\(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{A}, \mathtt{C}, \mathtt{G}, \mathtt{T}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the four bases of DNA;
\(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}, \ldots, \mathtt{z}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the 26 lowercase letters of English.

The set of all integers is not an alphabet, because it is not finite.











Definition 4 (String) Let \(\Sigma\) be an alphabet (Definition 3). The set \(\Sigma^*\) of strings over \(\Sigma\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026f) is the recursively defined set (Definition 2) with

base case: the empty string \(\lambda\), which has no symbols, is in \(\Sigma^*\);
recursive rule: if \(w \in \Sigma^*\) and \(x \in \Sigma\), then \(w x \in \Sigma^*\), where \(w x\) is the string \(w\) followed by the symbol \(x\).

Racket and Python write the empty string "".











Example 6 (Building a string of DNA bases) Let \(\Sigma = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{A}, \mathtt{C}, \mathtt{G}, \mathtt{T}\right\}\mathclose{}\). The string \(\mathtt{GAT}\) is in \(\Sigma^*\) (Definition 4), by three applications of the recursive rule:

\(\lambda \in \Sigma^*\) and \(\mathtt{G} \in \Sigma\), so \(\lambda \mathtt{G} = \mathtt{G}\) is in \(\Sigma^*\);
\(\mathtt{G} \in \Sigma^*\) and \(\mathtt{A} \in \Sigma\), so \(\mathtt{GA} \in \Sigma^*\);
\(\mathtt{GA} \in \Sigma^*\) and \(\mathtt{T} \in \Sigma\), so \(\mathtt{GAT} \in \Sigma^*\).

The string \(\mathtt{GAU}\) is not in \(\Sigma^*\), since the rule adds only symbols of \(\Sigma\), and \(\mathtt{U} \notin \Sigma\).











Definition 5 (Palindrome) A palindrome (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) is a string (Definition 4) that reads the same backward as forward: its \(i\)th symbol equals its \(i\)th symbol from the end, for every \(i\).











Example 7 (Some palindromes) Over the alphabet of lowercase letters, \(\mathtt{noon}\) and \(\mathtt{racecar}\) are palindromes (Definition 5), and so is \(\mathtt{abba}\), from Exercise: Completing a palindrome. The string \(\mathtt{recur}\) is not a palindrome: backward it reads \(\mathtt{rucer}\). The empty string and every string of one symbol are palindromes.






3 Recursion in Racket







Exercise 3 (Tracing a recursive Racket function) The Racket function binary takes a non-negative integer (Definition: Non-negative integers) n and returns a string:
(define (binary n)
  (if (< n 2)
      (number->string n)
      (string-append (binary (quotient n 2))
                     (number->string (remainder n 2)))))
Here

(if test a b) returns a when test is true and b when it is false;
(quotient n 2) is \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), the floor (Definition: Floor) of \(n / 2\);
(remainder n 2) is the remainder, 0 or 1, left after dividing n by 2;
number->string turns a number into the string of its digits;
string-append joins two strings into one.

Run (binary 6) by hand: write down each call of binary that it makes, and the string that each call returns.










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. Since \(6 \ge 2\), (binary 6) calls (binary 3), because \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor 6 / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = 3\), and puts "0", the remainder of 6 divided by 2, after its result. Since \(3 \ge 2\), (binary 3) calls (binary 1) and puts "1" after its result. Since \(1 < 2\), (binary 1) returns "1" without calling binary again. Replacing each call with what it returns:
(binary 6)
= (string-append (binary 3) "0")
= (string-append (string-append (binary 1) "1") "0")
= (string-append (string-append "1" "1") "0")
= (string-append "11" "0")
= "110"
So (binary 1) returns "1", (binary 3) returns "11", and (binary 6) returns "110". That is 6 written in base 2, since \(1 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot 1 = 6\).











Remark 1 (Three questions for writing a recursive function). A Racket function that calls itself, such as binary in Exercise 3, answers three questions:

Base case. Which inputs does it answer directly? For binary, the inputs 0 and 1, whose base-2 form is the single digit "0" or "1".
Recursive call. Which smaller input does it call itself on? For binary, the input \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), which is less than \(n\) when \(n \ge 2\).
Combination. How does it turn the result of the recursive call into its own answer? For binary, it puts the last base-2 digit of \(n\), the remainder of \(n\) divided by 2, after the result.

The base case is the branch of the if that does not call the function, and the recursive call and the combination make up the other branch.











Example 8 (Counting digits in Racket) The recursive definition of \(d\) in Example 3 becomes a Racket function line by line:
(define (digits n)
  (if (< n 10)
      1
      (+ 1 (digits (quotient n 10)))))
Following Remark 1:

the base case answers 1 for every input less than 10;
the recursive call is (digits (quotient n 10)), on \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), which is less than \(n\);
the combination adds 1 to the result of the recursive call.

(digits 2026) calls (digits 202), (digits 20) and (digits 2) in turn, as in Example 3, and returns 4.






4 Lists







Exercise 4 (Building a list with cons) In Racket, empty is the list with no elements, and (cons x xs) is the list whose first element is x, followed by the elements of the list xs. For example, (cons 5 empty) is the one-element list '(5). Write the list '(7 2 9) using only cons, empty and numbers.










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. Build the list from its last element forward:

(cons 9 empty) is '(9);
(cons 2 (cons 9 empty)) is '(2 9);
(cons 7 (cons 2 (cons 9 empty))) is '(7 2 9).

So '(7 2 9) is (cons 7 (cons 2 (cons 9 empty))).











Definition 6 (List) Let \(A\) be a set (Definition: Set). The set of lists of elements of \(A\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) is the recursively defined set (Definition 2) with

base case: the empty list, written \(\mathtt{empty}\), is a list;
recursive rule: if \(x \in A\) and \(L\) is a list, then \(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\) is a list, whose first element is \(x\) and whose rest is \(L\).

Racket writes the empty list as empty or '(), and \(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\) as (cons x L), and (first L) and (rest L) return the two parts of a list that is not empty. Racket also has the older names car for first and cdr for rest. Python writes the empty list [].











Example 9 (Taking a list apart) Let L be the list '(7 2 9) (Definition 6), which Solution 4 builds as (cons 7 (cons 2 (cons 9 empty))). Then

(first L) is 7, and (rest L) is '(2 9);
(first (rest L)) is 2;
(rest (rest (rest L))) is empty.

(first empty) raises an error, since the empty list is not built by cons and has no first element.











Definition 7 (Length of a list) The length \(\operatorname{len}(L)\) of a list \(L\) (Definition 6) is defined recursively, following the two parts of the definition of a list:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{len}(\mathtt{empty}) &= 0,
\\ \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\right)\mathclose{} &= 1 + \operatorname{len}(L).
\end{aligned}
\]











Example 10 (The length of '(7 2 9)) In Racket, the definition of length (Definition 7) is
(define (len L)
  (if (empty? L)
      0
      (+ 1 (len (rest L)))))
where (empty? L) tests whether L is the empty list. Replacing each call with the recursive rule:
(len '(7 2 9))
= (+ 1 (len '(2 9)))
= (+ 1 (+ 1 (len '(9))))
= (+ 1 (+ 1 (+ 1 (len '()))))
= (+ 1 (+ 1 (+ 1 0)))
= 3
Racket’s built-in length gives the same values.











Definition 8 (Appending two lists) The append \(\operatorname{app}(L, M)\) of two lists \(L\) and \(M\) (Definition 6), the list of the elements of \(L\) followed by the elements of \(M\), is defined recursively on \(L\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{app}(\mathtt{empty}, M) &= M,
\\ \operatorname{app}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L), M\right)\mathclose{} &= \operatorname{cons}\mathopen{}\left(x, \operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{}.
\end{aligned}
\]











Example 11 (Appending '(1 2) and '(3)) In Racket, the definition of append (Definition 8) is
(define (app L M)
  (if (empty? L)
      M
      (cons (first L) (app (rest L) M))))
The recursion takes L apart and leaves M alone:
(app '(1 2) '(3))
= (cons 1 (app '(2) '(3)))
= (cons 1 (cons 2 (app '() '(3))))
= (cons 1 (cons 2 '(3)))
= '(1 2 3)
Racket’s built-in append gives the same values.






5 Recursive algorithms







Exercise 5 (Is it a palindrome?) The algorithm pal, in the pseudocode of Remark: How to read the pseudocode in this chapter, tests whether a string is a palindrome (Definition 5):
procedure pal(s)        // s is a string s[1] s[2] ... s[n] of n symbols
    if n <= 1
        return true
    if s[1] != s[n]
        return false
    return pal(s[2..n-1])   // s without its first and last symbols
Here != means \(\ne\), and s[2..n-1] is the string of the symbols s[2] through s[n-1], which is the empty string when \(n = 2\), since the range 2..1 is empty. Run pal(level) by hand: write down each call of pal that it makes, and what each call returns.










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. 



Call
\(n\)
First and last symbols
What the call does




pal(level)
5
l, l
calls pal(eve)


pal(eve)
3
e, e
calls pal(v)


pal(v)
1

returns true



pal(v) returns true, so pal(eve) returns true, and so pal(level) returns true: \(\mathtt{level}\) is a palindrome.











Definition 9 (Recursive algorithm) An algorithm (Definition: Algorithm) is recursive (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) if it solves a problem by calling itself on smaller inputs of the same problem and using what those calls return. The inputs that it answers without calling itself are its base cases, as in Definition 1.











Example 12 (pal is recursive) The algorithm pal of Exercise 5 is recursive (Definition 9). On a string of \(n \ge 2\) symbols whose first and last symbols match, it calls itself on the string without those two symbols, which has \(n - 2\) symbols, and returns what that call returns.
It answers directly in two cases: when \(n \le 1\), since the empty string and a single symbol read the same backward, and when the first and last symbols differ. For example, pal(recur) finds that the first and last symbols are both r, and calls pal(ecu). That call finds e and u, which differ, and returns false, so pal(recur) returns false.






6 Proofs about recursive definitions







Exercise 6 (Guessing a formula) Compare each term \(a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_5\) of the sequence in Solution 1 with the power \(2^n\), and guess a formula for \(a_n\) that does not use the earlier terms.










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. 



\(n\)
0
1
2
3
4
5




\(a_n\)
2
3
5
9
17
33


\(2^n\)
1
2
4
8
16
32



Each term is one more than the power below it, so a good guess is \(a_n = 2^n + 1\). Six terms do not prove the guess for every \(n\).











Theorem 1 (A formula for the double-minus-one sequence) Let \(a_0, a_1, \ldots\) be the sequence with \(a_0 = 2\) and \(a_n = 2 a_{n-1} - 1\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) (Example 1). Then \(a_n = 2^n + 1\) for every non-negative integer \(n\).










ProofProof






Proof. We use induction (Definition: Proof by induction), following Remark: The shape of a proof by induction with \(n_0 = 0\). Let \(P(n)\) be the equation \(a_n = 2^n + 1\).
Base case. \(a_0 = 2 = 2^0 + 1\).
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 0\) be an integer, and suppose \(P(k)\): \(a_k = 2^k + 1\). The goal \(P(k + 1)\) is \(a_{k + 1} = 2^{k + 1} + 1\). Since \(k + 1 \ge 1\), the recursive rule gives \(a_{k + 1}\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k + 1}
&= 2 a_k - 1
&& \text{(recursive rule)}
\\&= 2 \mathopen{}\left(2^k + 1\right)\mathclose{} - 1
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= 2^{k + 1} + 2 - 1
\\&= 2^{k + 1} + 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(P(k + 1)\) holds, and by induction \(a_n = 2^n + 1\) for every non-negative integer \(n\).











Definition 10 (Structural induction) Structural induction (Wikipedia contributors 2026g) is a way to prove that every element of a recursively defined set (Definition 2) has a property \(P\), in two steps:

Base case. Show that every element that the set’s base case names has \(P\).
Inductive step. Show that whenever the recursive rule builds a new element from elements that have \(P\), the new element has \(P\) too.












Example 13 (Every element of \(S\) is odd) Let \(S\) be the set of Exercise 2. It is a recursively defined set (Definition 2), with base case \(1 \in S\) and recursive rule that if \(x \in S\), then \(x + 2 \in S\) and \(3x \in S\). We use structural induction (Definition 10) to show that every element of \(S\) is a positive odd (Definition: Even integer) integer.
Base case. The base case names 1, and \(1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1\) is positive and odd.
Inductive step. Let \(x \in S\) be a positive odd integer, so \(x = 2j + 1\) for some integer \(j \ge 0\). The recursive rule builds \(x + 2\) and \(3x\) from \(x\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
x + 2 &= 2(j + 1) + 1,
\\ 3x &= 6j + 3 = 2(3j + 1) + 1,
\end{aligned}
\]
which are positive and odd, since \(j + 1\) and \(3j + 1\) are non-negative integers.
So every element of \(S\) is a positive odd integer. Every positive odd integer \(2j + 1\) is in \(S\) too, since it comes from 1 by adding 2 a total of \(j\) times. So \(S\) is the set of positive odd integers, as Solution 2 found for the elements less than 12.











Remark 2 (Why structural induction works). Every element of a recursively defined set (Definition 2) comes from the base case by applying the recursive rule some number \(k \ge 0\) of times. Let \(Q(k)\) be the claim that every element built with \(k\) applications of the rule has the property \(P\). Strong induction (Definition: Proof by strong induction) on \(k\) proves \(Q(k)\) for every \(k \ge 0\):

an element built with 0 applications is named by the base case, so it has \(P\) by the base case of Definition 10;
an element built with \(k \ge 1\) applications comes, by its last application, from elements built with fewer applications, which have \(P\) by the strong induction hypothesis, so it has \(P\) by the inductive step.

So every element of the set has \(P\).











Theorem 2 (Appending adds lengths) For all lists \(L\) and \(M\) (Definition 6),
\[
\operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{} = \operatorname{len}(L) + \operatorname{len}(M),
\]
where \(\operatorname{len}\) is the length (Definition 7) and \(\operatorname{app}\) is the append (Definition 8).










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(M\) be a list. We use structural induction (Definition 10) on \(L\), with \(P(L)\) the equation \(\operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{} = \operatorname{len}(L) + \operatorname{len}(M)\).
Base case. The base case of Definition 6 names only the empty list, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}(\mathtt{empty}, M)\right)\mathclose{}
&= \operatorname{len}(M)
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{app} \text{)}
\\&= 0 + \operatorname{len}(M)
\\&= \operatorname{len}(\mathtt{empty}) + \operatorname{len}(M).
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{len} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Inductive step. The recursive rule builds \(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\) from an element \(x\) and a list \(L\). Suppose \(P(L)\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L), M\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}
\\&= \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}\mathopen{}\left(x, \operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{app} \text{)}
\\&= 1 + \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{len} \text{)}
\\&= 1 + \operatorname{len}(L) + \operatorname{len}(M)
&& \text{(induction hypothesis } P(L) \text{)}
\\&= \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\right)\mathclose{} + \operatorname{len}(M),
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{len} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is \(P\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\right)\mathclose{}\). By structural induction, \(P(L)\) holds for every list \(L\). Since \(M\) was any list, the equation holds for all lists \(L\) and \(M\).











Theorem 3 (The function \(d\) counts digits) Let \(d\) be the function of Example 3. For every natural number \(n\),
\[
10^{d(n) - 1} \le n < 10^{d(n)},
\]
so \(n\) has exactly \(d(n)\) decimal digits.










ProofProof






Proof. A natural number \(n\) has \(m\) digits exactly when \(10^{m - 1} \le n < 10^m\), since \(10^{m - 1}\), which is 1 followed by \(m - 1\) zeros, is the smallest natural number with \(m\) digits, and \(10^m\), which is 1 followed by \(m\) zeros, is the smallest with \(m + 1\). So the inequalities say that \(n\) has \(d(n)\) digits.
The recursive rule uses \(d\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\), not \(d(n - 1)\), so we use strong induction (Definition: Proof by strong induction). Let \(n\) be a natural number, and suppose the inequalities hold for every natural number less than \(n\).
If \(n \le 9\), then \(d(n) = 1\), and \(10^0 = 1 \le n < 10 = 10^1\).
If \(n \ge 10\), let \(q = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\). Then \(q \le n / 10 < q + 1\), so \(10q \le n < 10q + 10\). Also \(q \ge 1\), since \(n / 10 \ge 1\), and \(q < n\), so \(q\) is a natural number less than \(n\), and by the strong induction hypothesis
\[
10^{d(q) - 1} \le q < 10^{d(q)}.
\]
The recursive rule gives \(d(n) = 1 + d(q)\). For the lower bound,
\[
\begin{aligned}
n
&\ge 10 q
\\&\ge 10 \cdot 10^{d(q) - 1}
&& \text{(strong induction hypothesis)}
\\&= 10^{d(q)}
\\&= 10^{d(n) - 1}.
&& \text{(} d(n) = 1 + d(q) \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For the upper bound, \(q\) and \(10^{d(q)}\) are integers with \(q < 10^{d(q)}\), so \(q + 1 \le 10^{d(q)}\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
n
&< 10 (q + 1)
\\&\le 10 \cdot 10^{d(q)}
&& \text{(} q + 1 \le 10^{d(q)} \text{)}
\\&= 10^{d(q) + 1}
\\&= 10^{d(n)}.
&& \text{(} d(n) = 1 + d(q) \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So the inequalities hold for \(n\), and by strong induction they hold for every natural number \(n\).

NoteSource





Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Logic 1” and “Logic 2”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. The examples of propositions, the truth tables to decode, the list of English phrasings of a conditional, and the “only if” example come from those notes; the other exercises are new.
The definitions are included from the mathematics prerequisites notes, so they read the same in both places.

title: Propositional Logic
text:
2.1 Evaluating compound propositions







Exercise 3 (Evaluate a compound proposition) Suppose \(P\) is true, \(Q\) is false, and \(R\) is false. Is \((\neg P \lor Q) \land \neg R\) true or false?










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. Substitute the truth values, then evaluate from the innermost parentheses outward:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\neg P \lor Q) \land \neg R
&= (\neg \mathrm{T} \lor \mathrm{F}) \land \neg \mathrm{F} \\
&= (\mathrm{F} \lor \mathrm{F}) \land \mathrm{T} \\
&= \mathrm{F} \land \mathrm{T} \\
&= \mathrm{F}
\end{aligned}
\]
The proposition is false.











Exercise 4 (Evaluate another compound proposition) With the same truth values as Exercise 3 (\(P\) true, \(Q\) false, \(R\) false), is \(\neg (P \land Q) \lor R\) true or false?










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. \[
\begin{aligned}
\neg (P \land Q) \lor R
&= \neg (\mathrm{T} \land \mathrm{F}) \lor \mathrm{F} \\
&= \neg \mathrm{F} \lor \mathrm{F} \\
&= \mathrm{T} \lor \mathrm{F} \\
&= \mathrm{T}
\end{aligned}
\]
The proposition is true.

title: Propositional Logic
text:
2.2 Truth tables







Exercise 5 (How many cases?) Exercise 4 found the truth value of \(\neg (P \land Q) \lor R\) for one choice of truth values of \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\). How many different choices are there?










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. Each of \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\) is either true or false, independently of the other two, so there are \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 2^3 = 8\) choices. With \(n\) propositions there are \(2^n\).











Definition 7 (Truth table) A truth table for a proposition built from \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\) with logical connectives (Definition 3) has one row for each of the \(2^n\) combinations of truth values of \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\), and gives the truth value of the proposition in each row.

title: Propositional Logic
text:
3.1 The converse







Exercise 9 (Reverse an implication) For all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), “if \(x = y\), then \(x^2 = y^2\)” is true. Is “if \(x^2 = y^2\), then \(x = y\)” also true for all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\)?










SolutionSolution






Solution 9. No. Take \(x = 1\) and \(y = -1\). Then \(x^2 = 1 = y^2\), so the premise is true, but \(x \ne y\), so the conclusion is false.
Swapping the premise and the conclusion of a true implication can give a false one.











Definition 9 (Converse) The converse (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) of the proposition “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” is the proposition “if \(Q\), then \(P\)”.

title: Propositional Logic
text:
3.2 Conditionals in English







Exercise 10 (“Only if”) Rewrite “I go to class only if I am healthy” in the form “if \(P\), then \(Q\)”.










SolutionSolution






Solution 10. “If I go to class, then I am healthy.”
The sentence says that going to class requires being healthy, so whenever I go to class, I am healthy. It does not say “if I am healthy, then I go to class”; that is its converse (Definition 9), and a healthy person may still skip class.
In general, “\(P\) only if \(Q\)” means \(P \Rightarrow Q\).











Remark 5 (English phrasings of \(P \Rightarrow Q\)). Each of these sentences means \(P \Rightarrow Q\):

If \(P\), then \(Q\).
\(Q\) if \(P\).
\(Q\) whenever \(P\).
\(Q\), provided that \(P\).
Whenever \(P\), then also \(Q\).
\(P\) is a sufficient condition for \(Q\).
For \(Q\), it is sufficient that \(P\).
\(Q\) is a necessary condition for \(P\).
For \(P\), it is necessary that \(Q\).
\(P\) only if \(Q\).

title: Loop Invariants
text:
NoteSource





The topics of this chapter follow Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 worksheet on loop invariants:

what a loop invariant is;
the three parts of a loop invariant proof: initialization, maintenance and termination;
proving that a loop stops;
choosing an invariant strong enough to give the result;
invariants for a loop inside another loop.

Everything else is new: the algorithms, the exercises, the examples, the theorems and their proofs.




1 Preconditions and postconditions







Exercise 1 (Tracing a square-root loop) The algorithm root takes a non-negative integer (Definition: Non-negative integers) \(n\):
procedure root(n)        // n is a non-negative integer
    r := 0
    while (r + 1) * (r + 1) <= n
        r := r + 1
    return r
Run root(20) by hand. Each time the condition after while is tested, write down the value of r and whether the condition is true, and say which number root(20) returns.










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 



Test
r
\((r + 1)^2\)
\((r + 1)^2 \le 20\)?




1
0
1
true


2
1
4
true


3
2
9
true


4
3
16
true


5
4
25
false



The condition is false at the fifth test, so the loop stops there, and root(20) returns 4. The answer satisfies \(4^2 = 16 \le 20 < 25 = 5^2\): 4 is the largest integer whose square is at most 20.











Remark 1 (How to read the pseudocode in this chapter). The algorithms (Definition: Algorithm) in this chapter are written in pseudocode, not in a particular programming language:

x := e sets the variable x to the value of the expression e;
the indented lines under while are the body of the loop, and a while loop tests its condition before every pass through the body, running the body when the condition is true and stopping when it is false;
for i := a to b runs its body once for each of \(i = a, a + 1, \ldots, b\), and not at all if \(a > b\);
A[1..n] is an array of \(n\) entries A[1], …, A[n];
text after // is a comment, which the algorithm ignores.

In Solution 1, the body of root runs four times, and its condition is tested five times: once before each pass through the body, and once more when the loop stops.











Definition 1 (Floor) The floor \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) of a real number (Definition: Real numbers) \(x\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) is the largest integer (Definition: Integers) that is at most \(x\).











Example 1 (Some floors) By Definition 1,

\(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor 3.7\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = 3\), since 3 is an integer at most 3.7 and 4 is not;
\(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor 5\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = 5\), since 5 is already an integer;
\(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor-1.5\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = -2\), since \(-2\) is at most \(-1.5\) and \(-1\) is not.












Definition 2 (Precondition) A precondition of an algorithm (Definition: Algorithm) is a condition on its input that the algorithm assumes is true when it starts.











Definition 3 (Postcondition) A postcondition of an algorithm is a condition on its input and its output that is required to be true when the algorithm stops, provided that its precondition (Definition 2) was true when it started.











Example 2 (What root promises) For root from Exercise 1, the precondition (Definition 2) is

\(n\) is a non-negative integer,

and the postcondition (Definition 3) is

the returned value \(r\) is a non-negative integer with \(r^2 \le n < (r + 1)^2\).

For a non-negative integer \(r\), the two inequalities \(r^2 \le n < (r + 1)^2\) say that \(r \le \sqrt{n} < r + 1\), so the postcondition says that \(r = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor\sqrt{n}\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) (Definition 1), the largest integer whose square is at most \(n\). Solution 1 checks it for \(n = 20\), where \(r = 4\).











Definition 4 (Correct algorithm) An algorithm is correct for a given precondition (Definition 2) and postcondition (Definition 3) if, for every input that satisfies the precondition, the algorithm stops, and the postcondition is true when it stops.











Example 3 (A version of root that is not correct) Change r := 0 in root to r := 1, and keep the rest. On the input \(n = 0\), which satisfies the precondition of Example 2, the condition \((1 + 1)^2 \le 0\) is false at the first test, so the loop body never runs and the algorithm returns \(r = 1\). But \(1^2 = 1 > 0\), so the postcondition \(r^2 \le n\) is false. One input is enough to show that this version is not correct (Definition 4), even though it returns the right value for every \(n \ge 1\).
To show that an algorithm is correct, we need an argument that covers every input at once.






2 Loop invariants







Exercise 2 (One pass through the body of root) In root (Exercise 1), suppose that at some test of the condition after while, r is an integer with \(r^2 \le n\), and the condition \((r + 1)^2 \le n\) is true. Show that \(r^2 \le n\) is true again at the next test.










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Since the condition is true, the body runs once and replaces r with \(r' = r + 1\), and then the condition is tested again. At that next test,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(r')^2
&= (r + 1)^2
\\&\le n,
&& \text{(the condition was true)}
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(r^2 \le n\) is true again, for the new value of r.











Definition 5 (Guard of a loop) The guard of a while loop is the condition written after while: the loop tests it before each pass through the body, runs the body when it is true, and stops when it is false.











Example 4 (The guard of a for loop) The guard (Definition 5) of root (Exercise 1) is \((r + 1)^2 \le n\).
A for loop is a while loop written more briefly. The loop on the left does the same thing as the loop on the right, provided the body changes neither i nor b:
for i := a to b              i := a
    body                     while i <= b
                                 body
                                 i := i + 1
So the guard of for i := a to b is \(i \le b\), and the loop stops at the first test where \(i = b + 1\), or at once if \(a > b\).











Definition 6 (Loop invariant) A loop invariant of a loop is a statement about the loop’s variables that is true every time the loop’s guard (Definition 5) is tested, before the first pass through the body and after each pass, for every input that satisfies the algorithm’s precondition (Definition 2).











Example 5 (A statement that holds at every test of root) In the run of root(20) in Solution 1, r takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 at the five tests of the guard. The statement “\(r^2 \le n\)” is true at all five tests, as a loop invariant (Definition 6) must be, and Solution 2 shows, for every \(n\), that a pass through the body never turns it from true to false. The statement “\(r < 4\)”, by contrast, is true at the first four tests but false at the fifth, so it is not a loop invariant of root.











Theorem 1 (The loop invariant theorem) Let \(I\) be a statement about the variables of a while loop whose guard (Definition 5) is \(G\). Suppose that

\(I\) is true at the first test of the guard, and
whenever \(I\) and \(G\) are both true at a test of the guard, \(I\) is true at the next test.

Then \(I\) is a loop invariant (Definition 6) of the loop. In particular, if the loop stops, then \(I\) is true and \(G\) is false when it stops.










ProofProof






Proof. We use induction (Definition: Proof by induction) on the number of passes through the body. For each non-negative integer \(k\), let \(P(k)\) be the claim

if the body runs at least \(k\) times, then \(I\) is true at the test of the guard that follows the first \(k\) passes.

The test that follows the first \(0\) passes is the first test.
Base case. \(P(0)\) is hypothesis 1.
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 1\), suppose \(P(k - 1)\) holds, and suppose the body runs at least \(k\) times. Then it runs at least \(k - 1\) times, so by \(P(k - 1)\), \(I\) is true at the test that follows the first \(k - 1\) passes. The \(k\)th pass comes right after that test, and the body runs only when the guard is true, so \(G\) is also true at that test. By hypothesis 2, \(I\) is true at the next test, which is the test that follows the first \(k\) passes. So \(P(k)\) holds.
By induction, \(P(k)\) holds for every \(k \ge 0\). Every test of the guard follows the first \(k\) passes for some \(k \ge 0\), so \(I\) is true at every test, and \(I\) is a loop invariant. The loop stops only at a test where \(G\) is false, and \(I\) is true at that test too.











Remark 2 (The three parts of a loop invariant proof). A proof that an algorithm with one loop is correct (Definition 4) usually names a statement \(I\) and shows three things.
Initialization. Assuming the precondition, \(I\) is true at the first test of the guard.
Maintenance. If \(I\) and the guard are both true at a test, then \(I\) is true at the next test.
Termination. The loop stops, and when it stops, \(I\) together with the guard being false implies the postcondition.
Initialization and maintenance are the two hypotheses of Theorem 1, and they play the roles of the base case and the inductive step of a proof by induction (Definition: Proof by induction). The theorem then says that \(I\) is a loop invariant, so the proof does not have to repeat the induction each time. Termination is the part an induction proof does not have: the theorem says what is true if the loop stops, not that it does.











Example 6 (root is correct) We show that root (Exercise 1) is correct (Definition 4) for the precondition and postcondition of Example 2. Let \(n\) be a non-negative integer, and let \(I\) be the statement

r is a non-negative integer and \(r^2 \le n\).

Initialization. At the first test, \(r = 0\), which is a non-negative integer, and \(r^2 = 0 \le n\), since \(n \ge 0\).
Maintenance. Suppose \(I\) and the guard \((r + 1)^2 \le n\) are true at a test. The body replaces r with \(r + 1\), which is again a non-negative integer, and Solution 2 shows that \((r + 1)^2 \le n\). So \(I\) is true at the next test.
Termination. By Theorem 1, \(I\) is true at every test. A non-negative integer \(r\) satisfies \(r \le r^2\) (if \(r = 0\), both sides are \(0\), and if \(r \ge 1\), then \(r^2 = r \cdot r \ge r \cdot 1\)), so \(r \le r^2 \le n\) at every test. Each pass through the body increases r by 1, starting from 0, so if the body runs at least \(k\) times, then \(r = k\) at the test after the first \(k\) passes, and so \(k \le n\). So the body runs at most \(n\) times, and the loop stops. When it stops, \(I\) is true and the guard is false, so
\[
r^2 \le n
\quad\text{and}\quad
n < (r + 1)^2,
\]
and root returns this \(r\), a non-negative integer. That is the postcondition.






3 Termination







Exercise 3 (A loop that halves) The algorithm halvings takes a natural number (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) \(n\) and counts how many times \(n\) can be halved, rounding down, before it reaches 1:
procedure halvings(n)    // n is a natural number
    k := n
    c := 0
    while k >= 2
        k := floor(k / 2)
        c := c + 1
    return c
Here floor(x) is the floor \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) (Definition 1) of \(x\). Explain why the loop stops for every natural number \(n\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. First, k is a natural number at every test of the guard. At the first test \(k = n\), a natural number. If \(k\) is a natural number and the guard \(k \ge 2\) is true, then \(k / 2 \ge 1\), so the new value \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor k / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is an integer that is at least 1. So, by Theorem 1, “k is a natural number” is a loop invariant.
Second, each pass through the body makes k smaller: the new value is \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor k / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} \le k / 2 < k\), since \(k > 0\). Both values are integers, so k decreases by at least 1.
So, if the body runs at least \(j\) times, then at the test after the first \(j\) passes, \(1 \le k \le n - j\), and so \(j \le n - 1\). The body runs at most \(n - 1\) times, and the loop stops.











Definition 7 (Loop variant) A loop variant of a loop is an integer-valued expression in the loop’s variables that is at least 0 at every test of the loop’s guard (Definition 5), and that is smaller after each pass through the body than it was before that pass, for every input that satisfies the algorithm’s precondition (Definition 2).











Example 7 (Loop variants of halvings and root) Solution 3 shows that k is a loop variant (Definition 7) of halvings: it is an integer that is at least 1, and so at least 0, at every test, and each pass through the body makes it smaller. A loop can have more than one loop variant: k - 1 is another one, since it is at least 0 at every test and decreases by the same amount as k.
The termination part of Example 6 is an argument about the loop variant \(n - r\) of root. It is an integer, it is at least 0 at every test because \(r \le n\) there, and each pass through the body increases r by 1, so it decreases \(n - r\) by 1.











Theorem 2 (A loop with a variant stops) If a loop has a loop variant (Definition 7) whose value at the first test of the guard is \(v_0\), then the body runs at most \(v_0\) times, and so the loop stops.










ProofProof






Proof. Write \(v\) for the loop variant. For each non-negative integer \(k\), let \(P(k)\) be the claim

if the body runs at least \(k\) times, then \(v \le v_0 - k\) at the test that follows the first \(k\) passes.

We prove \(P(k)\) for every \(k \ge 0\) by induction (Definition: Proof by induction).
Base case. The test that follows the first \(0\) passes is the first test, where \(v = v_0\).
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 1\), suppose \(P(k - 1)\) holds, and suppose the body runs at least \(k\) times. By \(P(k - 1)\), \(v \le v_0 - (k - 1)\) at the test that follows the first \(k - 1\) passes. The \(k\)th pass makes the integer \(v\) smaller, so it lowers \(v\) by at least 1, and \(v \le v_0 - k\) at the next test. So \(P(k)\) holds.
Now suppose the body runs at least \(k\) times. By \(P(k)\), \(v \le v_0 - k\) at the test that follows the first \(k\) passes, and \(v \ge 0\) at every test, so \(0 \le v_0 - k\), that is, \(k \le v_0\). So the body cannot run \(v_0 + 1\) times.











Example 8 (A countdown timer) The algorithm countdown counts down a timer that starts at \(x\) minutes and 0 seconds, one second per pass:
procedure countdown(x)   // x is a non-negative integer
    y := 0               // x is the minutes, y the seconds
    while x > 0 or y > 0
        if y > 0
            y := y - 1
        else
            x := x - 1
            y := 59
Neither x nor y is a loop variant (Definition 7): x stays the same while y counts down, and y jumps from 0 to 59 when x goes down. The total number of seconds left, \(60x + y\), is one.
To see this, first let \(I\) be the statement “x and y are integers with \(x \ge 0\) and \(0 \le y \le 59\)”. At the first test, \(x \ge 0\) and \(y = 0\), so \(I\) is true. Suppose \(I\) and the guard are true at a test. If \(y > 0\), the body replaces y with \(y - 1\), which is between 0 and 58, and leaves x alone. Otherwise \(y = 0\), so the guard says \(x > 0\), and the body replaces x with \(x - 1 \ge 0\) and y with 59. Either way \(I\) is true at the next test, so by Theorem 1, \(I\) is a loop invariant.
So \(60x + y \ge 0\) at every test. Each pass through the body lowers \(60x + y\) by exactly 1: if \(y > 0\), the new value is \(60x + (y - 1)\), and if \(y = 0\), the new value is
\[
\begin{aligned}
60(x - 1) + 59
&= 60x - 1
\\&= (60x + y) - 1.
&& \text{(since } y = 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(60x + y\) is a loop variant. Write \(x_0\) for the input value of x. The variant starts at \(60 x_0\), so by Theorem 2 the body runs at most \(60 x_0\) times, and the loop stops. When it stops, the guard is false, so \(x \le 0\) and \(y \le 0\), and \(I\) gives \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\), so \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\), where \(60x + y = 0\). The variant went down by exactly 1 each time, so the body ran exactly \(60 x_0\) times, once for each second.











Remark 3 (A loop nobody knows how to stop). The process of Example: A proposition whose truth value nobody knows is the loop
while n != 1
    if n is even
        n := n / 2
    else
        n := 3 * n + 1
on a positive integer \(n\). Nobody knows whether it stops for every positive integer \(n\): that is the Collatz conjecture (Wikipedia contributors 2026a). So nobody has found a loop variant (Definition 7) for it, since Theorem 2 would then prove that it always stops. Termination is a separate claim from what an invariant gives, and it can be the hard part.






4 Choosing a strong enough invariant







Exercise 4 (The two ends of a reversal) The algorithm reverse reverses an array A[1..n], where \(n \ge 0\), by swapping its outermost entries and moving inward:
procedure reverse(A, n)  // A[1..n] is an array, n >= 0
    i := 1
    j := n
    while i < j
        swap A[i] and A[j]
        i := i + 1
        j := j - 1
Show that \(i + j = n + 1\) is a loop invariant (Definition 6) of its loop.










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. We check the two hypotheses of Theorem 1.
Initialization. At the first test, \(i = 1\) and \(j = n\), so \(i + j = n + 1\).
Maintenance. Suppose \(i + j = n + 1\) and the guard \(i < j\) are true at a test. The swap does not change i or j, and the body then replaces i with \(i + 1\) and j with \(j - 1\). At the next test,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(i + 1) + (j - 1)
&= i + j
\\&= n + 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
So, by Theorem 1, \(i + j = n + 1\) is a loop invariant.











Remark 4 (A true invariant can be too weak). The postcondition (Definition 3) of reverse is about the entries of A: writing B[1..n] for the array as it was before the loop, it says that \(A[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\) for every \(k\) with \(1 \le k \le n\). The loop invariant \(i + j = n + 1\) of Solution 4 is true, but it says nothing about A, so no amount of reasoning from it, and from the guard being false, can reach this postcondition.
The invariant, together with the guard being false, has to imply the postcondition. Here the guard mentions only i and j, so the invariant itself has to say something about the entries of A. A good way to find one is to ask what the loop has finished so far, and what it has not touched yet, at a test partway through the loop.











Example 9 (reverse is correct) Let B[1..n] be the array A as it was before the loop of Exercise 4. At a test partway through, the loop has swapped the entries outside positions \(i\) to \(j\), and has not touched the entries from \(i\) to \(j\). So let \(I\) be the statement made of these three parts:

(a) \(i + j = n + 1\) and \(i \le j + 1\);
(b) \(A[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\) for every \(k\) with \(1 \le k < i\) or \(j < k \le n\);
(c) \(A[k] = B[k]\) for every \(k\) with \(i \le k \le j\).

Initialization. At the first test, \(i = 1\) and \(j = n\). Part (a) holds because \(1 + n = n + 1\) and \(1 \le n + 1\), since \(n \ge 0\). No \(k\) between 1 and \(n\) has \(k < 1\) or \(k > n\), so (b) says nothing. Nothing has changed yet, so \(A[k] = B[k]\) for every \(k\), and (c) holds.
Maintenance. Suppose \(I\) and the guard \(i < j\) are true at a test. By (c), \(A[i] = B[i]\) and \(A[j] = B[j]\) before the swap. By (a), \(j = n + 1 - i\) and \(i = n + 1 - j\). So after the swap,
\[
A[i] = B[j] = B[n + 1 - i]
\quad\text{and}\quad
A[j] = B[i] = B[n + 1 - j],
\]
and no other entry changes. The body then replaces i with \(i' = i + 1\) and j with \(j' = j - 1\).

Part (a): \(i' + j' = i + j = n + 1\), as in Solution 4. Since \(i\) and \(j\) are integers and \(i < j\), we have \(i + 1 \le j\), so \(i' \le j = j' + 1\).
Part (b): a \(k\) with \(k < i'\) has \(k < i\), where the swap did not change \(A[k]\) and (b) already held, or \(k = i\), just shown. A \(k\) with \(k > j'\) has \(k > j\) or \(k = j\), in the same way.
Part (c): a \(k\) with \(i' \le k \le j'\) has \(i < k < j\), so the swap did not change \(A[k]\), and \(A[k] = B[k]\) by (c).

So \(I\) is true at the next test.
Termination. By Theorem 1, \(I\) is true at every test. By (a), \(i \le j + 1\), so \(j - i + 1 \ge 0\) at every test, and each pass lowers \(j - i + 1\) by 2. So \(j - i + 1\) is a loop variant (Definition 7), and by Theorem 2 the loop stops. When it stops, the guard is false, so \(i \ge j\), and with (a), \(i = j\) or \(i = j + 1\). Now let \(1 \le k \le n\).

If \(k < i\) or \(k > j\), then \(A[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\) by (b).
Otherwise \(i \le k \le j\), which can only happen when \(i = j = k\). Then (a) gives \(2k = n + 1\), so \(k = n + 1 - k\), and (c) gives \(A[k] = B[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\).

So \(A[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\) for every \(k\), which is the postcondition of Remark 4. The middle entry of an array of odd length is the one that never moves.






5 Nested loops







Exercise 5 (Looking for a repeated entry) The algorithm has_repeat decides whether some value appears twice in an array A[1..n], where \(n \ge 1\), by comparing every pair of positions:
procedure has_repeat(A, n)   // A[1..n] is an array, n >= 1
    found := false
    for i := 1 to n - 1
        for j := i + 1 to n
            if A[i] = A[j]
                found := true
    return found
Run has_repeat on the array \(A = (3, 1, 4, 1)\), with \(n = 4\). List the pairs \((i, j)\) that the inner loop compares, in order, and give the first pair at which found becomes true.










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. 



\((i, j)\)
\(A[i]\)
\(A[j]\)
found after the comparison




\((1, 2)\)
3
1
false


\((1, 3)\)
3
4
false


\((1, 4)\)
3
1
false


\((2, 3)\)
1
4
false


\((2, 4)\)
1
1
true


\((3, 4)\)
4
1
true



The inner loop compares the six pairs in the table, in that order. found first becomes true at \((2, 4)\), since \(A[2] = A[4] = 1\), and it stays true, so has_repeat returns true.











Remark 5 (Proving a nested loop correct). A loop inside another loop gets its own loop invariant (Definition 6). The proof usually goes from the inside out:

prove the inner loop’s invariant, using the outer loop’s invariant at the test where the inner loop starts;
read off what the inner loop has done when it stops;
use that in the maintenance step of the outer loop’s invariant.

Each for loop is a while loop (Example 4), so each invariant is a statement about the tests of that loop’s guard.











Example 10 (has_repeat is correct) In has_repeat (Exercise 5), call a pair of positions \((p, q)\) a match if \(1 \le p < q \le n\) and \(A[p] = A[q]\). The postcondition is that has_repeat returns true if A has a match, and false if it has none. The algorithm never changes A. We follow Remark 5.
The inner loop. Fix a pass of the outer loop with index \(i\), where \(1 \le i \le n - 1\), and suppose that, when the inner loop starts,

found is true exactly when there is a match \((p, q)\) with \(p < i\),

which is the outer loop’s invariant \(K\), proved in the next part. Let \(J\) be the statement

\(i + 1 \le j \le n + 1\), and found is true exactly when there is a match \((p, q)\) with \(p < i\), or with \(p = i\) and \(q < j\).


Initialization: at the first test, \(j = i + 1 \le n\). No \(q\) has \(i < q < i + 1\), so \(J\) says the same as the supposition above.
Maintenance: suppose \(J\) and the guard \(j \le n\) are true at a test. A match with \(p < i\), or with \(p = i\) and \(q < j + 1\), is either one of the matches that \(J\) describes or the pair \((i, j)\). If \(A[i] = A[j]\), the body sets found to true, and \((i, j)\) is such a match. If not, found does not change, and \((i, j)\) is not a match. Either way, after j becomes \(j + 1 \le n + 1\), \(J\) is true at the next test.
Termination: by Theorem 1, \(J\) is a loop invariant, so \(n + 1 - j \ge 0\) at every test, and each pass lowers \(n + 1 - j\) by 1. So \(n + 1 - j\) is a loop variant (Definition 7), and the inner loop stops (Theorem 2). It stops when \(j \le n\) is false, so, with \(j \le n + 1\), \(j = n + 1\). Every match has \(q \le n < n + 1\), so, when the inner loop stops,

found is true exactly when there is a match \((p, q)\) with \(p < i\) or \(p = i\), that is, with \(p < i + 1\).


The outer loop. Let \(K\) be the statement

\(1 \le i \le n\), and found is true exactly when there is a match \((p, q)\) with \(p < i\).


Initialization: at the first test, \(i = 1 \le n\), since \(n \ge 1\), found is false, and no match has \(p < 1\).
Maintenance: suppose \(K\) and the guard \(i \le n - 1\) are true at a test. Then the inner loop runs, and when it stops, found is true exactly when there is a match with \(p < i + 1\). After i becomes \(i + 1 \le n\), \(K\) is true at the next test.
Termination: by Theorem 1, \(K\) is a loop invariant, so \(n - i \ge 0\) at every test, and each pass lowers \(n - i\) by 1. So \(n - i\) is a loop variant, and the outer loop stops. It stops when \(i \le n - 1\) is false, so, with \(i \le n\), \(i = n\). Every match has \(p < q \le n\), so \(p < n\). So, when the outer loop stops, found is true exactly when A has a match, and the algorithm returns found.
