title: Proving Non-Conditional Statements
text:
NoteSource





Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Proving Non-Conditional Statements, Disproof”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. These come from those notes:

the outline of an “if and only if” proof;
the outline of an existence proof that names an element;
proving that several propositions are equivalent with a cycle of conditionals;
the constructive example of half of a positive number;
the non-constructive example of an irrational power of an irrational number;
disproving a proposition by proving its negation.

The exercises are new.




1 Proving if and only if







Exercise 1 (A sum of squares equal to zero) Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Prove: \(x^2 + y^2 = 0\) if and only if \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\) (Definition: If and only if).
Hint: prove the two directions one at a time.










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. If \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\), then \(x^2 + y^2 = 0\). Suppose \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\). Then \(x^2 + y^2 = 0^2 + 0^2 = 0\).
If \(x^2 + y^2 = 0\), then \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\). Suppose \(x^2 + y^2 = 0\). A square of a real number is never negative, so \(y^2 \ge 0\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2
&= -y^2
&& \text{(subtract } y^2 \text{ from both sides of } x^2 + y^2 = 0 \text{)}
\\&\le 0.
&& \text{(} y^2 \ge 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Also \(x^2 \ge 0\), so \(x^2 = 0\), and so \(x = 0\). The same steps with \(x\) and \(y\) swapped give \(y = 0\).











Theorem 1 (A biconditional is two conditionals) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\),
\[
(P \Leftrightarrow Q) \equiv \mathopen{}\left((P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)\right)\mathclose{}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. The fifth and last columns of this truth table (Definition: Truth table) match in every row (Definition: If and only if, Definition: Implies, Definition: And):











\(P\)
\(Q\)
\(P \Rightarrow Q\)
\(Q \Rightarrow P\)
\((P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)\)
\(P \Leftrightarrow Q\)




T
T
T
T
T
T


T
F
F
T
F
F


F
T
T
F
F
F


F
F
T
T
T
T



So the two propositions are logically equivalent (Definition: Logical equivalence).











Example 1 (Proving both directions) Claim: let \(n\) be an integer. Then \(n\) is even if and only if \(n + 2\) is even.
By Theorem 1, it is enough to prove two conditionals.

If \(n\) is even, then \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\) (Definition: Even integer), so \(n + 2 = 2k + 2 = 2(k + 1)\), and \(k + 1\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof). So \(n + 2\) is even.
If \(n + 2\) is even, then \(n + 2 = 2m\) for some integer \(m\), so \(n = 2m - 2 = 2(m - 1)\), and \(m - 1\) is an integer. So \(n\) is even.












Remark 1 (The shape of an “if and only if” proof). A proof of “\(P\) if and only if \(Q\)” has two parts:

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose \(P\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(Q\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Suppose \(Q\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(P\).

Each part is a proof of a conditional, so each can be a direct proof (Definition: Direct proof), a proof by contrapositive (Definition: Proof by contrapositive), or a proof by contradiction (Definition: Proof by contradiction), and the two parts need not use the same method.











Theorem 2 (A cycle of conditionals) Let \(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_k\) be propositions. If \(P_1 \Rightarrow P_2\), \(P_2 \Rightarrow P_3\), \(\ldots\), \(P_{k-1} \Rightarrow P_k\) and \(P_k \Rightarrow P_1\) are all true, then \(P_1, \ldots, P_k\) all have the same truth value.










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose one of the propositions, \(P_i\), is true. By modus ponens (Theorem: Common rules of inference), \(P_i \Rightarrow P_{i+1}\) makes \(P_{i+1}\) true, then \(P_{i+1} \Rightarrow P_{i+2}\) makes \(P_{i+2}\) true, and so on around the cycle, with \(P_k \Rightarrow P_1\) leading from \(P_k\) back to \(P_1\), until every proposition in the list is true. So either all of \(P_1, \ldots, P_k\) are true, or none of them is true, and then all of them are false.











Example 2 (Three ways to say “odd”) Let \(n\) be an integer, and consider

\(P_1\): \(n\) is odd;
\(P_2\): \(n + 1\) is even;
\(P_3\): \(n - 1\) is even.

By Theorem 2, three conditionals show that all three have the same truth value.

\(P_1 \Rightarrow P_2\): if \(n = 2k + 1\) (Definition: Odd integer), then \(n + 1 = 2k + 2 = 2(k + 1)\).
\(P_2 \Rightarrow P_3\): if \(n + 1 = 2m\), then \(n - 1 = 2m - 2 = 2(m - 1)\).
\(P_3 \Rightarrow P_1\): if \(n - 1 = 2j\), then \(n = 2j + 1\).

In each step the new multiplier, \(k + 1\), \(m - 1\) or \(j\), is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof). Proving all six conditionals between pairs would have taken twice as many steps.






2 Proving existence







Exercise 2 (A solution in integers) Show that there are integers \(x\) and \(y\) with \(5x + 3y = 1\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Take \(x = 2\) and \(y = -3\). Then \(5x + 3y = 5 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot(-3) = 10 - 9 = 1\). So integers with \(5x + 3y = 1\) exist (Definition: Existential quantifier). Other pairs work too, such as \(x = -1\) and \(y = 2\).











Definition 1 (Constructive proof) A constructive proof of a proposition \(\exists x \in S,\ P(x)\) (Definition: Existential quantifier) names a particular element of \(S\) and shows that \(P\) is true of it (Wikipedia contributors 2026). A proposition with several existential quantifiers, such as “there are integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(m + n = 1\)”, gets a constructive proof that names one element for each quantifier.











Example 3 (Half of a positive number) Claim: for every positive real number \(x\), there is a positive real number \(y\) with \(y < x\).
Let \(x\) be a positive real number. We give a constructive proof of “there is a positive real number \(y\) with \(y < x\)” for this \(x\): take \(y = \frac{x}{2}\). Then \(y > 0\), because \(x > 0\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
x - y
&= x - \frac{x}{2}
&& \text{(substitute } y = \tfrac{x}{2} \text{)}
\\&= \frac{x}{2}
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\\&> 0,
&& \text{(} x > 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(y < x\). The element named, \(\frac{x}{2}\), depends on \(x\), which a “for every \(x\), there is a \(y\)” statement allows.
The solution to Exercise 2 is also a constructive proof: it names the integers \(2\) and \(-3\).











Definition 2 (Non-constructive proof) A non-constructive proof of a proposition \(\exists x \in S,\ P(x)\) shows that it is true without naming any element \(x\) of \(S\) for which \(P(x)\) is true (Wikipedia contributors 2026).











Example 4 (An irrational power of an irrational number) Claim: there are irrational numbers \(x\) and \(y\) (Definition: Irrational numbers) for which \(x^y\) is rational (Definition: Rational numbers).
The number \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational (Theorem: \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational). Consider \(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\), and take two cases (Definition: Proof by cases).
Case 1: \(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\) is rational. Then \(x = \sqrt{2}\) and \(y = \sqrt{2}\) work.
Case 2: \(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\) is irrational. Then take \(x = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(y = \sqrt{2}\), both irrational, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^y
&= \mathopen{}\left(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\right)\mathclose{}^{\sqrt{2}}
&& \text{(substitute } x \text{ and } y \text{)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2} \cdot\sqrt{2}}
&& \text{(a power of a power multiplies the exponents)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}^{2}
&& \text{(} \sqrt{2} \cdot\sqrt{2} = 2 \text{)}
\\&= 2,
\end{aligned}
\]
which is rational, since \(2 = \frac{2}{1}\).
Every number is rational or irrational, so one of the cases holds, and the claim is true. The proof does not say which case holds, so it does not name a pair \(x, y\) that works.






3 Disproof







Exercise 3 (Prove or disprove) Prove or disprove: for every real number \(x\), if \(x^2 > 1\), then \(x > 1\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. The proposition is false. Take \(x = -2\). Then \(x^2 = 4 > 1\), but \(x > 1\) is false. So \(x = -2\) makes “if \(x^2 > 1\), then \(x > 1\)” false (Definition: Implies), and so it is a counterexample (Definition: Counterexample) to the proposition.











Definition 3 (Disproof) A disproof of a proposition \(P\) is a proof (Definition: Proof) of its negation, \(\neg P\) (Definition: Not).











Example 5 (No integer squares to two) Claim to disprove: there is an integer \(n\) with \(n^2 = 2\).
By Theorem: Negating a quantifier, its negation is “for every integer \(n\), \(n^2 \ne 2\)”. We prove the negation by cases (Definition: Proof by cases). Let \(n\) be an integer.

If \(n\) is \(-1\), \(0\) or \(1\), then \(n^2\) is \(1\), \(0\) or \(1\), which is not \(2\).
Otherwise \(n \le -2\) or \(n \ge 2\), so \(\mathopen{}\left|n\right|\mathclose{} \ge 2\), and \(n^2 = \mathopen{}\left|n\right|\mathclose{}^2 \ge 2^2 = 4\), so \(n^2 \ne 2\).












Exercise 4 (An equation with a solution) Prove or disprove: there are integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 4n = 2\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. The proposition is true. Take \(m = 1\) and \(n = -1\). Then \(6m + 4n = 6 - 4 = 2\).











Exercise 5 (An equation without a solution) Prove or disprove: there are integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 4n = 3\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. The proposition is false. Applying Theorem: Negating a quantifier to each of its two quantifiers in turn, its negation is “for all integers \(m\) and \(n\), \(6m + 4n \ne 3\)”, and we prove that. Let \(m\) and \(n\) be integers. Then \(6m + 4n = 2(3m + 2n)\), and \(3m + 2n\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(6m + 4n\) is even (Definition: Even integer). But \(3 = 2 \cdot 1 + 1\) is odd (Definition: Odd integer), and no integer is both even and odd (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(6m + 4n \ne 3\).






References

Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 syllabus opens the course with an introduction to functional programming; this chapter, its examples and its exercises are new.
The definitions of expression, function, argument and value are included from the mathematics prerequisites notes, so they read the same in both places.




1 Expressions







Remark 1 (Running Racket). This course writes its programs in Racket, a programming language that grew out of Scheme, a dialect of Lisp. Racket comes with DrRacket, the program you use to write and run Racket code, and Lab 1 walks through using it. Each Racket file in this course starts with the line #lang racket. The Racket Guide is the reference for anything these notes do not cover.











Exercise 1 (Operation first) Racket writes \(7 - 2\) as (- 7 2), with the operation first and the parentheses around the whole expression. Guess what each Racket expression returns:

(* (+ 1 2) (- 10 4))
(- 20 (* 3 (+ 1 1)))
(+ 1 2 3 4)

Then write \((2 + 3) \cdot 4 - 1\) in Racket.










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. Work from the innermost parentheses outward.

(+ 1 2) is 3 and (- 10 4) is 6, so the expression is (* 3 6), which returns 18.
(+ 1 1) is 2, so (* 3 (+ 1 1)) is 6, and (- 20 6) returns 14.
+ can take any number of operands, and adds them all, so the expression returns 10.

The expression \((2 + 3) \cdot 4 - 1\) subtracts 1 from the product of \(2 + 3\) and 4, so in Racket it is (- (* (+ 2 3) 4) 1), which returns 19.











Definition 1 (Function (map, mapping, transformation)) A function \(f\) from a set \(A\) to a set \(B\), (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) written \(f : A \to B\), assigns to each element \(a \in A\) exactly one element \(f(a) \in B\).
A function is also called a map (or mapping) or a transformation; on this site the three words mean the same thing, although some authors reserve “transformation” for a function from a set to itself.











Definition 2 (Expression) An expression (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) is a string of symbols, built from constants, variables, operations and function names according to the rules of the notation. When its variables are read as inputs, an expression denotes a function: it fixes the output for each input.











Definition 3 (Racket expression, prefix notation) A Racket expression (Definition 2) is one of:

a constant, such as the number 7;
a name, such as x or +;
an application (f e1 ... en): an expression f for an operation or function, followed by its operands e1, …, en, which are expressions too, all inside one pair of parentheses.

Writing the operation before its operands is called prefix notation. Racket needs no precedence rules, because the nesting of the parentheses says which operation comes first: (* (+ 2 3) 4) adds first, and (+ 2 (* 3 4)) multiplies first.











Remark 2 (How Racket evaluates an application). To evaluate an application (f e1 ... en) (Definition 3), Racket evaluates each operand e1, …, en to a value, then applies f to those values. In part 1 of Exercise 1:
(* (+ 1 2) (- 10 4))
= (* 3 (- 10 4))
= (* 3 6)
= 18
Each = replaces one application by its value, and the evaluation ends with a value, which cannot be simplified further.






2 Functions







Exercise 2 (Reading a definition) This Racket code defines a function named h:
(define (h x)
  (- (* x x) (* 2 x)))

Write \(h(x)\) as a formula in ordinary mathematical notation.
What does (h 5) return?
What does (h (h 3)) return?











SolutionSolution






Solution 2. 

\(h(x) = x^2 - 2x\), since (* x x) is \(x^2\) and (* 2 x) is \(2x\).
\(h(5) = 25 - 10 = 15\), so (h 5) returns 15.
Racket first evaluates the argument (h 3), which is \(9 - 6 = 3\), and then applies h to it, so (h (h 3)) is (h 3) again and returns 3.












Definition 4 (Argument (input)) An argument (or input) of a function \(f : A \to B\) is an element \(a \in A\) that \(f\) is applied to.











Definition 5 (Value (output)) The value (or output) of a function \(f : A \to B\) at an argument \(a \in A\) is the element \(f(a) \in B\) that \(f\) assigns to \(a\).











Definition 6 (Defining a function in Racket) The Racket definition
(define (f x1 ... xn)
  body)
defines a function named f with parameters x1, …, xn: names that stand for its arguments (Definition 4). To evaluate an application (f a1 ... an), Racket evaluates the arguments a1, …, an, replaces each parameter in body by the value of its argument, and evaluates the result. The value of the application is the value (Definition 5) of f at those arguments.











Example 1 (Replacing a parameter by its argument) With h from Exercise 2, Definition 6 evaluates (h 5) in four steps:
(h 5)
= (- (* 5 5) (* 2 5))
= (- 25 (* 2 5))
= (- 25 10)
= 15
The first step replaces x by 5 in the body of h, just as computing \(h(5)\) replaces \(x\) by 5 in \(x^2 - 2x\). Each later step replaces one application by its value (Remark 2).






3 Cases







Exercise 3 (Choosing a case) A museum sets its ticket price, in dollars, by age:
(define (ticket-price age)
  (cond [(< age 5) 0]
        [(< age 18) 8]
        [else 12]))
Each line in square brackets pairs a test with a value.

Guess what (ticket-price 4), (ticket-price 5), (ticket-price 17) and (ticket-price 70) return.
Write the function as a formula with cases, for a whole number of years \(a \ge 0\).











SolutionSolution






Solution 3. 

Racket tries the tests in order and returns the value beside the first true one:

(ticket-price 4) returns 0, since \(4 < 5\).
(ticket-price 5) returns 8, since \(5 < 5\) is false but \(5 < 18\) is true.
(ticket-price 17) returns 8, since \(17 < 18\).
(ticket-price 70) returns 12, since neither test is true, so the else line applies.

The second case holds only when the first test is false, so its condition is \(5 \le a < 18\), not just \(a < 18\):
\[
p(a) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } a < 5, \\
8 & \text{if } 5 \le a < 18, \\
12 & \text{if } a \ge 18.
\end{cases}
\]












Definition 7 (True and false in Racket) Racket writes the two truth values as #t (true) and #f (false). A comparison such as (< 4 5) or (= 3 7) returns one of them, and and, or and not combine them: (and (< 1 2) (< 3 2)) returns #f.











Definition 8 (if and cond) The expression (if test a b) evaluates test, and returns the value of a if test is true and the value of b if it is false.
The expression
(cond [test1 a1]
      [test2 a2]
      ...
      [else an])
evaluates the tests in order and returns the value of the expression beside the first true one, or the value of an if none is true. Like a function defined by cases in mathematics, each case of a cond applies only when every case before it fails.
if and cond look like applications (Definition 3), but they are not: an application evaluates all of its operands (Remark 2), while if and cond evaluate only the tests they need and the one branch they return. and, or and define are not applications either.











Example 2 (Absolute value with if) The absolute value \[
\mathopen{}\left|x\right|\mathclose{} =
\begin{cases}
-x & \text{if } x < 0, \\
x & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\] has two cases, so one if (Definition 8) is enough:
(define (absolute x)
  (if (< x 0)
      (- x)
      x))
(absolute -7) returns 7, and (absolute 2) returns 2. Racket already has this function, under the name abs.






4 Pure functions







Exercise 4 (Same call, different answer) This Python code hands out ID numbers:
count = 0

def next_id():
    global count
    count = count + 1
    return count

The program calls next_id() twice in a row. What does each call return?
Is there a mathematical function \(f\) (Definition 1) with no arguments whose value is what next_id() returns every time it is called?











SolutionSolution






Solution 4. 

The first call changes count from 0 to 1 and returns 1. The second call changes count from 1 to 2 and returns 2.
No. A function with no arguments has exactly one value, but next_id() returned 1 and then 2. What it returns depends on the variable count, which is not an argument and which each call changes.












Definition 9 (Side effect) A side effect of a piece of code is any change it makes besides returning a value, such as changing a variable, printing, or writing a file. next_id in Exercise 4 has a side effect: it changes count.











Definition 10 (Pure function) A function in a program is pure (Wikipedia contributors 2026e) if

it returns the same value whenever it is called with the same arguments, and
it has no side effects (Definition 9).

A pure function computes a mathematical function (Definition 1) of its arguments.











Definition 11 (Functional programming) Functional programming (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) is a style of programming in which a program is built by defining and applying pure functions (Definition 10), rather than by running statements that change variables.











Remark 3 (Why this course uses functional programming). In a program built from pure functions (Definition 10), an expression can be replaced by its value anywhere it appears without changing what the program does. That is what makes evaluation by substitution (Example 1) work, and it is also how algebra works: \(h(5)\) can be replaced by 15 in any formula. So a pure function can be checked with the same reasoning as a formula, and this course proves facts about programs that way.
next_id in Exercise 4 is not pure, so next_id() + next_id() cannot be simplified to 2 * next_id(). On a fresh start, next_id() + next_id() returns 3, from \(1 + 2\), but 2 * next_id() returns 2. Racket can change variables too, with set!, but this course does not use it.






5 Functions as values







Exercise 5 (A function as an argument) The function twice takes a function f and a value x:
(define (twice f x)
  (f (f x)))

(define (add-three x)
  (+ x 3))
Guess what each expression returns:

(twice add-three 10)
(twice h 4), with h from Exercise 2
(twice add-three (twice add-three 0))











SolutionSolution






Solution 5. Replace f and x in the body (f (f x)) (Definition 6):

(twice add-three 10) is (add-three (add-three 10)), which is (add-three 13), which returns 16.
(twice h 4) is (h (h 4)). Since \(h(4) = 16 - 8 = 8\) and \(h(8) = 64 - 16 = 48\), it returns 48.
The argument (twice add-three 0) returns 6, so the whole expression is (twice add-three 6), which returns 12.












Definition 12 (Higher-order function) A higher-order function (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) is a function that takes a function as an argument, or returns a function as its value. twice in Exercise 5 is a higher-order function.











Example 3 (map and filter) Racket’s (list 5 7 9) makes the list of 5, 7 and 9, which Racket prints as '(5 7 9). Two built-in higher-order functions (Definition 12) work on lists:

(map f L) applies f to each element of the list L, and returns the list of results. With add-three from Exercise 5, (map add-three (list 5 7 9)) returns '(8 10 12).
(filter p L) returns the list of the elements x of L for which (p x) is true. (filter even? (list 5 6 7 8)) returns '(6 8).

Neither one changes L; each returns a new list.






6 Anonymous functions







Exercise 6 (A function with no name) The function pair-with takes a list L and a value y:
(define (pair-with L y)
  (map (lambda (x) (list x y)) L))
Guess what each expression returns:

((lambda (x) (* x x)) 7)
(map (lambda (x) (* 2 x)) (list 1 2 3))
(pair-with (list 1 2 3) "a")











SolutionSolution






Solution 6. (lambda (x) (* x x)) is the function that squares its argument, written in place without a name.

Applying it to 7 returns 49.
map (Example 3) applies the doubling function to each element, and returns '(2 4 6).
In the body of pair-with, y is "a", so map applies the function \(x \mapsto (x, \text{"a"})\) to each element, and returns '((1 "a") (2 "a") (3 "a")).












Definition 13 (lambda) The Racket expression
(lambda (x1 ... xn)
  body)
is a lambda expression. Its value is the function with parameters x1, …, xn whose value at its arguments is the value of body, found as in Definition 6. The function has no name. The body may use any name defined where the lambda expression appears, as the body of the lambda in pair-with (Exercise 6) uses y.
The definition (define (f x) body) is shorthand for (define f (lambda (x) body)): it gives the name f to the function the lambda expression makes.
Video: Jerry Cain uses lambda with map in Scheme, the language Racket grew out of, in Stanford CS 107 Lecture 22 (Cain 2008).











Remark 4 (Where the name comes from). The word lambda comes from the lambda calculus, a model of computation in which a function is written \(\lambda x.\, e\), the function that takes \(x\) to the value of the expression \(e\). The lambda calculus has only three features: functions, applying a function to an argument, and variables. It has no numbers, strings or loops (Crichton 2019). Applying \(\lambda x.\, e\) to an argument replaces each \(x\) in \(e\) by that argument, as in evaluation by substitution (Example 1). The function in Exercise 6 that squares its argument is \(\lambda x.\, x \cdot x\).
Media: Will Crichton’s notes on the lambda calculus, from Stanford’s CS 242, Programming Languages, go further (Crichton 2019).











Example 4 (A function that returns a function) The function adder takes a number d and returns a function:
(define (adder d)
  (lambda (x) (+ x d)))
(adder 3) returns the function \(x \mapsto x + 3\), which still knows that d is 3 after adder has returned. So adder is a higher-order function (Definition 12), and its value can be used anywhere a function can:

((adder 3) 4) returns 7.
(twice (adder 3) 10), with twice from Exercise 5, returns 16.
(map (adder 1) (list 5 7 9)) returns '(6 8 10).

title: Inference and Direct Proof
text:
NoteSource





Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Logic 4, Proofs Intro, Direct Proof”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. The rules of inference, the definition of “divides”, the observation that a definition’s “if” means “if and only if”, the template for a direct proof, and the ideas of proof by cases and “without loss of generality” come from those notes; the exercises are new.
The definitions of logical entailment, the integers, even and odd integers, and proof are included from the mathematics prerequisites notes, so they read the same in both places.




1 Rules of inference







Exercise 1 (Which conclusions are safe?) Let \(P\) be “the tests pass”, \(Q\) be “the build is deployed” and \(R\) be “the build is rolled back”. Each argument below lists some propositions, then “so”, then one more proposition. For each argument, decide whether the proposition after “so” must be true whenever all of the propositions before it are true.

\(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(P\), so \(Q\).
\(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(Q\), so \(P\).
\(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(\neg Q\), so \(\neg P\).
\(P \lor R\) and \(\neg R\), so \(P\).











SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 

Yes. \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false (Definition: Implies), so if \(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(P\) are both true, \(Q\) is true.
No. If the tests fail but someone deploys the build by hand, \(P\) is false and \(Q\) is true. Then \(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(Q\) are both true, and \(P\) is false.
Yes. \(\neg Q\) is true, so \(Q\) is false (Definition: Not). If \(P\) were true, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) would be false, so \(P\) is false and \(\neg P\) is true.
Yes. \(\neg R\) is true, so \(R\) is false (Definition: Not). \(P \lor R\) is true only if \(P\) or \(R\) is true (Definition: Or), so \(P\) is true.












Definition 1 (Argument) An argument is a list of propositions (Definition: Proposition (statement)), called its premises, together with one more proposition, called its conclusion. An argument is written with “so” or \(\therefore\) before its conclusion.











Remark 1 (Two uses of “premise” and “conclusion”). The premise and conclusion of a conditional \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (Remark: Names for the parts, and other notation) are its parts \(P\) and \(Q\). The premises and conclusion of an argument (Definition 1) are whole propositions: in argument 1 of Exercise 1, the premises are \(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(P\), and the conclusion is \(Q\).











Definition 2 (Logical entailment (logical consequence, deductive consequence)) Propositions or predicates \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\) (Definition: Proposition (statement), Definition: Predicate) logically entail (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) a proposition or predicate \(Q\) when every choice of values for their variables that makes all of \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\) true also makes \(Q\) true. Then \(Q\) is a logical consequence, or deductive consequence, of \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\).











Example 1 (Entailment in the deployment arguments) In Exercise 1, the premises of arguments 1, 3 and 4 (Definition 1) logically entail their conclusions (Definition 2). The premises of argument 2 do not: the values \(P\) false and \(Q\) true make both premises true and the conclusion false.











Definition 3 (Rule of inference) A rule of inference is a pattern of argument (Definition 1), written in terms of propositions \(P, Q, \ldots\), whose premises logically entail its conclusion (Definition 2) whatever propositions are put in place of \(P, Q, \ldots\). It is written with its premises above a line and its conclusion below: \[
\frac{P_1, \ldots, P_n}{Q}.
\]











Example 2 (Modus ponens) Argument 1 of Exercise 1 follows the pattern \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad P}{Q},
\] called modus ponens. It is a rule of inference (Definition 3): by Solution 1, its premises entail its conclusion for any propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), not only for tests and builds.











Theorem 1 (Common rules of inference) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), each of the following is a rule of inference (Definition 3):

modus ponens: \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad P}{Q}
\]
modus tollens: \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad \neg Q}{\neg P}
\]
disjunctive syllogism: \[
\frac{P \lor Q, \quad \neg P}{Q}
\]
simplification: \[
\frac{P \land Q}{P}
\]
conjunction: \[
\frac{P, \quad Q}{P \land Q}
\]
addition: \[
\frac{P}{P \lor Q}
\]











ProofProof






Proof. For each rule, suppose every premise is true, and show that the conclusion is true.

\(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false (Definition: Implies). \(P\) is true and \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is true, so \(Q\) is not false.
\(\neg Q\) is true, so \(Q\) is false (Definition: Not). If \(P\) were true, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) would be false, so \(P\) is false and \(\neg P\) is true.
\(\neg P\) is true, so \(P\) is false. \(P \lor Q\) is true only if \(P\) or \(Q\) is true (Definition: Or), so \(Q\) is true.
\(P \land Q\) is true only if both \(P\) and \(Q\) are true (Definition: And), so \(P\) is true.
\(P\) and \(Q\) are both true, so \(P \land Q\) is true (Definition: And).
\(P\) is true, so \(P \lor Q\) is true (Definition: Or).












Example 3 (Modus tollens on a slow page) “If the cache is warm, then the page loads in under a second” and “the page did not load in under a second” together give “the cache is not warm”, by modus tollens (Theorem 1).











Remark 2 (Two arguments that are not rules of inference). Argument 2 of Exercise 1, \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad Q}{P},
\] is called affirming the consequent, since it concludes \(P\) from the consequent \(Q\) of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (Remark: Names for the parts, and other notation). It is not a rule of inference (Definition 3): \(P\) false and \(Q\) true make its premises true and its conclusion false.
Denying the antecedent, \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad \neg P}{\neg Q},
\] fails for the same values of \(P\) and \(Q\). Both read like modus ponens or modus tollens (Theorem 1), which is why they are common mistakes.






2 Even, odd and divisible







Exercise 2 (Two times something, plus maybe one) Write each of \(14\), \(15\), \(-7\) and \(0\) as \(2k\) or as \(2k + 1\), for an integer \(k\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. 

\(14 = 2 \cdot 7\).
\(15 = 2 \cdot 7 + 1\).
\(-7 = 2 \cdot (-4) + 1\).
\(0 = 2 \cdot 0\).












Definition 4 (Integers) The integers (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) are the whole numbers, together with their negatives and \(0\):
\[\mathbb{Z} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left\{\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\]
An integer is an element of \(\mathbb{Z}\).











Definition 5 (Positive integers) The integers (Definition 4) greater than \(0\) are the positive integers.











Definition 6 (Negative integers) The integers (Definition 4) less than \(0\) are the negative integers.











Example 4 (Integers and non-integers)  

\(-7\), \(0\), and \(12\) are integers.
\(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(-2.5\) are not integers.
\(\frac{6}{3}\) is an integer, because \(\frac{6}{3} = 2\).












Definition 7 (Even integer) An integer (Definition 4) \(n\) is even (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) if \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\).











Definition 8 (Odd integer) An integer (Definition 4) \(n\) is odd (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) if \(n = 2k + 1\) for some integer \(k\).











Example 5 (Even and odd integers)  

\(6\) is even, because \(6 = 2 \cdot 3\).
\(0\) is even, because \(0 = 2 \cdot 0\).
\(-3\) is odd, because \(-3 = 2 \cdot(-2) + 1\).
\(7\) is odd, because \(7 = 2 \cdot 3 + 1\).
\(2.5\) is neither even nor odd, because it is not an integer.












Remark 3 (Facts about integers used without proof). These notes use two facts about the integers (Definition 4) without proving them:

the sum, difference and product of two integers are integers;
every integer is even or odd (Definition 7, Definition 8), and none is both.












Remark 4 (A definition’s “if” means “if and only if”). Definition 7 says that \(n\) is even “if” \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\), but it means “if and only if” (Definition: If and only if): an integer is even exactly when it can be written as \(2k\). So a proof can use a definition in both directions: to show that \(n\) is even, write \(n\) as \(2k\); and from “\(n\) is even”, conclude that \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\).











Definition 9 (Divides) Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers (Definition 4). We say that \(a\) divides \(b\), written \(a \mid b\), if \(b = a c\) for some integer \(c\). When \(a\) does not divide \(b\), we write \(a \nmid b\).











Example 6 (Divisors)  

\(3 \mid 12\), because \(12 = 3 \cdot 4\).
\(-2 \mid 6\), because \(6 = (-2) \cdot (-3)\).
\(3 \nmid 13\): \(3 c\) increases with \(c\), \(3 \cdot 4 = 12\) and \(3 \cdot 5 = 15\), and there is no integer between \(4\) and \(5\), so no integer \(c\) gives \(3 c = 13\).
Every integer \(a\) divides \(0\), because \(0 = a \cdot 0\).
\(0\) divides only \(0\), because \(0 \cdot c = 0\) for every integer \(c\).












Remark 5 (Divisibility in Racket). For a nonzero integer a, Racket’s (remainder b a) returns 0 exactly when \(a \mid b\) (Definition 9), so (zero? (remainder b a)) tests divisibility. (zero? (remainder 12 3)) returns #t and (zero? (remainder 13 3)) returns #f, as in Example 6. (remainder 12 0) raises an error, so a Racket test of \(a \mid b\) has to handle \(a = 0\) on its own.






3 Direct proof







Exercise 3 (An odd input) Show that if \(n\) is an odd integer, then \(3 n + 5\) is even.






TipHint



What does Definition 8 let you write in place of \(n\)?












SolutionSolution






Solution 3. Suppose \(n\) is an odd integer. By Definition 8, \(n = 2 k + 1\) for some integer \(k\). Then \[
3 n + 5 = 3 (2 k + 1) + 5 = 6 k + 3 + 5 = 6 k + 8 = 2 (3 k + 4).
\] Since \(3 k + 4\) is an integer (Remark 3), \(3 n + 5\) is even, by Definition 7.











Definition 10 (Proof) A proof (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) of a proposition (Definition: Proposition (statement)) is a finite list of statements that ends with that proposition, in which each statement is

an assumption,
a definition,
a previously proved result, or
a consequence of earlier statements in the list, by one rule of logic or algebra.












Example 7 (A proof, statement by statement) Solution 3 is a proof (Definition 10) of “\(3 n + 5\) is even” in which “\(n\) is an odd integer” is an assumption. Its statements are:

the assumption: \(n\) is an odd integer;
a definition: \(n = 2 k + 1\) for some integer \(k\), by Definition 8;
consequences by algebra: \(3 n + 5 = 6 k + 8 = 2 (3 k + 4)\);
a definition: \(3 n + 5\) is even, by Definition 7, since \(3 k + 4\) is an integer.












Definition 11 (Direct proof) A direct proof of a conditional \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (Definition: Implies) is a proof (Definition 10) of \(Q\) in which \(P\) is an assumption.











Example 8 (A direct proof) Solution 3 is a direct proof (Definition 11) of “if \(n\) is an odd integer, then \(3 n + 5\) is even”: it assumes \(P\), “\(n\) is an odd integer”, and ends with \(Q\), “\(3 n + 5\) is even”.











Remark 6 (The shape of a direct proof). A direct proof (Definition 11) of “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” has this shape:

Suppose \(P\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(Q\).

Write the first and last lines first, then fill in the middle, usually by replacing each defined term with its definition (Remark 4).
A direct proof proves \(P \Rightarrow Q\): when \(P\) is true, the proof shows that \(Q\) is true, and when \(P\) is false, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is true anyway (Definition: Implies).
When the statement is about every element of a set, as in “for every odd integer \(n\)” (Definition: Universal quantifier), the proof starts from an arbitrary element: “Suppose \(n\) is an odd integer.” Since the proof uses nothing about \(n\) except that \(n\) is odd, the same steps work for every odd integer.











Exercise 4 (Divisors of divisors) Let \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) be integers. Prove that if \(a \mid b\) and \(b \mid c\), then \(a \mid c\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. Suppose \(a \mid b\) and \(b \mid c\). By Definition 9, \(b = a j\) and \(c = b k\) for some integers \(j\) and \(k\). Then \[
c = b k = (a j) k = a (j k).
\] Since \(j k\) is an integer (Remark 3), \(a \mid c\), by Definition 9.






4 Proof by cases







Exercise 5 (Even for every integer) Prove that \(n^2 + n\) is even for every integer \(n\).






TipHint



Every integer is even or odd (Remark 3). Handle the two kinds separately.












SolutionSolution






Solution 5. Let \(n\) be an integer. Every integer is even or odd (Remark 3), so one of these cases holds.
Case 1: \(n\) is even. By Definition 7, \(n = 2 k\) for some integer \(k\), and \[
n^2 + n = (2 k)^2 + 2 k = 4 k^2 + 2 k = 2 (2 k^2 + k).
\]
Case 2: \(n\) is odd. By Definition 8, \(n = 2 k + 1\) for some integer \(k\), and \[
n^2 + n = (2 k + 1)^2 + (2 k + 1) = (4 k^2 + 4 k + 1) + (2 k + 1) = 4 k^2 + 6 k + 2 = 2 (2 k^2 + 3 k + 1).
\]
In each case, \(n^2 + n\) is \(2\) times an integer (Remark 3), so \(n^2 + n\) is even, by Definition 7.











Definition 12 (Proof by cases) A proof by cases splits the situation into cases that together cover every possibility, and proves the conclusion separately in each case.











Example 9 (Two cases) Solution 5 is a proof by cases (Definition 12): every integer is even or odd (Remark 3), so its two cases cover every integer \(n\).











Exercise 6 (Larger plus smaller) For real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), let \(\max(x, y)\) be the larger of \(x\) and \(y\) and \(\min(x, y)\) the smaller (both equal \(x\) when \(x = y\)). Prove that \(\max(x, y) + \min(x, y) = x + y\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Either \(x \le y\) or \(y \le x\). Both sides of the equation stay the same when \(x\) and \(y\) are swapped, so without loss of generality, suppose \(x \le y\). Then \(\max(x, y) = y\) and \(\min(x, y) = x\), so \[
\max(x, y) + \min(x, y) = y + x = x + y.
\]











Remark 7 (Without loss of generality). Solution 6 is a proof by cases (Definition 12) with two cases, \(x \le y\) and \(y \le x\). The proof of the second case is the proof of the first with the names \(x\) and \(y\) swapped, which changes neither side of the equation. “Without loss of generality, suppose \(x \le y\)” says this, and writes out only the first case. Use it only when the other cases really are the same proof with names changed.

title: State Machines and Finite Automata
text:
NoteSource





The topics of this chapter follow the course calendar, and their order follows Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes introducing the theory of computation. These come from those notes:

the three parts of the theory of computation, computability, complexity and automata theory, with the halting problem and the P versus NP problem as examples of the first two;
automata as the precise form of “computer”, and the question of whether a machine accepts a string as the precise form of “problem”;
a state machine drawn as a directed graph, with an arrow into the initial state and a double circle for an accepting state.

These follow the course’s handout on graph extensions:

a finite automaton seen as a directed graph whose vertices are states and whose labeled edges are transitions, with a start state and accepting states;
reading a string one symbol at a time, following the edge labeled with each symbol, and accepting the string when the machine ends in an accepting state.

The transition function, runs, the extended transition function, languages, dead states, complements and state-transition tables are added here. The notes do not cover nondeterministic automata or regular expressions, so this chapter does not either. The examples, the exercises, the Racket functions and the proofs are new.




1 State machines







Exercise 1 (A door with a lock) A door is always in one of three conditions: closed, open or locked. Four actions can be done to it:

o: push it open, which opens a closed door and does nothing to a locked or an open one;
c: shut it, which closes an open door and does nothing otherwise;
l: turn the key to lock, which locks a closed door and does nothing otherwise;
u: turn the key to unlock, which unlocks a locked door, leaving it closed, and does nothing otherwise.

The door starts closed, and these actions are done in this order:
\[
\mathtt{o}, \mathtt{l}, \mathtt{c}, \mathtt{l}, \mathtt{o}, \mathtt{u}, \mathtt{o}.
\]
In which condition is the door at the end?










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. Follow the door one action at a time:














action

o
l
c
l
o
u
o




condition
closed
open
open
closed
locked
locked
closed
open



The first l does nothing, because the door is open, and the second o does nothing, because the door is locked. At the end the door is open.











Remark 1 (Where state machines come from). The theory of computation (Wikipedia contributors 2026h) asks what computers can do. It has three parts:

computability theory asks which problems a computer can solve at all. For example, no program can decide, for every program \(P\) and input \(I\), whether \(P\) stops when it runs on \(I\); this is the halting problem (Wikipedia contributors 2026d).
complexity theory asks how much time the problems that can be solved need. Whether every problem whose answers can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly is the P versus NP problem (Wikipedia contributors 2026e), which no one had solved as of 2026.
automata theory makes “computer” and “problem” precise, so that the other two parts can prove things about them. A computer becomes an abstract machine, called an automaton (plural automata), and a problem becomes the question of which strings (Definition: String) the machine answers yes for.

The halting problem and the P versus NP problem are about machines that can do anything a general program can, called Turing machines (Wikipedia contributors 2026i). This chapter studies the simplest automata, which remember only one of finitely many situations. They are far less powerful than Turing machines, and cannot model a general program.











Definition 1 (State machine) A state machine \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0)\) consists of

a nonempty finite set \(S\) (Definition: Set), whose elements are called states;
an alphabet \(\Sigma\) (Definition: Alphabet), whose symbols are called inputs;
a function (Definition: Function (map, mapping, transformation)) \(\delta : S \times \Sigma \to S\) on the Cartesian product (Definition: Cartesian product) \(S \times \Sigma\), called the transition function;
an initial state \(s_0 \in S\).

When \(M\) is in state \(s\) and reads the input \(x\), it moves to the state \(\delta(s, x)\). Names and tuples for these machines vary between sources: for example, the finite-state machines of (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) also carry a set of final states in the tuple.











Example 1 (The door as a state machine) The door of Exercise 1 is a state machine (Definition 1) with

states \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{closed}, \text{open}, \text{locked}\right\}\mathclose{}}\);
inputs \(\Sigma = {\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{o}, \mathtt{c}, \mathtt{l}, \mathtt{u}\right\}\mathclose{}}\);
initial state \(s_0 = \text{closed}\);
the transition function \(\delta\) with

\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{o}) &= \text{open},
& \delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{c}) &= \text{closed},
\\
\delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{l}) &= \text{locked},
& \delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{u}) &= \text{closed},
\\
\delta(\text{open}, \mathtt{o}) &= \text{open},
& \delta(\text{open}, \mathtt{c}) &= \text{closed},
\\
\delta(\text{open}, \mathtt{l}) &= \text{open},
& \delta(\text{open}, \mathtt{u}) &= \text{open},
\\
\delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{o}) &= \text{locked},
& \delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{c}) &= \text{locked},
\\
\delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{l}) &= \text{locked},
& \delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{u}) &= \text{closed}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The set \(S \times \Sigma\) has \(3 \cdot 4 = 12\) pairs, and \(\delta\) gives one state for each of them, including the pairs where the action does nothing, such as \(\delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{o}) = \text{locked}\).











Definition 2 (State diagram) The state diagram (Wikipedia contributors 2026f) of a state machine \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0)\) (Definition 1) is the directed graph (Definition: Directed graph (digraph)) with

vertex set \(S\);
for each state \(s\) and each input \(x\), one edge from \(s\) to \(\delta(s, x)\), labeled \(x\).

The labels are extra data attached to the edges: the directed graph itself is only its vertices and edges. It is drawn with an extra arrow, which starts at no state, pointing to the initial state \(s_0\). Two inputs \(x \ne y\) with \(\delta(s, x) = \delta(s, y)\) give parallel edges (Definition: Parallel edges) of the directed graph, which are drawn as one arrow labeled with all of their inputs.











Example 2 (The state diagram of the door) Figure 1 is the state diagram (Definition 2) of the door (Example 1). The loop at closed is labeled \(\mathtt{c}, \mathtt{u}\): it stands for two parallel loops, one labeled \(\mathtt{c}\) and one labeled \(\mathtt{u}\), since \(\delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{c}) = \delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{u}) = \text{closed}\).



Figure 1: The state diagram of the door.

















Remark 2 (Every state has one edge for each input). In the state diagram (Definition 2) of a state machine with inputs \(\Sigma\), each state \(s\) is the start of exactly one edge labeled \(x\) for each input \(x\), because \(\delta(s, x)\) is one state. So every state has out-degree (Definition: Out-degree) \({\mathopen{}\left|\Sigma\right|\mathclose{}}\), counting each label of a drawn arrow as its own edge. In Figure 1 every state has out-degree 4. The in-degrees (Definition: In-degree) add up to the same total, \(3 \cdot 4 = 12\), as Theorem: Degrees in a directed graph says.






2 Runs







Exercise 2 (Following the door) The door (Example 1) starts closed, and these actions are done in this order:
\[
\mathtt{l}, \mathtt{o}, \mathtt{u}, \mathtt{o}, \mathtt{l}.
\]
Write down the whole sequence of conditions the door passes through, starting with the condition it is in before the first action.










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. The sequence starts with closed, and each later condition is \(\delta\) of the condition before it and the action:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{l}) &= \text{locked},
\\
\delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{o}) &= \text{locked},
\\
\delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{u}) &= \text{closed},
\\
\delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{o}) &= \text{open},
\\
\delta(\text{open}, \mathtt{l}) &= \text{open}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So the sequence is
\[
\text{closed}, \text{locked}, \text{locked}, \text{closed}, \text{open}, \text{open}:
\]
six conditions for five actions. In Figure 1, they are the states met by following, from closed, the arrows labeled \(\mathtt{l}\), \(\mathtt{o}\), \(\mathtt{u}\), \(\mathtt{o}\) and \(\mathtt{l}\) in turn.











Definition 3 (Run) Let \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0)\) be a state machine (Definition 1), let \(s \in S\), and let \(w = x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n\) be a string (Definition: String) of \(n \ge 0\) inputs \(x_i \in \Sigma\). The run of \(M\) on \(w\) from \(s\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) is the sequence of states
\[
r_0, r_1, \ldots, r_n
\]
with \(r_0 = s\) and \(r_i = \delta(r_{i - 1}, x_i)\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\). The run of \(M\) on \(w\), with no state named, is the run from the initial state \(s_0\).











Example 3 (A run of the door) The run (Definition 3) of the door (Example 1) on the string \(\mathtt{oclu}\) is
\[
\text{closed}, \text{open}, \text{closed}, \text{locked}, \text{closed},
\]
since \(\delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{o}) = \text{open}\), \(\delta(\text{open}, \mathtt{c}) = \text{closed}\), \(\delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{l}) = \text{locked}\) and \(\delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{u}) = \text{closed}\). The string has 4 inputs, and the run has 5 states. The run on the empty string \(\lambda\) is the one state closed.











Definition 4 (Extended transition function) Let \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0)\) be a state machine (Definition 1). Its extended transition function \(\delta^* : S \times \Sigma^* \to S\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) gives the state that \(M\) reaches from a state \(s\) by reading a string \(w \in \Sigma^*\) (Definition: String). It is defined recursively (Definition: Recursive definition), following the recursive definition of \(\Sigma^*\):

base case: \(\delta^*(s, \lambda) = s\);
recursive rule: if \(w \in \Sigma^*\) and \(x \in \Sigma\), then \(\delta^*(s, w x) = \delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta^*(s, w), x\right)\mathclose{}\).












Example 4 (Unfolding the extended transition function) For the door (Example 1), the recursive rule of Definition 4 peels off the last input three times:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta^*(\text{closed}, \mathtt{lou})
&= \delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta^*(\text{closed}, \mathtt{lo}), \mathtt{u}\right)\mathclose{}
\\&= \delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta^*(\text{closed}, \mathtt{l}), \mathtt{o}\right)\mathclose{}, \mathtt{u}\right)\mathclose{}
\\&= \delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta^*(\text{closed}, \lambda), \mathtt{l}\right)\mathclose{}, \mathtt{o}\right)\mathclose{}, \mathtt{u}\right)\mathclose{}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The base case gives \(\delta^*(\text{closed}, \lambda) = \text{closed}\), and then evaluating from the inside out,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta(\text{closed}, \mathtt{l}), \mathtt{o}\right)\mathclose{}, \mathtt{u}\right)\mathclose{}
&= \delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{o}), \mathtt{u}\right)\mathclose{}
\\&= \delta(\text{locked}, \mathtt{u})
\\&= \text{closed}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(\delta^*(\text{closed}, \mathtt{lou}) = \text{closed}\).











Theorem 1 (A run ends where the extended transition function says) Let \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0)\) be a state machine (Definition 1), let \(s \in S\), and let \(r_0, \ldots, r_n\) be the run (Definition 3) of \(M\) on a string \(w = x_1 \cdots x_n\) from \(s\). Then
\[
r_n = \delta^*(s, w),
\]
where \(\delta^*\) is the extended transition function (Definition 4).










ProofProof






Proof. We show, by induction (Definition: Proof by induction) on \(k = 0, 1, \ldots, n\), that \(r_k = \delta^*(s, x_1 \cdots x_k)\), where \(x_1 \cdots x_0\) is the empty string \(\lambda\).
Base case. For \(k = 0\), \(r_0 = s = \delta^*(s, \lambda)\), by Definition 3 and the base case of Definition 4.
Inductive step. Suppose \(r_{k - 1} = \delta^*(s, x_1 \cdots x_{k - 1})\) for some \(k\) with \(1 \le k \le n\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_k
&= \delta(r_{k - 1}, x_k)
&& \text{(definition of the run)}
\\&= \delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta^*(s, x_1 \cdots x_{k - 1}), x_k\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= \delta^*(s, x_1 \cdots x_{k - 1} x_k).
&& \text{(recursive rule for } \delta^* \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
By induction, the equation holds for every \(k \le n\), and \(k = n\) gives \(r_n = \delta^*(s, w)\).











Theorem 2 (A run is the only walk that spells its string) Let \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0)\) be a state machine (Definition 1), let \(s \in S\), and let \(w = x_1 \cdots x_n\) be a string over \(\Sigma\). In the state diagram (Definition 2) of \(M\), there is exactly one walk (Definition: Walk) \(v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n\) from \(s\) in which each edge \(e_i\) is labeled \(x_i\), and its vertices \(v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_n\) are the run (Definition 3) of \(M\) on \(w\) from \(s\).










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(r_0, \ldots, r_n\) be the run of \(M\) on \(w\) from \(s\).
There is such a walk. For each \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), the state diagram has an edge \(e_i\) from \(r_{i - 1}\) to \(\delta(r_{i - 1}, x_i) = r_i\), labeled \(x_i\). So \(r_0, e_1, r_1, \ldots, e_n, r_n\) is a walk from \(r_0 = s\) whose edges are labeled \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\).
There is only one. Let \(v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n\) be any walk from \(s\) with each \(e_i\) labeled \(x_i\). We show, by induction (Definition: Proof by induction) on \(k\), that \(v_k = r_k\) for \(k = 0, \ldots, n\). For \(k = 0\), \(v_0 = s = r_0\). Suppose \(v_{k - 1} = r_{k - 1}\) for some \(k\) with \(1 \le k \le n\). The edge \(e_k\) starts at \(v_{k - 1} = r_{k - 1}\) and is labeled \(x_k\), and the only such edge in the state diagram goes to \(\delta(r_{k - 1}, x_k) = r_k\). So \(v_k = r_k\). The edge \(e_k\) is that one edge, so the edges of the two walks are the same too.






3 Deterministic finite automata







Exercise 3 (Every a needs a b) A program reads a string (Definition: String) of the symbols \(\mathtt{a}\) and \(\mathtt{b}\), and must check that every \(\mathtt{a}\) in it is immediately followed by a \(\mathtt{b}\). Which of these strings pass the check?
\[
\mathtt{abab}, \quad \mathtt{aab}, \quad \mathtt{ba}, \quad \mathtt{bbab}, \quad \lambda
\]










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. The strings \(\mathtt{abab}\) and \(\mathtt{bbab}\) pass: each of their \(\mathtt{a}\)s has a \(\mathtt{b}\) right after it. The empty string \(\lambda\) passes too, since it has no \(\mathtt{a}\) that could fail. The string \(\mathtt{aab}\) fails, because its first \(\mathtt{a}\) is followed by an \(\mathtt{a}\), and \(\mathtt{ba}\) fails, because its \(\mathtt{a}\) is followed by nothing.
To check a string from left to right, the program only has to remember one of three things about what it has read so far: that every \(\mathtt{a}\) so far has its \(\mathtt{b}\), that the last symbol was an \(\mathtt{a}\) still waiting for its \(\mathtt{b}\), or that the check has already failed.











Definition 5 (Deterministic finite automaton (DFA)) A deterministic finite automaton, or DFA, (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0, F)\) is a state machine \((S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0)\) (Definition 1) together with a subset (Definition: Subset) \(F \subseteq S\), whose elements are called accepting states. Its state diagram is the state diagram (Definition 2) of the state machine, with each accepting state drawn as a double circle.
It is deterministic because each state and input give exactly one next state, \(\delta(s, x)\).











Example 5 (A DFA for every a needing a b) Figure 2 is the state diagram of the DFA (Definition 5) \(A = (S, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)\) with \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{q_0, q_1, q_2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \(\Sigma = {\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \(F = {\mathopen{}\left\{q_0\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta(q_0, \mathtt{a}) &= q_1, & \delta(q_0, \mathtt{b}) &= q_0,
\\
\delta(q_1, \mathtt{a}) &= q_2, & \delta(q_1, \mathtt{b}) &= q_0,
\\
\delta(q_2, \mathtt{a}) &= q_2, & \delta(q_2, \mathtt{b}) &= q_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Its states are the three things to remember in Solution 3: \(q_0\) for “every \(\mathtt{a}\) so far has its \(\mathtt{b}\)”, \(q_1\) for “the last symbol was an \(\mathtt{a}\) still waiting”, and \(q_2\) for “the check has failed”.



Figure 2: The DFA \(A\), which checks that every \(\mathtt{a}\) is followed by a \(\mathtt{b}\).

















Definition 6 (Accepting a string) A DFA (Definition 5) \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0, F)\) accepts a string \(w \in \Sigma^*\) (Definition: String) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) if \(\delta^*(s_0, w) \in F\), where \(\delta^*\) is the extended transition function (Definition 4). Otherwise \(M\) rejects \(w\). By Theorem 1, \(M\) accepts \(w\) exactly when the run (Definition 3) of \(M\) on \(w\) ends at an accepting state.











Example 6 (Tracing three strings) These are the runs (Definition 3) of the DFA \(A\) of Example 5 on three strings of Exercise 3:

So \(A\) accepts (Definition 6) \(\mathtt{abab}\), which passes the check of Exercise 3, and rejects \(\mathtt{aab}\) and \(\mathtt{ba}\), which fail it. Its run on \(\lambda\) is \(q_0\) alone, so it accepts \(\lambda\).











Example 7 (The door as a DFA) Choosing the accepting states \(F = {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{open}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) makes the door (Example 1) a DFA (Definition 5), \(D\), drawn in Figure 3. It accepts (Definition 6) the strings after which the door is open. For example, it accepts \(\mathtt{o}\), \(\mathtt{luo}\) and \(\mathtt{ol}\), whose runs end at open, and rejects \(\lambda\), \(\mathtt{oc}\) and \(\mathtt{lo}\), whose runs end at closed, closed and locked.



Figure 3: The door as a DFA whose one accepting state is open.

















Definition 7 (Language) A language over an alphabet \(\Sigma\) (Definition: Alphabet) (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) is a subset (Definition: Subset) of \(\Sigma^*\), the set of all strings over \(\Sigma\) (Definition: String).











Example 8 (Languages over a and b) Let \(\Sigma = {\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}\right\}\mathclose{}}\). Each of these sets is a language (Definition 7) over \(\Sigma\):

the empty set \(\emptyset\) (Definition: Empty set), which has no strings;
\({\mathopen{}\left\{\lambda\right\}\mathclose{}}\), which has one string, the empty string;
\({\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{b}, \mathtt{ba}, \mathtt{baa}\right\}\mathclose{}}\), which has three strings;
the set of strings with an even number of symbols, which is infinite;
\(\Sigma^*\) itself.

The first two are different languages: \(\emptyset\) has no elements, and \({\mathopen{}\left\{\lambda\right\}\mathclose{}}\) has one.











Definition 8 (Language of an automaton) The language of a DFA \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0, F)\) (Definition 5) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) is the language (Definition 7)
\[
L(M) = {\mathopen{}\left\{w \in \Sigma^* : M \text{ accepts } w\right\}\mathclose{}}
\]
of the strings that \(M\) accepts (Definition 6).











Example 9 (The language of the door) The language (Definition 8) \(L(D)\) of the door DFA (Example 7) is the set of strings over \({\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{o}, \mathtt{c}, \mathtt{l}, \mathtt{u}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) after which the door is open. So \(\mathtt{o}, \mathtt{luo}, \mathtt{ol} \in L(D)\) and \(\lambda, \mathtt{oc}, \mathtt{lo} \notin L(D)\). Every string in \(L(D)\) contains an \(\mathtt{o}\), since a run starts at closed, and the only arrow into open from another state is labeled \(\mathtt{o}\). The converse fails: \(\mathtt{oc}\) contains an \(\mathtt{o}\) but is not in \(L(D)\).











Theorem 3 (The language of the a-and-b checker) The language (Definition 8) of the DFA \(A\) of Example 5 is
\[
L(A) = {\mathopen{}\left\{w \in {\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}\right\}\mathclose{}}^* : \text{every } \mathtt{a} \text{ in } w \text{ is immediately followed by a } \mathtt{b}\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Sort the strings over \({\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) into three classes:

class 0: no two \(\mathtt{a}\)s in a row, and not ending in \(\mathtt{a}\);
class 1: no two \(\mathtt{a}\)s in a row, and ending in \(\mathtt{a}\);
class 2: two \(\mathtt{a}\)s in a row somewhere.

Every string is in exactly one class. A string has every \(\mathtt{a}\) immediately followed by a \(\mathtt{b}\) exactly when it is in class 0, since an \(\mathtt{a}\) that is not followed by a \(\mathtt{b}\) is followed either by an \(\mathtt{a}\) (class 2) or by nothing (class 1). Let \(P(w)\) be the statement
\[
\text{if } w \text{ is in class } k, \text{ then } \delta^*(q_0, w) = q_k.
\]
We prove \(P(w)\) for every \(w\) by structural induction (Definition: Structural induction) on the recursive definition of strings (Definition: String).
Base case. The empty string \(\lambda\) is in class 0, and \(\delta^*(q_0, \lambda) = q_0\) (Definition 4), so \(P(\lambda)\) holds.
Inductive step. Suppose \(P(w)\), and let \(x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}\right\}\mathclose{}}\). By Definition 4, \(\delta^*(q_0, w x) = \delta\mathopen{}\left(\delta^*(q_0, w), x\right)\mathclose{}\). We split into cases on the class of \(w\).

\(w\) in class 0. By \(P(w)\), \(\delta^*(q_0, w) = q_0\). Since \(w\) does not end in \(\mathtt{a}\), adding \(x\) makes no two \(\mathtt{a}\)s in a row, so \(w x\) has none, as \(w\) has none. If \(x = \mathtt{a}\), then \(w x\) is in class 1, and \(\delta(q_0, \mathtt{a}) = q_1\). If \(x = \mathtt{b}\), then \(w x\) is in class 0, and \(\delta(q_0, \mathtt{b}) = q_0\).
\(w\) in class 1. By \(P(w)\), \(\delta^*(q_0, w) = q_1\). If \(x = \mathtt{a}\), then \(w x\) ends in two \(\mathtt{a}\)s, so it is in class 2, and \(\delta(q_1, \mathtt{a}) = q_2\). If \(x = \mathtt{b}\), then \(w x\) still has no two \(\mathtt{a}\)s in a row and ends in \(\mathtt{b}\), so it is in class 0, and \(\delta(q_1, \mathtt{b}) = q_0\).
\(w\) in class 2. By \(P(w)\), \(\delta^*(q_0, w) = q_2\). Then \(w x\) has two \(\mathtt{a}\)s in a row too, so it is in class 2, and \(\delta(q_2, x) = q_2\).

In every case \(\delta^*(q_0, w x) = q_k\) for the class \(k\) of \(w x\), so \(P(w x)\) holds. By structural induction, \(P(w)\) holds for every string \(w\).
Now let \(w\) be any string, in class \(k\). By \(P(w)\), \(\delta^*(q_0, w) = q_k\), and \(A\) accepts \(w\) (Definition 6) exactly when \(q_k \in F = {\mathopen{}\left\{q_0\right\}\mathclose{}}\), that is, when \(k = 0\). So \(A\) accepts exactly the strings of class 0, which are the strings with every \(\mathtt{a}\) immediately followed by a \(\mathtt{b}\).











Definition 9 (Dead state) A dead state of a DFA \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0, F)\) (Definition 5) is a state \(d \notin F\) with \(\delta(d, x) = d\) for every input \(x \in \Sigma\).











Example 10 (The dead state of the checker) In the DFA \(A\) of Example 5, \(q_2\) is a dead state (Definition 9): it is not accepting, and both of its arrows lead back to it. Once a run (Definition 3) reaches \(q_2\), every later state of the run is \(q_2\), so the run ends at \(q_2\) and \(A\) rejects the string. For example, \(A\) rejects every string that starts with \(\mathtt{aa}\), whatever comes after it.











Theorem 4 (Swapping the accepting states) Let \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0, F)\) be a DFA (Definition 5), and let
\[
M' = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0, S \setminus F)
\]
be the DFA with the same states, inputs, transitions and initial state, whose accepting states are the states that are not accepting in \(M\). Then \(L(M')\) (Definition 8) is the complement (Definition: Complement) \(\Sigma^* \setminus L(M)\) of \(L(M)\) in \(\Sigma^*\).










ProofProof






Proof. The extended transition function \(\delta^*\) (Definition 4) is built from \(S\), \(\Sigma\) and \(\delta\) alone, so \(M\) and \(M'\) have the same \(\delta^*\). Let \(w \in \Sigma^*\). By the language of a DFA (Definition 8) and the definition of accepting (Definition 6),
\[
\begin{aligned}
w \in L(M')
&\iff M' \text{ accepts } w
&& \text{(language of a DFA)}
\\&\iff \delta^*(s_0, w) \in S \setminus F
&& \text{(definition of accepting)}
\\&\iff \delta^*(s_0, w) \notin F
&& \text{(since } \delta^*(s_0, w) \in S \text{)}
\\&\iff M \text{ does not accept } w
&& \text{(definition of accepting)}
\\&\iff w \notin L(M).
&& \text{(language of a DFA)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(L(M')\) is the set of strings in \(\Sigma^*\) that are not in \(L(M)\).
The step from \(\delta^*(s_0, w) \in S \setminus F\) to \(\delta^*(s_0, w) \notin F\) uses that \(\delta\) is a function on all of \(S \times \Sigma\), so that \(\delta^*(s_0, w)\) is a state of \(S\) for every string \(w\). Some drawings of automata leave out a dead state (Definition 9) and the arrows into it, so that some states have no arrow for some input. Swapping the accepting states of such a drawing does not give the complement: a string whose run would enter the missing dead state is rejected before and after the swap. Put the dead state back before swapping.











Example 11 (The strings that fail the check) Swapping the accepting states of the DFA \(A\) of Example 5 gives the DFA \(A'\) of Figure 4, whose accepting states are \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). By Theorem 4 and Theorem 3, \(A'\) accepts exactly the strings in which some \(\mathtt{a}\) is not immediately followed by a \(\mathtt{b}\): those with two \(\mathtt{a}\)s in a row, and those that end in \(\mathtt{a}\). It accepts \(\mathtt{aab}\) and \(\mathtt{ba}\) and rejects \(\mathtt{abab}\) and \(\lambda\). In \(A'\), the state \(q_2\) is no longer a dead state (Definition 9), since it is accepting.



Figure 4: The DFA \(A'\), which accepts the strings that \(A\) rejects.












4 Designing a DFA







Exercise 4 (Recognizing decimal numerals) A program reads numbers written with digits and at most one decimal point. To keep the alphabet small, write \(\mathtt{d}\) for any one of the ten digits, so the alphabet (Definition: Alphabet) is \(\Sigma = {\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{d}, \mathtt{.}\right\}\mathclose{}}\). A numeral is one or more \(\mathtt{d}\)s, optionally followed by a point \(\mathtt{.}\) and one or more \(\mathtt{d}\)s. So \(\mathtt{d}\), \(\mathtt{ddd}\) and \(\mathtt{dd.d}\) are numerals, and \(\lambda\), \(\mathtt{.d}\), \(\mathtt{d.}\) and \(\mathtt{d.d.d}\) are not.
Draw the state diagram of a DFA (Definition 5) whose language (Definition 8) is the set of numerals.










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. Read from left to right, a numeral goes through four stages, and a string that is not a numeral can go wrong at any point. Give the DFA one state for each thing it has to remember:

\(n_0\): nothing has been read yet;
\(n_1\): one or more \(\mathtt{d}\)s and nothing else, which is a numeral, so \(n_1\) is accepting;
\(n_2\): one or more \(\mathtt{d}\)s and then a point, which is not a numeral yet;
\(n_3\): one or more \(\mathtt{d}\)s, a point and one or more \(\mathtt{d}\)s, which is a numeral, so \(n_3\) is accepting;
\(n_4\): the string has already gone wrong, which is a dead state (Definition 9).

A \(\mathtt{d}\) moves \(n_0\) to \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) to \(n_3\), and keeps \(n_1\) at \(n_1\) and \(n_3\) at \(n_3\). A point moves \(n_1\) to \(n_2\). A point anywhere else goes wrong: at the start, right after another point, or after the digits that follow a point. Figure 5 draws this DFA. For example, its run (Definition 3) on \(\mathtt{dd.d}\) is \(n_0, n_1, n_1, n_2, n_3\), which ends at an accepting state, and its run on \(\mathtt{d.}\) is \(n_0, n_1, n_2\), which does not.



Figure 5: A DFA whose language is the set of numerals.

















Remark 3 (Designing a DFA). Solution 4 follows a method that works for many languages (Definition 7):

Read a string from left to right, and ask what has to be remembered about the part read so far to decide the rest.
Make one state for each different thing to remember, and add a dead state (Definition 9) if a string can go wrong in a way that no later input repairs.
Make a state accepting when the part read so far, on its own, is in the language.
For each state and each input, decide which state the input leads to.
Check the DFA on short strings that should be accepted and on short strings that should be rejected.

A DFA has finitely many states, so this works only when finitely many things need to be remembered.











Example 12 (Counting 0s modulo 3) Consider the strings over \({\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) whose number of \(\mathtt{0}\)s leaves remainder 2 when it is divided by 3: 2, 5, 8, and so on. To design a DFA (Definition 5) whose language is this set of strings, it is enough to remember the remainder of the number of \(\mathtt{0}\)s read so far when it is divided by 3. So the DFA \(T\) of Figure 6 has three states, \(t_0\), \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), with \(t_k\) standing for “the remainder is \(k\)”. A \(\mathtt{1}\) does not change the count, so it keeps each state where it is. A \(\mathtt{0}\) adds one to the count, so it moves \(t_0\) to \(t_1\), \(t_1\) to \(t_2\), and \(t_2\) back to \(t_0\). The initial state is \(t_0\), since no \(\mathtt{0}\)s have been read, and \(t_2\) is the one accepting state.
The run (Definition 3) of \(T\) on \(\mathtt{1001}\) is \(t_0, t_0, t_1, t_2, t_2\), so \(T\) accepts that string, which has two \(\mathtt{0}\)s. The run on \(\mathtt{0100}\) is \(t_0, t_1, t_1, t_2, t_0\), so \(T\) rejects it, since it has three \(\mathtt{0}\)s. \(T\) rejects \(\lambda\), which has no \(\mathtt{0}\)s, and accepts \(\mathtt{00000}\), which has five. No state of \(T\) is a dead state (Definition 9), since \(\delta(t_k, \mathtt{0})\) is a different state from \(t_k\) for each \(k\).



Figure 6: The DFA \(T\), which accepts the strings whose number of \(\mathtt{0}\)s leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3.












5 State-transition tables







Exercise 5 (Reading a DFA from a table) A DFA has states \(p_0\), \(p_1\), \(p_2\) and \(p_3\), inputs \(\mathtt{0}\) and \(\mathtt{1}\), initial state \(p_0\) and one accepting state, \(p_3\). Its transitions are given by this table, in which the entry in the row of a state and the column of an input is the state that the input leads to:

Definition 10 (State-transition table) The state-transition table (Wikipedia contributors 2026g) of a DFA \(M = (S, \Sigma, \delta, s_0, F)\) (Definition 5) has one row for each state and one column for each input, and the entry in the row of \(s\) and the column of \(x\) is \(\delta(s, x)\). The initial state is marked with \(\to\) and each accepting state with \(*\).

Example 15 (What the table’s DFA accepts) Figure 7 draws the DFA \(W\) of Exercise 5. Its language (Definition 8) is the set of strings over \({\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) that contain \(\mathtt{110}\) as three symbols in a row. Each state records how much of \(\mathtt{110}\) the last symbols read have matched:

\(p_0\): none of it;
\(p_1\): the last symbol read is a \(\mathtt{1}\) that follows no other \(\mathtt{1}\), the start of \(\mathtt{110}\);
\(p_2\): the last two symbols read are \(\mathtt{11}\);
\(p_3\): \(\mathtt{110}\) has appeared, and \(p_3\) is accepting, with both of its arrows leading back to it.

A \(\mathtt{0}\) read at \(p_1\) goes back to \(p_0\), since a string ending in \(\mathtt{10}\) has matched none of \(\mathtt{110}\), while a \(\mathtt{1}\) read at \(p_2\) stays at \(p_2\), since a string ending in \(\mathtt{111}\) still ends in \(\mathtt{11}\). So \(W\) accepts \(\mathtt{0101100}\), as in Solution 5, and rejects \(\mathtt{101011}\), which does not contain \(\mathtt{110}\).



Figure 7: The DFA \(W\), which accepts the strings that contain \(\mathtt{110}\).

















Remark 4 (A table is like a labeled adjacency list). The row of a state \(s\) in a state-transition table (Definition 10) lists the ends of the edges that start at \(s\) in the state diagram (Definition 2), one for each input, like the list of \(s\) in an adjacency list (Definition: Adjacency list) of a directed graph. The table also says which edge has which label, which an adjacency list does not. Every row has exactly \({\mathopen{}\left|\Sigma\right|\mathclose{}}\) entries, as Remark 2 says.
The likeness stops when two inputs lead from \(s\) to the same state. Then the state diagram has parallel edges (Definition: Parallel edges), for which Definition: Adjacency list does not define an adjacency list, and the row of \(s\) names that state more than once, as the row of \(q_2\) in Example 13 does.






6 Automata in Racket







Exercise 6 (One step in Racket) In Racket, the table of the DFA \(A\) (Example 13) can be stored as a list with one list for each state, which starts with the state and goes on with a list (x t) for each input x, where t is the state that x leads to:
(define pairs-table
  '((q0 (#\a q1) (#\b q0))
    (q1 (#\a q2) (#\b q0))
    (q2 (#\a q2) (#\b q2))))

(define (step table s x)
  (second (assoc x (rest (assoc s table)))))
Here #\a is the character a, and assoc is as in Exercise: Looking up a vertex. What does (step pairs-table 'q1 #\b) return?










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. (assoc 'q1 pairs-table) is the row '(q1 (#\a q2) (#\b q0)), and its rest is '((#\a q2) (#\b q0)). (assoc #\b ...) finds '(#\b q0) in that list, and its second element is 'q0. So (step pairs-table 'q1 #\b) returns 'q0, which is \(\delta(q_1, \mathtt{b})\) (Example 5).











Example 16 (Running a DFA in Racket) With step as in Exercise 6, run returns the run (Definition 3) from a state s on a list xs of inputs, and accepts? says whether a DFA accepts (Definition 6) the string whose inputs are the list xs:
(define (run table s xs)
  (if (empty? xs)
      (list s)
      (cons s (run table (step table s (first xs)) (rest xs)))))

(define (accepts? table start accepting xs)
  (if (member (last (run table start xs)) accepting)
      #t
      #f))

(last L) is the last element of the list L.
(member x L) is #f if x is not in the list L, and a list that is not #f if it is.
(string->list w) is the list of the characters of the string w.

(run pairs-table 'q0 (string->list "abab")) returns '(q0 q1 q0 q1 q0), and (run pairs-table 'q0 (string->list "aab")) returns '(q0 q1 q2 q2), the runs of Example 6. (accepts? pairs-table 'q0 '(q0) (string->list "abab")) returns #t, (accepts? pairs-table 'q0 '(q0) (string->list "ba")) returns #f, and (accepts? pairs-table 'q0 '(q0) (string->list "")) returns #t, since \(A\) accepts \(\lambda\). Let \(w\) be the string whose symbols are the elements of xs, in order. run reads the first symbol of \(w\) first, as Definition 3 does, so by Theorem 1 the last state of (run table s xs) is \(\delta^*(s, w)\).











Example 17 (Checking numerals in Racket) In the form of Exercise 6, the DFA of Solution 4 is the table below, with the symbol 'digit for the input \(\mathtt{d}\) and the symbol 'point for the input \(\mathtt{.}\):
(define numeral-table
  '((n0 (digit n1) (point n4))
    (n1 (digit n1) (point n2))
    (n2 (digit n3) (point n4))
    (n3 (digit n3) (point n4))
    (n4 (digit n4) (point n4))))
To check real text, classify turns each character into an input, and numeral? runs the DFA with accepts? from Example 16:
(define (classify c)
  (cond [(char<=? #\0 c #\9) 'digit]
        [(char=? c #\.) 'point]
        [else 'other]))

(define (numeral? text)
  (let ([xs (map classify (string->list text))])
    (and (not (member 'other xs))
         (accepts? numeral-table 'n0 '(n1 n3) xs))))

(char<=? #\0 c #\9) is true when the character c is one of the ten digits 0 to 9.
(cond [test1 a] [test2 b] [else c]) returns a if test1 is true, otherwise b if test2 is true, and otherwise c.
(map f L) applies f to each element of the list L.
(and p q) is #f if p is #f, and is q otherwise.

A character that is neither a digit nor a point is classified 'other, which is not an input of the DFA, so numeral? returns #f for any text that contains one, without running the DFA. Then
(map numeral? '("3.14" "2026" "7." ".5" "1.2.3" "d.d" "-3" "\u00BD"))
returns '(#t #t #f #f #f #f #f #f): "3.14" and "2026" are numerals, and the others are not. The letter d in "d.d" is classified 'other, not 'digit, and so is the one character of "\u00BD", the fraction one half, even though Racket’s char-numeric? counts it as numeric.
