title: Contrapositive and Contradiction
text:
NoteSource





Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Contrapositive Proof” and “Proof by Contradiction”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. These come from those notes:

the definition of congruence modulo \(n\), and the point that it is not the mod operator;
the human and mammal illustration of a contrapositive;
the example of a product not divisible by \(5\);
the truth table showing why a proof by contradiction works;
the outlines of a proof by contrapositive, a proof by contradiction, and a proof of a conditional by contradiction;
the definition and examples of a prime number, and the fact that every integer above one has a prime divisor;
the statement that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational (the proof here is different);
Euclid’s proof that there are infinitely many primes.

The exercises are new.
The definitions of the contrapositive, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, and rational and irrational numbers, their examples of a proof by contradiction and of rational and irrational numbers, and the theorem that a conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, are included from the mathematics prerequisites notes, so they read the same in both places.




1 Congruence modulo \(n\)







Exercise 1 (Differences divisible by five) For each integer \(a\) in the list \(23\), \(38\), \(50\), \(-7\), compute \(a - 8\), and decide whether \(5 \mid (a - 8)\) (Definition: Divides).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 

\(23 - 8 = 15 = 5 \cdot 3\), so \(5 \mid (23 - 8)\).
\(38 - 8 = 30 = 5 \cdot 6\), so \(5 \mid (38 - 8)\).
\(50 - 8 = 42\). Since \(5 \cdot 8 = 40 < 42 < 45 = 5 \cdot 9\), no integer \(c\) has \(5c = 42\), so \(5 \nmid (50 - 8)\).
\(-7 - 8 = -15 = 5 \cdot(-3)\), so \(5 \mid (-7 - 8)\).












Definition 1 (Congruence modulo \(n\)) Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers (Definition: Integers), and let \(n\) be a positive integer. We say that \(a\) is congruent to \(b\) modulo \(n\), written \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\), if \(n \mid (a - b)\) (Definition: Divides) (Wikipedia contributors 2026d). When \(a\) is not congruent to \(b\) modulo \(n\), we write \(a \not\equiv b \pmod{n}\).











Example 1 (Congruences)  

By Solution 1, \(23 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\), \(38 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\) and \(-7 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\), but \(50 \not\equiv 8 \pmod{5}\).
A 24-hour clock that reads \(19\) shows the same hour as a 12-hour clock that reads \(7\), and \(19 \equiv 7 \pmod{12}\), because \(19 - 7 = 12 = 12 \cdot 1\).












Remark 1 (Two meanings of \(\equiv\), and the mod operator). The symbol \(\equiv\) also means logical equivalence (Definition: Logical equivalence). The “\((\operatorname{mod} n)\)” after it says which meaning is in use: \(23 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\) is a statement about two integers, and \(P \equiv Q\) is a statement about two propositions.
Congruence is related to the mod operator of a programming language, but it is not the same thing. In Racket, (modulo 23 5) is the number \(3\), while \(23 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\) is a proposition (Definition: Proposition (statement)), which is true or false.






2 Proof by contrapositive







Exercise 2 (An odd sum) Let \(x\) and \(y\) be integers. Prove: if \(x + y\) is odd, then \(x \ne y\).
First try a direct proof (Definition: Direct proof), starting from “Suppose \(x + y\) is odd.” Then try starting from “Suppose \(x = y\).”










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. The direct start gives \(x + y = 2k + 1\) for some integer \(k\) (Definition: Odd integer), which says little about whether \(x\) and \(y\) are equal.
The second start goes further. Suppose \(x = y\). Then \(x + y = x + x = 2x\), and \(x\) is an integer, so \(x + y\) is even (Definition: Even integer). No integer is both even and odd (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(x + y\) is not odd.
That proves “if \(x = y\), then \(x + y\) is not odd”. Why proving this proposition proves the one we were asked about is the subject of this section.











Definition 2 (Contrapositive) The contrapositive (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) of the proposition “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” is the proposition “if \(\neg Q\), then \(\neg P\)”.











Example 2 (Contrapositives)  

The contrapositive of “if \(x\) is a human, then \(x\) is a mammal” is “if \(x\) is not a mammal, then \(x\) is not a human”.
In Exercise 2, \(P\) is “\(x + y\) is odd” and \(Q\) is “\(x \ne y\)”. The negation of \(Q\) is “\(x = y\)” (Definition: Not), so the contrapositive is “if \(x = y\), then \(x + y\) is not odd”, which is what Solution 2 proved.












Theorem 1 (A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive) For any propositions \(P\) and \(Q\),
\[
(P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv (\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P).
\]










ProofProof






Proof. By the definition of implies, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false exactly when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false. By the same definition, \(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\) is false exactly when \(\neg Q\) is true and \(\neg P\) is false, that is, exactly when \(Q\) is false and \(P\) is true. So the two propositions are false in the same row of a truth table and true in the other three, which is Definition: Logically equivalent.











Example 3 (A proposition and its contrapositive) Take “if today is Saturday, then today is a weekend day”, which is true.
Its contrapositive is “if today is not a weekend day, then today is not Saturday”. It is also true, as Theorem 1 says it must be: Monday through Friday are the days that are not weekend days, and none of them is Saturday.











Definition 3 (Proof by contrapositive) A proof by contrapositive (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) of a proposition “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” is a direct proof of its contrapositive, “if \(\neg Q\), then \(\neg P\)”: it assumes that \(Q\) is false and reaches the conclusion that \(P\) is false. By Theorem 1, proving the contrapositive proves the original proposition.











Example 4 (A product not divisible by \(5\)) Claim: let \(x\) and \(y\) be integers. If \(5 \nmid xy\), then \(5 \nmid x\) and \(5 \nmid y\).
A direct proof would start from \(5 \nmid xy\), which says only that \(xy\) is not \(5\) times an integer, and gives no equation to work with. By De Morgan’s laws (Theorem: De Morgan’s laws), the negation of “\(5 \nmid x\) and \(5 \nmid y\)” is “\(5 \mid x\) or \(5 \mid y\)”, so the contrapositive (Definition 2) is “if \(5 \mid x\) or \(5 \mid y\), then \(5 \mid xy\)”. We prove it by cases (Definition: Proof by cases).
Case 1: \(5 \mid x\). Then \(x = 5c\) for some integer \(c\) (Definition: Divides), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
xy
&= (5c) y
&& \text{(substitute } x = 5c \text{)}
\\&= 5 (c y),
&& \text{(regroup the product)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(c y\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(5 \mid xy\).
Case 2: \(5 \mid y\). Then \(y = 5d\) for some integer \(d\), so \(xy = x (5d) = 5 (x d)\), and \(x d\) is an integer, so \(5 \mid xy\).
In both cases \(5 \mid xy\), which proves the contrapositive and so the claim (Theorem 1). For example, \(x = 3\) and \(y = 7\) give \(xy = 21\), which \(5\) does not divide, and indeed \(5\) divides neither \(3\) nor \(7\).











Remark 2 (The shape of a proof by contrapositive). A proof by contrapositive (Definition 3) of “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” has this shape:

Suppose \(\neg Q\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(\neg P\).

Use it when \(\neg Q\) gives you more to work with than \(P\) does. In Exercise 2, \(\neg Q\) was the equation \(x = y\), while \(P\) said only that \(x + y\) is odd.











Exercise 3 (A square not divisible by three) Let \(n\) be an integer. Prove: if \(3 \nmid n^2\), then \(3 \nmid n\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. We prove the contrapositive (Definition 3): if \(3 \mid n\), then \(3 \mid n^2\).
Suppose \(3 \mid n\). Then \(n = 3c\) for some integer \(c\) (Definition: Divides), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
n^2
&= (3c)^2
&& \text{(substitute } n = 3c \text{)}
\\&= 9 c^2
&& \text{(square each factor)}
\\&= 3 (3 c^2),
&& \text{(write } 9 = 3 \cdot 3 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(3 c^2\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(3 \mid n^2\). By Theorem 1, this proves the original proposition.






3 Proof by contradiction







Exercise 4 (No solution in integers) Show that there are no integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 9n = 1\).
Hint: suppose there were. What would \(6m + 9n = 1\) say about \(3\) and \(1\)?










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. Suppose there are integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 9n = 1\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
1
&= 6m + 9n
&& \text{(the assumption, read from right to left)}
\\&= 3 (2m + 3n),
&& \text{(distributive law, read from right to left)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(2m + 3n\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(3 \mid 1\) (Definition: Divides).
But \(3 \nmid 1\): since \(3 \cdot 0 = 0 < 1 < 3 = 3 \cdot 1\), no integer \(c\) has \(3c = 1\). So \(3 \mid 1\) and \(3 \nmid 1\), which is impossible. The assumption must be false, so there are no integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 9n = 1\).











Definition 4 (Proof by contradiction) A proof by contradiction (Wikipedia contributors 2026f) of a proposition \(P\) assumes that \(P\) is false, and derives from that assumption a proposition that is known to be false.











Example 5 (No integer is both even and odd) Suppose, for contradiction, that some integer \(n\) is both even and odd (definition). Then \(n = 2j\) and \(n = 2k + 1\) for some integers \(j\) and \(k\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
2j &= 2k + 1
&& \text{(both equal } n \text{)}
\\
2j - 2k &= 1
&& \text{(subtract } 2k \text{ from both sides)}
\\
2(j - k) &= 1
&& \text{(distributive law)}
\\
j - k &= \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(divide both sides by } 2 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The third line uses the distributive law. But \(j - k\) is an integer, and \(\frac{1}{2}\) is not, so the last line is false. So no integer is both even and odd. For example, \(6 = 2 \cdot 3\) is even, and \(6 = 2k + 1\) would need \(k = 2.5\), which is not an integer.











Theorem 2 (Why a proof by contradiction works) For propositions \(P\) and \(C\),
\[
P \equiv \mathopen{}\left(\neg P \Rightarrow (C \land \neg C)\right)\mathclose{}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. \(C \land \neg C\) is false in every row (Definition: And, Definition: Not), so it is a contradiction (Definition: Contradiction). So, by Definition: Implies, \(\neg P \Rightarrow (C \land \neg C)\) is true exactly in the rows where \(\neg P\) is false, which are the rows where \(P\) is true:

The first and last columns match in every row (Definition: Logical equivalence).











Example 6 (The six and nine proof, read through the theorem) In Solution 4, \(P\) is “there are no integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 9n = 1\)”, and \(C\) is “\(3 \mid 1\)”. The solution assumed \(\neg P\), that such integers exist, and derived both \(C\) and \(\neg C\). That proves \(\neg P \Rightarrow (C \land \neg C)\), so, by Theorem 2, it proves \(P\).











Remark 3 (The shape of a proof by contradiction). A proof by contradiction (Definition 4) of a proposition \(P\) has this shape:

Suppose \(\neg P\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(C\) and \(\neg C\).

Two things differ from a proof by contrapositive (Remark 2). \(P\) need not be a conditional. And the proof does not know \(C\) in advance: any proposition \(C\) for which the argument derives both \(C\) and \(\neg C\) will do.











Remark 4 (Proving a conditional by contradiction). To prove “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” by contradiction, suppose its negation, which is “\(P\) and \(\neg Q\)” (Theorem: Negating a conditional):

Suppose \(P\) and \(\neg Q\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(C\) and \(\neg C\).

A proof by contrapositive (Remark 2) assumes only \(\neg Q\), and has the fixed goal \(\neg P\). A proof by contradiction assumes both \(P\) and \(\neg Q\), and any contradiction will do.











Example 7 (A number plus its reciprocal) Claim: let \(x\) be a real number. If \(x > 0\), then \(x + \frac{1}{x} \ge 2\).
Suppose, for contradiction, that \(x > 0\) and \(x + \frac{1}{x} < 2\). Since \(x > 0\), multiplying both sides by \(x\) keeps the inequality, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2 + 1
&< 2x
&& \text{(multiply both sides by } x > 0 \text{)}
\\
x^2 - 2x + 1
&< 0
&& \text{(subtract } 2x \text{ from both sides)}
\\
(x - 1)^2
&< 0.
&& \text{(square of a difference)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(C\) be “\((x - 1)^2 \ge 0\)”. \(C\) is true, because a square of a real number is never negative, and the last line says \(\neg C\). That is a contradiction, so the claim holds. The proof used \(x > 0\) in the first step, and the contradiction it reached is not \(x \le 0\). For example, \(x = 4\) gives \(4 + \frac{1}{4} = 4.25 \ge 2\).











Exercise 5 (Squares one apart) Prove that there are no positive integers \(x\) and \(y\) with \(x^2 - y^2 = 1\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(x\) and \(y\) are positive integers with \(x^2 - y^2 = 1\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
1
&= x^2 - y^2
&& \text{(the assumption, read from right to left)}
\\&= (x - y)(x + y).
&& \text{(difference of squares)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(x \ge 1\) and \(y \ge 1\), \(x + y \ge 2\). Dividing both sides by \(x + y\) gives \(x - y = \frac{1}{x + y}\), and \(0 < \frac{1}{x + y} \le \frac{1}{2}\), so \(x - y\) is strictly between \(0\) and \(1\) and is not an integer. But \(x - y\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof). That is a contradiction, so there are no such \(x\) and \(y\).






4 Irrational numbers







Exercise 6 (Bounds on a fraction for \(\sqrt{2}\)) Suppose \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers with \(\frac{a}{b} = \sqrt{2}\). Use \(1 < 2 < 4\) to show that \(b < a < 2b\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. Square roots keep the order of positive numbers, so \(1 < 2 < 4\) gives \(1 < \sqrt{2} < 2\), that is, \(1 < \frac{a}{b} < 2\). Multiplying each part by \(b\), which is positive, keeps the order, and gives \(b < a < 2b\).











Definition 5 (Rational numbers) A rational number (Wikipedia contributors 2026h) is a number that can be written as a fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are integers (Definition: Integers) and \(b \ne 0\). The set of rational numbers is written \(\mathbb{Q}\):
\[\mathbb{Q} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left\{\frac{a}{b} : a \in \mathbb{Z},\ b \in \mathbb{Z},\ b \ne 0\right\}\mathclose{}\]











Example 8 (Rational numbers)  

\(\frac{3}{4}\) is rational, with \(a = 3\) and \(b = 4\).
\(0.75\) is rational, because \(0.75 = \frac{3}{4}\).
Every integer is rational: for example, \(-5 = \frac{-5}{1}\).
\(0.333\ldots\), with the \(3\)s repeating forever, is rational, because \(0.333\ldots = \frac{1}{3}\).












Definition 6 (Irrational numbers) An irrational number (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) is a real number (Definition: Real numbers) that is not rational (Definition 5).











Example 9 (Irrational numbers)  

\(\sqrt{2} = 1.41421\ldots\), the square root of \(2\), is irrational: no fraction of integers \(\frac{a}{b}\) squares to \(2\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026i).
\(\pi = 3.14159\ldots\) is irrational (Wikipedia contributors 2026g).
\(1.5\) is not irrational, because \(1.5 = \frac{3}{2}\) is rational.












Remark 5 (Smallest elements). These notes use one more fact about the integers without proving it (Wikipedia contributors 2026j):

every set of positive integers that has at least one element has a smallest element.

For example, the set of positive integers \(b\) for which \(\frac{3}{4} b\) is an integer has the elements \(4\), \(8\), \(12\) and so on, and its smallest element is \(4\).











Theorem 3 (\(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational) The square root of \(2\) is irrational (Definition 6) (Wikipedia contributors 2026i).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational (Definition 5). Then \(\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}\) for some integers \(a\) and \(b\) with \(b \ne 0\). Since \(\sqrt{2} > 0\), we can take \(a\) and \(b\) positive (if \(b < 0\), replace \(a\) and \(b\) with \(-a\) and \(-b\)). So the set of positive integers \(b\) for which \(\sqrt{2}\, b\) is an integer has an element, and by Remark 5 it has a smallest element. Let \(b\) be that smallest element, and let \(a = \sqrt{2}\, b\), a positive integer.
By Solution 6, \(b < a < 2b\), so \(b' = a - b\) is an integer with \(0 < b' < b\). Let \(a' = 2b - a\), also an integer. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{2}\, b'
&= \sqrt{2}\, (a - b)
&& \text{(definition of } b' \text{)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}\, a - \sqrt{2}\, b
&& \text{(distributive law)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}\, \sqrt{2}\, b - a
&& \text{(substitute } a = \sqrt{2}\, b \text{ in the first term, and } \sqrt{2}\, b = a \text{ in the second)}
\\&= 2b - a
&& \text{(} \sqrt{2}\, \sqrt{2} = 2 \text{)}
\\&= a'.
&& \text{(definition of } a' \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(b'\) is a positive integer for which \(\sqrt{2}\, b'\) is an integer, and \(b' < b\). That contradicts the choice of \(b\) as the smallest such integer. So \(\sqrt{2}\) is not rational.











Example 10 (The step in the proof, on a fraction near \(\sqrt{2}\)) The proof of Theorem 3 turns a fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\) into \(\frac{2b - a}{a - b}\). Applied to \(\frac{7}{5} = 1.4\), whose square is \(\frac{49}{25} = 1.96\), it gives \(\frac{10 - 7}{7 - 5} = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5\), whose square is \(\frac{9}{4} = 2.25\). Neither fraction is exactly \(\sqrt{2}\), and the step moved from denominator \(5\) to the smaller denominator \(2\). If some fraction were exactly \(\sqrt{2}\), the step would give another fraction exactly equal to \(\sqrt{2}\), with a smaller positive denominator, and a smallest positive denominator could not exist.






5 Infinitely many primes







Exercise 7 (Which are prime?) Which of \(51\), \(53\) and \(57\) have no positive divisors other than \(1\) and themselves? Hint: try dividing by \(2\), \(3\), \(5\) and \(7\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 7. 

\(51 = 3 \cdot 17\), so \(3\) divides \(51\) (Definition: Divides).
\(57 = 3 \cdot 19\), so \(3\) divides \(57\).
\(53\) is not divisible by \(2\), \(3\), \(5\) or \(7\), because it lies strictly between two multiples of each: \(2 \cdot 26 = 52 < 53 < 54 = 2 \cdot 27\), \(3 \cdot 17 = 51 < 53 < 54 = 3 \cdot 18\), \(5 \cdot 10 = 50 < 53 < 55 = 5 \cdot 11\), and \(7 \cdot 7 = 49 < 53 < 56 = 7 \cdot 8\). A divisor \(d\) of \(53\) with \(1 < d < 53\) would pair with \(\frac{53}{d}\), and one of the two would be at most \(7\), because \(8 \cdot 8 = 64 > 53\). It would be one of \(2, \ldots, 7\), and \(4\) or \(6\) would make \(2\) a divisor too, since \(2\) divides both (Exercise: Divisors of divisors). So \(53\) has no positive divisors other than \(1\) and \(53\).












Definition 7 (Prime number) An integer \(n \ge 2\) is prime if its only positive divisors (Definition: Divides) are \(1\) and \(n\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026e).











Example 11 (Prime and not prime)  

\(2\), \(3\), \(5\), \(7\), \(11\) and \(13\) are prime.
\(9\) is not prime, because \(3 \mid 9\), and \(3\) is neither \(1\) nor \(9\).
\(1\) is not prime, because Definition 7 applies only to integers \(n \ge 2\).












Remark 6 (Every integer above one has a prime divisor). These notes use one more fact without proving it:

every integer \(n \ge 2\) is divisible by at least one prime (Definition 7).

For example, \(91\) is divisible by the primes \(7\) and \(13\), since \(91 = 7 \cdot 13\).











Theorem 4 (There are infinitely many primes) There are infinitely many prime numbers (Definition 7) (Wikipedia contributors 2026b).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, and list them all as \(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k\). The list is not empty, because \(2\) is prime. Let
\[
N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1.
\]
Each \(p_i \ge 2\), so \(N \ge 3\), and by Remark 6 some prime \(p\) divides \(N\): \(N = p s\) for some integer \(s\). The list holds every prime, so \(p\) is one of \(p_1, \ldots, p_k\), and so \(p\) also divides their product: \(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k = p t\) for some integer \(t\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
1
&= N - p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k
&& \text{(definition of } N \text{)}
\\&= p s - p t
&& \text{(substitute both products)}
\\&= p (s - t).
&& \text{(distributive law, read from right to left)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(s - t\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), \(p \mid 1\). But \(p \ge 2\), and \(p \cdot 0 = 0 < 1 < p = p \cdot 1\), so no integer \(c\) has \(p c = 1\), and \(p \nmid 1\). That is a contradiction, so there are infinitely many primes.











Example 12 (The number \(N\) in the proof) The proof of Theorem 4 does not claim that \(N\) is prime.

From the list \(2, 3, 5\), \(N = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 + 1 = 31\), which is prime.
From the list \(2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13\), \(N = 30030 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509\), which is not prime. Its prime divisors \(59\) and \(509\) are not in the list, which is what the proof needs: every list of primes misses some prime.







6 Choosing a method







Remark 7 (Which method to try). 

Try a direct proof (Definition: Direct proof) first.
Try the contrapositive (Definition 3) when \(\neg Q\) is the easier assumption (Remark 2).
Try contradiction (Definition 4) when the proposition says that something does not exist or is not true, as in “no integers satisfy”, “is irrational” or “infinitely many”: its negation hands you an object to work with.

Definition 1 (Logical equivalence) Two propositions \(A\) and \(B\), each built from some of the propositions \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\), are logically equivalent, written \(A \equiv B\), if they have the same truth value in every row of a truth table (Definition: Truth table), that is, for every combination of truth values of \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\).











Example 1 (An equivalence) By Exercise 1, \(P \lor (P \land Q) \equiv P\) (Definition 1): the truth table of \(P \lor (P \land Q)\) has the same column as \(P\), in a table with columns for both \(P\) and \(Q\).











Remark 1 (Notation for logical equivalence). \(A \equiv B\) (Definition 1) is a claim about \(A\) and \(B\), not a new proposition built from them with a logical connective (Definition: Logical connective). Some books write \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) or \(A \iff B\) for it instead, which is easy to confuse with the biconditional (Definition: If and only if); these notes use \(\equiv\).
Logical equivalence can be chained: if \(A \equiv B\) and \(B \equiv C\), then \(A \equiv C\), since in each row \(A\) has the value of \(B\), which has the value of \(C\).











Exercise 2 (Not both) A continuous integration server runs two test suites. Let \(P\) be “the unit tests pass” and \(Q\) be “the integration tests pass”.
Is “it is not the case that both suites pass”, \(\neg (P \land Q)\), logically equivalent (Definition 1) to “neither suite passes”, \(\neg P \land \neg Q\)?










SolutionSolution

Theorem 1 (Equivalence is a tautological biconditional) For propositions \(A\) and \(B\), \(A \equiv B\) (Definition 1) exactly when \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) is a tautology (Definition 2).










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition: If and only if, \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) is true in a row of the truth table exactly when \(A\) and \(B\) have the same truth value in that row. So \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) is true in every row exactly when \(A\) and \(B\) have the same truth value in every row, which is what \(A \equiv B\) means.











Example 4 (An equivalence as a tautology) Since \(P \lor (P \land Q) \equiv P\) (Example 1), Theorem 1 says that \((P \lor (P \land Q)) \Leftrightarrow P\) is a tautology.

Example 5 (Distributing “and”) For an integer \(x\), “\(x\) is even, and \(x > 0\) or \(x < 0\)” is logically equivalent, by law 1 of Theorem 2, to “\(x\) is even and \(x > 0\), or \(x\) is even and \(x < 0\)”.











Remark 3 (Checking an equivalence in Racket). A truth table is a loop over every combination of truth values, so a program can check an equivalence. In Racket, for*/and runs its body for every combination of p and q, and returns #f as soon as the body returns #f, and #t if it never does:
(for*/and ([p '(#t #f)]
           [q '(#t #f)])
  (equal? (or p (and p q)) p))
This returns #t, as Exercise 1 found. Replacing the body with (equal? (not (and p q)) (and (not p) (not q))) returns #f, as Exercise 2 found.






2 Negation







Exercise 4 (When is the door locked?) A door opens when the badge is valid, the PIN is correct, and it is a weekday. Let \(B\) be “the badge is valid”, \(N\) be “the PIN is correct” and \(W\) be “it is a weekday”, so the door stays locked when \(\neg (B \land N \land W)\) is true.
Describe when the door stays locked with a sentence that puts “not” only in front of \(B\), \(N\) or \(W\), never in front of a compound proposition.










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. The door stays locked when the badge is not valid, the PIN is not correct, or it is not a weekday: \(\neg B \lor \neg N \lor \neg W\). \(B \land N \land W\) is false exactly when at least one of \(B\), \(N\) and \(W\) is false.











Theorem 3 (Double negation) For a proposition \(P\), \(\neg \neg P \equiv P\) (Definition 1).

Example 6 (Not unreadable) “It is not the case that the file is not readable” means “the file is readable” (Theorem 3).











Theorem 4 (Replacing a part by an equivalent part) If \(A \equiv B\) (Definition 1), then replacing \(A\) by \(B\) inside a larger proposition gives a proposition logically equivalent to the larger one. In particular, \(\neg A \equiv \neg B\).










ProofProof






Proof. The truth value of the larger proposition in a row of its truth table depends on the truth value of \(A\) in that row, not on how \(A\) is written. \(A\) and \(B\) have the same truth value in every row, so the two larger propositions do too.











Example 7 (Replacing a part) Since \(P \lor (P \land Q) \equiv P\) (Example 1), Theorem 4 gives \(R \land (P \lor (P \land Q)) \equiv R \land P\) and \(\neg (P \lor (P \land Q)) \equiv \neg P\).











Theorem 5 (De Morgan’s laws) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026):

\(\neg (P \land Q) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg Q\);
\(\neg (P \lor Q) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q\).











ProofProof

Law 2 follows from law 1. Law 1 holds for any two propositions, so it holds for \(\neg P\) and \(\neg Q\): \[
\neg (\neg P \land \neg Q) \equiv \neg \neg P \lor \neg \neg Q.
\] By double negation (Theorem 3) and Theorem 4, the right side is logically equivalent to \(P \lor Q\), so \[
\neg (\neg P \land \neg Q) \equiv P \lor Q.
\] Negating both sides (Theorem 4) gives \[
\neg \neg (\neg P \land \neg Q) \equiv \neg (P \lor Q),
\] and by double negation the left side is logically equivalent to \(\neg P \land \neg Q\). So \(\neg (P \lor Q) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q\).











Example 8 (Neither coordinate positive) For real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), by law 2 of Theorem 5, “not (\(x > 0\) or \(y > 0\))” is logically equivalent to “\(x \le 0\) and \(y \le 0\)”.











Exercise 5 (A broken deployment rule) A team’s rule is “if the tests pass, then the build is deployed”. Let \(P\) be “the tests pass” and \(Q\) be “the build is deployed”. The rule is broken on the days when \(\neg (P \Rightarrow Q)\) is true.
Write \(\neg (P \Rightarrow Q)\) without \(\Rightarrow\), and in English.










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. The rule is broken on a day when the tests pass and the build is not deployed: \(P \land \neg Q\). On a day when the tests fail, the rule is not broken, whether or not the build is deployed.
“If the tests pass, then the build is not deployed”, \(P \Rightarrow \neg Q\), is not the negation: on a day when the tests fail, it is true, and so is the rule.











Theorem 6 (Negating a conditional) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), \(\neg (P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv P \land \neg Q\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition: Implies, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false exactly when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false, so \(\neg (P \Rightarrow Q)\) is true exactly in that row. \(P \land \neg Q\) is true exactly when \(P\) is true and \(\neg Q\) is true, which is the same row.











Example 9 (When a search claim fails) The negation of “if the list is sorted, then binary search finds the key” is “the list is sorted and binary search does not find the key” (Theorem 6).











Corollary 1 (A conditional without the arrow) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), \(P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg P \lor Q\).










ProofProof






Proof. By double negation (Theorem 3), \(P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg \neg (P \Rightarrow Q)\). By Theorem 6 and Theorem 4, \(\neg \neg (P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv \neg (P \land \neg Q)\). By De Morgan’s law 1 (Theorem 5), \(\neg (P \land \neg Q) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg \neg Q\), and by double negation again, that is logically equivalent to \(\neg P \lor Q\).











Example 10 (A rule as an “or”) By Corollary 1, “if the tests pass, then the build is deployed” is logically equivalent to “the tests fail or the build is deployed”.






3 Negating quantified propositions







Exercise 6 (Not every test passes) Let \(T\) be the set of tests in a test suite, and let \(P(t)\) be “test \(t\) passes”. The report “every test passes” is \(\forall t \in T, P(t)\).
Write the negation of this report in English and in symbols, without putting \(\neg\) in front of a quantifier.










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. “Some test fails”: \(\exists t \in T, \neg P(t)\). “Every test passes” is false exactly when at least one test does not pass.
“Every test fails”, \(\forall t \in T, \neg P(t)\), is not the negation: when some tests pass and some fail, both it and “every test passes” are false.











Theorem 7 (Negating a quantifier) For a set \(S\) and a predicate \(P(x)\) (Definition: Predicate) whose domain (Definition: Domain (domain of discourse, universe of discourse)) is \(S\):

\(\neg (\forall x \in S, P(x))\) and \(\exists x \in S, \neg P(x)\) have the same truth value;
\(\neg (\exists x \in S, P(x))\) and \(\forall x \in S, \neg P(x)\) have the same truth value.











ProofProof






Proof. 

By Definition: Universal quantifier, \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) is false exactly when \(P(x)\) is false for at least one \(x\) in \(S\), which by Definition: Existential quantifier is when \(\exists x \in S, \neg P(x)\) is true.
By Definition: Existential quantifier, \(\exists x \in S, P(x)\) is false exactly when \(P(x)\) is false for every \(x\) in \(S\), which by Definition: Universal quantifier is when \(\forall x \in S, \neg P(x)\) is true.












Example 11 (No natural square root of 2) By part 2 of Theorem 7, \(\neg (\exists n \in \mathbb{N}, n^2 = 2)\) has the same truth value as \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, n^2 \ne 2\).











Remark 4 (De Morgan’s laws for quantifiers). Theorem 7 is often written \(\neg \forall x, P(x) \equiv \exists x, \neg P(x)\) and \(\neg \exists x, P(x) \equiv \forall x, \neg P(x)\). These notes say “has the same truth value” instead, because \(P(x)\) is a predicate, not a proposition, so Definition 1, which compares truth tables, does not apply.
On a finite set \(S = \{a, b\}\), \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) has the same truth value as \(P(a) \land P(b)\), and \(\exists x \in S, P(x)\) has the same truth value as \(P(a) \lor P(b)\), so Theorem 7 is De Morgan’s laws (Theorem 5) applied to \(P(a)\) and \(P(b)\).
Racket shows the same pattern on a list: (not (andmap even? (list 2 4 5))) and (ormap odd? (list 2 4 5)) both return #t.











Remark 5 (Pushing a negation inward). To negate a proposition built with \(\neg\), \(\land\), \(\lor\), \(\Rightarrow\) and quantifiers, move the \(\neg\) inward one step at a time:

across a quantifier, with Theorem 7, which swaps \(\forall\) and \(\exists\);
across \(\land\) or \(\lor\), with De Morgan’s laws (Theorem 5);
across \(\Rightarrow\), with Theorem 6;
across another \(\neg\), with double negation (Theorem 3).

Stop when every \(\neg\) sits in front of a proposition with no connective or quantifier inside it. The result is easier to read and to check than a \(\neg\) in front of the whole proposition.











Exercise 7 (Completing a palindrome) Let \(W\) be the set of words made of the letters a and b, including the empty word, and write \(s t\) for word \(s\) followed by word \(t\). A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as abba.
Write the negation of \[
\forall s \in W,\ \exists t \in W,\ s t \text{ is a palindrome}
\] without putting \(\neg\) in front of a quantifier.










SolutionSolution






Solution 7. Apply Theorem 7 twice, from the outside in. First, the negation has the truth value of \[
\exists s \in W,\ \neg (\exists t \in W,\ s t \text{ is a palindrome}).
\] For each word \(s\), Theorem 7 says that \(\neg (\exists t \in W,\ s t \text{ is a palindrome})\) has the truth value of \(\forall t \in W,\ s t \text{ is not a palindrome}\). These have the same truth value for every \(s\), so the \(\exists s\) propositions built from them do too (Definition: Existential quantifier), and the negation has the truth value of \[
\exists s \in W,\ \forall t \in W,\ s t \text{ is not a palindrome}.
\] In English: some word cannot be made into a palindrome by adding letters at its end.











Exercise 8 (Which one is true?) Which is true: \(\forall s \in W,\ \exists t \in W,\ s t \text{ is a palindrome}\), from Exercise 7, or its negation?










SolutionSolution






Solution 8. The original is true, so its negation is false. For any word \(s\), let \(t\) be \(s\) written backwards; then \(s t\) reads the same backwards. For example, for \(s = \text{aab}\), \(t = \text{baa}\) and \(s t = \text{aabbaa}\).






References

title: Graphs
text:
NoteSource





The topics of this chapter, and their order, follow the course calendar and Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes on graphs. These come from those notes:

a graph as a set of vertices and a set of edges, each edge with one or two endpoints;
loops, parallel (multiple) edges, simple graphs and directed graphs;
adjacent vertices, the degree of a vertex, with a loop counted twice, and the in-degree and out-degree in a directed graph;
the handshake theorem, the fact that a graph has an even number of vertices of odd degree, and the sums of the in-degrees and out-degrees;
complete graphs \(K_n\), cycle graphs \(C_n\), bipartite graphs and subgraphs;
adjacency lists and adjacency matrices, with parallel edges counted in the matrix, and when a list takes less space than a matrix;
walks (which the notes call paths), circuits and cycles, connected graphs and connected components, and strongly connected directed graphs;
counting walks with the powers of the adjacency matrix, proved by induction on the length.

The pseudocode for breadth-first and depth-first search, and the use of a queue and of recursion in them, follow the course’s handout on graph extensions. Euler circuits and trails and Hamiltonian cycles follow the course calendar, with the definitions cited with them. Incident edges, neighborhoods and weakly connected directed graphs are added here. The proofs of the handshake theorem, of the even number of vertices of odd degree and of counting walks follow the lecture notes. The examples, the exercises, the Racket functions and the other proofs are new.




1 Graphs







Exercise 1 (Computers and cables) An office has six computers, named \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\), \(e\) and \(f\). A cable joins the two computers in each of these eight pairs:
\[
{\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{a, c\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{c, e\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{d, e\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{d, f\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{e, f\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]
Draw a point for each computer and a line for each cable. How many cables have computer \(d\) at one end?










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. Figure 1 is one drawing. The cables with \(d\) at one end are \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{d, e\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{d, f\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so there are three of them.



Figure 1: The computers and cables of Exercise 1.

















Definition 1 (Graph) A graph \(G = (V, E)\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026o) consists of

a nonempty finite set \(V\) (Definition: Finite set), whose elements are called the vertices of \(G\);
a finite set \(E\), whose elements are called the edges of \(G\);
for each edge, a set of one or two vertices, called the endpoints of the edge.

An edge joins its endpoints. To stress that its edges have no direction, \(G\) is also called an undirected graph.











Example 1 (The office graph) The computers and cables of Exercise 1 form a graph (Definition 1) \(G = (V, E)\), with one vertex for each computer and one edge for each cable:
\[
\begin{aligned}
V &= {\mathopen{}\left\{a, b, c, d, e, f\right\}\mathclose{}},
\\
E &= {\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{a, c\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{c, e\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{d, e\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{d, f\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{e, f\right\}\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here each edge is written as the set of its endpoints: the edge \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}\) joins the vertices \(b\) and \(d\). Figure 1 draws \(G\). We call \(G\) the office graph.











Remark 1 (A drawing is not the graph). A graph (Definition 1) says only which vertices are the endpoints of which edges. A drawing of it adds things that are not part of the graph: where the points are, how long and how curved the lines are, and whether two lines cross. Two drawings that put the points in different places draw the same graph, as long as they join the same pairs of points.
Graphs here are different objects from graphs of functions (Definition: Graph of a function), just as directed graphs of relations were (Remark: Two uses of the word “graph”).











Definition 2 (Loop) A loop (Wikipedia contributors 2026t) is an edge of a graph (Definition 1) that has only one endpoint. It joins that vertex to itself.











Definition 3 (Parallel edges) Two different edges of a graph (Definition 1) are parallel edges (Wikipedia contributors 2026u) if they have the same set of endpoints.











Example 2 (A loop and two parallel edges) The graph in Figure 2 has vertices \(p\), \(q\), \(r\) and \(s\), and five edges:

a loop (Definition 2) at \(p\);
an edge joining \(p\) and \(q\);
two parallel edges (Definition 3) joining \(q\) and \(r\);
an edge joining \(r\) and \(s\).

The two edges joining \(q\) and \(r\) have the same set of endpoints, \({\mathopen{}\left\{q, r\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so writing an edge as the set of its endpoints does not tell them apart. We name them instead, say \(e_1\) and \(e_2\), and say that each has endpoints \(q\) and \(r\).



Figure 2: A graph with a loop at \(p\) and two parallel edges between \(q\) and \(r\).

















Example 3 (The bridges of Königsberg) The city of Königsberg was built on four pieces of land, divided by a river, with seven bridges between them (Wikipedia contributors 2026x). Name the pieces of land \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\), where \(A\) is an island. Two bridges joined \(A\) and \(B\), two joined \(A\) and \(C\), and one bridge joined each of the pairs \({\mathopen{}\left\{A, D\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{B, D\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{C, D\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
Figure 3 draws the graph (Definition 1) with a vertex for each piece of land and an edge for each bridge. It has two pairs of parallel edges (Definition 3), and no loops (Definition 2).



Figure 3: The bridges of Königsberg as a graph: a vertex for each piece of land, and an edge for each bridge.

















Definition 4 (Simple graph) A graph (Definition 1) is simple (Wikipedia contributors 2026o) if it has no loops (Definition 2) and no parallel edges (Definition 3).











Example 4 (Simple or not)  

The office graph of Example 1 is simple (Definition 4): each of its edges has two endpoints, and no two of its edges have the same endpoints.
The graph of Example 2 is not simple, since it has a loop and two parallel edges.
The bridge graph of Example 3 is not simple, since it has parallel edges.

In a simple graph, each edge is the only edge with its two endpoints, so writing each edge as the set of its endpoints, as in Example 1, names every edge exactly once.











Definition 5 (Directed graph (digraph)) A directed graph, or digraph, \(G = (V, E)\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026l) consists of

a nonempty finite set \(V\) of vertices;
a finite set \(E\) of edges;
for each edge, a vertex where it starts and a vertex where it ends.

An edge that starts at \(u\) and ends at \(v\) goes from \(u\) to \(v\). Two different edges of a directed graph are parallel edges (Definition 3) if they start at the same vertex and end at the same vertex. When \(G\) has no parallel edges, we write each edge from \(u\) to \(v\) as the ordered pair \((u, v)\) (Definition: Ordered pair). An edge that starts and ends at the same vertex is a loop, as in Definition 2.











Example 5 (Links between web pages) A small website has four pages: home, about, blog and contact. Figure 4 draws the directed graph (Definition 5) with a vertex for each page and an edge from page \(u\) to page \(v\) when \(u\) links to \(v\). Its edges are
\[
\begin{aligned}
& (\text{home}, \text{about}), (\text{home}, \text{blog}), (\text{about}, \text{contact}),
\\
& (\text{blog}, \text{home}), (\text{blog}, \text{blog}), (\text{blog}, \text{contact}), (\text{contact}, \text{home}).
\end{aligned}
\]
The blog links to itself, so the edge \((\text{blog}, \text{blog})\) is a loop. The edges \((\text{home}, \text{blog})\) and \((\text{blog}, \text{home})\) are different edges: one starts at home and the other starts at blog.



Figure 4: The links between the four pages of a website.

















Remark 2 (Relations and directed graphs). Let \(R\) be a relation on a set \(A\). The drawing of Definition: Directed graph of a relation draws the directed graph (Definition 5) with vertex set \(A\) and edge set \(R\). That directed graph has no parallel edges, since \(R\) is a set and has each pair at most once. Going the other way, the edges of a directed graph with no parallel edges form a relation on its vertex set. The links of Example 5 form the relation “links to” on the set of four pages.

Definition 6 (Adjacent vertices (neighbors)) Two vertices \(u\) and \(v\) of a graph (Definition 1) are adjacent, or neighbors, if some edge has endpoints \(u\) and \(v\).











Example 6 (Neighbors in the office graph) In the office graph (Example 1), the neighbors (Definition 6) of \(b\) are \(a\), \(c\) and \(d\). The vertices \(a\) and \(f\) are not adjacent, since no edge has endpoints \(a\) and \(f\). In the graph of Example 2, the loop at \(p\) makes \(p\) adjacent to itself.











Definition 7 (Incident) An edge of a graph (Definition 1) is incident with each of its endpoints.











Example 7 (Edges at a vertex of the office graph) In the office graph (Example 1), the edges incident (Definition 7) with \(e\) are \({\mathopen{}\left\{c, e\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{d, e\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{e, f\right\}\mathclose{}}\). The edge \({\mathopen{}\left\{c, e\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is incident with \(c\) and with \(e\), and with no other vertex.











Definition 8 (Neighborhood) The neighborhood \(N(v)\) of a vertex \(v\) of a graph (Definition 1) is the set of neighbors (Definition 6) of \(v\).











Example 8 (Neighborhoods with a loop and parallel edges) In the graph of Example 2,
\[
N(p) = {\mathopen{}\left\{p, q\right\}\mathclose{}}, \qquad N(q) = {\mathopen{}\left\{p, r\right\}\mathclose{}}, \qquad N(r) = {\mathopen{}\left\{q, s\right\}\mathclose{}}, \qquad N(s) = {\mathopen{}\left\{r\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]
The loop at \(p\) puts \(p\) in its own neighborhood (Definition 8). The two parallel edges joining \(q\) and \(r\) put \(r\) in \(N(q)\) only once, since \(N(q)\) is a set.











Definition 9 (Degree) The degree \(\deg(v)\) of a vertex \(v\) of a graph (Definition 1) (Wikipedia contributors 2026j) is the number of edges that have \(v\) as an endpoint, where each loop (Definition 2) at \(v\) counts twice.











Example 9 (Degrees with a loop) In the graph of Example 2 (Figure 2), \(\deg(p) = 2 + 1 = 3\) (Definition 9), since the loop at \(p\) counts twice and one more edge joins \(p\) to \(q\). Both parallel edges (Definition 3) count at \(q\) and at \(r\), so
\[
\deg(q) = 3, \quad \deg(r) = 3, \quad \deg(s) = 1.
\]
Each edge has two ends, and a loop has both of its ends at the same vertex. Counting a loop twice makes \(\deg(v)\) the number of ends of edges at \(v\).











Theorem 1 (The handshake theorem) For every graph \(G = (V, E)\) (Definition 1),
\[
\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2 {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}},
\]
where \(\deg(v)\) is the degree (Definition 9) of \(v\) and \({\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}}\) is the number of edges (Definition: Cardinality). It is called the handshake theorem (Wikipedia contributors 2026r) because, when the vertices are the people at a party and the edges are the handshakes between them, it says that the numbers of hands that the people shook add up to twice the number of handshakes.










ProofProof






Proof. Each edge has two ends. An edge with two endpoints has one end at each endpoint, and a loop has both ends at its one endpoint. We count the set of all ends of all edges in two ways.
Counted edge by edge, each edge gives two ends, so there are \(2 {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}}\) ends.
Counted vertex by vertex, the ends at \(v\) are one end of each non-loop edge with endpoint \(v\) and two ends of each loop at \(v\). That is \(\deg(v)\) ends, by Definition 9, and each end is at exactly one vertex, so there are \(\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v)\) ends.
The two counts count the same set, so they are equal.











Example 10 (Checking the handshake theorem) In the office graph (Example 1), the degrees add up to 16 (Solution 2), and \(2 {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}} = 2 \cdot 8 = 16\). In the graph of Example 2, the degrees of Example 9 add up to \(3 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 10\), and \(2 {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}} = 2 \cdot 5 = 10\), as Theorem 1 says.











Corollary 1 (An even number of odd degrees) Every graph (Definition 1) has an even number of vertices of odd degree (Definition 9).










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(G = (V, E)\) be a graph, let \(O\) be the set of vertices of odd degree, and let \(N\) be the set of vertices of even degree. By Theorem 1,
\[
\sum_{v \in O} \deg(v) = 2 {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}} - \sum_{v \in N} \deg(v).
\]
The right side is an even number minus a sum of even numbers, so it is even (Definition: Even integer). The left side is a sum of \({\mathopen{}\left|O\right|\mathclose{}}\) odd numbers. Pair the odd numbers off two at a time. The sum of each pair is even. If \({\mathopen{}\left|O\right|\mathclose{}}\) were odd, one odd number would be left over, and the left side would be an even number plus an odd number, which is odd. So \({\mathopen{}\left|O\right|\mathclose{}}\) cannot be odd, and it is even.











Example 11 (Degrees that no graph has) No graph has five vertices with degrees 4, 3, 3, 2 and 1. Such a graph would have three vertices of odd degree, the two of degree 3 and the one of degree 1, and Corollary 1 says that the number of vertices of odd degree is even. Equivalently, by Theorem 1, the degrees would add up to \(4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 13\), which is not twice a number of edges.











Definition 10 (Out-degree) The out-degree \(\deg^+(v)\) of a vertex \(v\) of a directed graph (Definition 5) (Wikipedia contributors 2026l) is the number of edges that start at \(v\).











Definition 11 (In-degree) The in-degree \(\deg^-(v)\) of a vertex \(v\) of a directed graph (Definition 5) (Wikipedia contributors 2026l) is the number of edges that end at \(v\).











Theorem 2 (Degrees in a directed graph) For every directed graph \(G = (V, E)\) (Definition 5),
\[
\sum_{v \in V} \deg^+(v) = {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}} = \sum_{v \in V} \deg^-(v),
\]
where \(\deg^+\) is the out-degree (Definition 10) and \(\deg^-\) is the in-degree (Definition 11).










ProofProof






Proof. Each edge starts at exactly one vertex, so sorting the edges by the vertex where they start puts each edge in exactly one group. The group of \(v\) has \(\deg^+(v)\) edges, so the sizes of the groups add up to \(\sum_{v \in V} \deg^+(v) = {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}}\). Sorting the edges by the vertex where they end gives \(\sum_{v \in V} \deg^-(v) = {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}}\) in the same way.

3 Special graphs and subgraphs







Exercise 3 (A chess tournament) A chess club has 8 members, and every two members play each other exactly once. How many games are played?










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. Draw a vertex for each member and an edge for each game. Each member plays the 7 others, so each vertex has degree 7 (Definition 9). By Theorem 1, \(2 {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}} = 8 \cdot 7 = 56\), so there are \({\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}} = 28\) games.











Definition 12 (Complete graph) For a positive integer \(n\), a complete graph \(K_n\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026e) is a simple graph (Definition 4) with \(n\) vertices in which every two different vertices are adjacent (Definition 6). Two complete graphs with \(n\) vertices differ only in the names of their vertices, so we write \(K_n\) for any of them.











Example 13 (The tournament graph) The graph of Solution 3, with a vertex for each member and an edge for each game, is a complete graph on 8 vertices, \(K_8\) (Definition 12).











Definition 13 (Cycle graph) For an integer \(n \ge 3\), a cycle graph \(C_n\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026i) is a simple graph (Definition 4) with vertices \(v_1, \ldots, v_n\) and the \(n\) edges
\[
{\mathopen{}\left\{v_1, v_2\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{v_2, v_3\right\}\mathclose{}}, \ldots, {\mathopen{}\left\{v_{n - 1}, v_n\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{v_n, v_1\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]
Going along these edges in order from \(v_1\) visits every vertex and returns to \(v_1\). Two cycle graphs with \(n\) vertices differ only in the names of their vertices, so we write \(C_n\) for any of them.











Example 14 (A round table) Nine people sit around a round table. The graph with a vertex for each person, and an edge between each two people who sit next to each other, is a cycle graph on 9 vertices, \(C_9\) (Definition 13): going around the table visits each person once, and each person sits next to exactly two others.











Definition 14 (Bipartite graph) A graph \(G = (V, E)\) (Definition 1) is bipartite (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) if there are two sets \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) with \(V_1 \cup V_2 = V\) and \(V_1 \cap V_2 = \emptyset\) (Definition: Union, Definition: Intersection), such that every edge has one endpoint in \(V_1\) and the other endpoint in \(V_2\).











Example 15 (The cube graph is bipartite) Let \(Q_3\) be the graph whose vertices are the eight bit strings of length 3, with an edge between two strings when they differ in exactly one position (Wikipedia contributors 2026s). For example, \(000\) and \(010\) are adjacent (Definition 6), but \(000\) and \(011\) are not. Figure 5 draws \(Q_3\) as the corners and edges of a cube.
Let \(V_1\) be the strings with an even number of ones, and \(V_2\) the strings with an odd number of ones:
\[
V_1 = {\mathopen{}\left\{000, 011, 101, 110\right\}\mathclose{}}, \qquad V_2 = {\mathopen{}\left\{001, 010, 100, 111\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]
Changing one position of a string changes its number of ones by exactly one, from even to odd or from odd to even. So every edge has one endpoint in \(V_1\) and the other in \(V_2\), and \(Q_3\) is bipartite (Definition 14).



Figure 5: The cube graph \(Q_3\), with the strings in \(V_1\) shaded.

















Definition 15 (Subgraph) A subgraph of a graph \(G = (V, E)\) (Definition 1) is a graph \(H = (W, F)\) with \(W \subseteq V\) and \(F \subseteq E\) (Definition: Subset), where each edge of \(F\) has the same endpoints in \(H\) as in \(G\). Since \(H\) is a graph, the endpoints of each edge of \(F\) are in \(W\).











Example 16 (Leaving out a computer) Take the computer \(b\) out of the office (Example 1), with its cables \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}\). What is left is a subgraph (Definition 15) of the office graph, with vertex set \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, c, d, e, f\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and the five edges
\[
{\mathopen{}\left\{a, c\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{c, e\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{d, e\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{d, f\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{e, f\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]
Taking out \(b\) but keeping the edge \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}\) would not give a subgraph, since one endpoint of that edge would not be a vertex.

if \(G\) is a graph, the neighbors of \(v\) (Definition 6);

Definition 17 (Adjacency matrix) Let \(G\) be a graph (Definition 1) or a directed graph (Definition 5), and list its vertices in a chosen order as \(v_1, \ldots, v_n\). The adjacency matrix of \(G\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) is the \(n \times n\) matrix (Definition: Matrix) \(A_G\) whose entry \(a_{ij}\) in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is

if \(G\) is a graph, the number of edges with endpoints \(v_i\) and \(v_j\);
if \(G\) is a directed graph, the number of edges from \(v_i\) to \(v_j\).

So a loop at \(v_i\) adds 1 to the diagonal entry \(a_{ii}\).











Example 18 (The adjacency matrix of the office graph) With its vertices in the order \(a, b, c, d, e, f\), the office graph (Example 1) has the adjacency matrix (Definition 17)

\\

Example 19 (Counting parallel edges) With its vertices in the order \(A, B, C, D\), the bridge graph of Example 3 has the adjacency matrix (Definition 17)
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 2 & 2 & 1
\\
2 & 0 & 0 & 1
\\
2 & 0 & 0 & 1
\\
1 & 1 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The entries 2 count the two parallel edges (Definition 3) between \(A\) and \(B\) and the two between \(A\) and \(C\).











Example 20 (The adjacency matrix of a directed graph) With its vertices in the order home, about, blog, contact, the directed graph of Example 5 has the adjacency matrix (Definition 17)
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 1 & 0
\\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\\
1 & 0 & 1 & 1
\\
1 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The entry in row 1 and column 3 is 1, since home links to blog, and so is the entry in row 3 and column 1, since blog links to home. The entry in row 2 and column 1 is 0, since about does not link to home, although home links to about. The 1 in row 3 and column 3 is the loop at blog. This is the matrix of the relation “links to” (Definition: Matrix of a relation, Remark 2).











Remark 3 (What the adjacency matrix shows). Let \(A_G = (a_{ij})\) be the adjacency matrix (Definition 17) of \(G\).

If \(G\) is a graph, then \(a_{ij} = a_{ji}\) for all \(i\) and \(j\), since an edge with endpoints \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) has endpoints \(v_j\) and \(v_i\).
If \(G\) is a graph with no loops (Definition 2), then row \(i\) adds up to \(\deg(v_i)\) (Definition 9). Some books put 2 on the diagonal for each loop (Wikipedia contributors 2026b), which makes the rows add up to the degrees even with loops.
If \(G\) is a directed graph, then row \(i\) adds up to the out-degree \(\deg^+(v_i)\) (Definition 10), and column \(i\) adds up to the in-degree \(\deg^-(v_i)\) (Definition 11).

An adjacency list (Definition 16) of a graph with no loops has \(2 {\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}}\) entries, by Theorem 1, and an adjacency matrix has \(n^2\) entries. When there are few edges, as in Exercise 4, the list is shorter. When most pairs of vertices are adjacent, the matrix is about as long, and it answers “are \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) adjacent?” with a single entry.

Exercise 5 (Looking up a vertex) In Racket, the adjacency list of the office graph (Example 17) can be stored as a list with one list for each vertex, which starts with the vertex and goes on with its neighbors:

  '((a b c)
    (b a c d)
    (c a b e)

The quote ' makes Racket read what follows as data, so '(a b c) is the same list as (list 'a 'b 'c). (assoc x L) returns the first element of the list L whose first element is x, and #f if there is none. What does (assoc 'd office) return?










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. It returns '(d b e f), the element of office that starts with d. Its rest, '(b e f), lists the neighbors of \(d\) (Definition 6).











Example 21 (Neighbors and degrees in Racket) With office as in Exercise 5, these functions return the neighbors (Definition 6) and the degree (Definition 9) of a vertex of a graph with no loops or parallel edges:
(define (neighbors G v)
  (rest (assoc v G)))

(define (degree G v)
  (length (neighbors G v)))
(neighbors office 'b) returns '(a c d), and (degree office 'b) returns 3. (for/sum ([x L]) body) adds up the values of body for each element x of the list L, so

6 Walks, trails and paths







Exercise 6 (A route through every computer) In the office of Exercise 1, a message passes from computer to computer along cables. Give a route for a message that starts at \(a\), ends at \(f\), and passes through every computer exactly once.










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. One route is \(a, c, b, d, e, f\). Each two computers next to each other in it are joined by a cable: \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, c\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{c, b\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{d, e\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{e, f\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are all edges in Figure 1. Another is \(a, b, c, e, d, f\).











Definition 18 (Walk) Let \(G\) be a graph (Definition 1) and let \(n \ge 0\) be an integer. A walk of length \(n\) from a vertex \(u\) to a vertex \(v\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026v) is a sequence
\[
v_0, e_1, v_1, e_2, v_2, \ldots, e_n, v_n
\]
of vertices \(v_i\) and edges \(e_i\), with \(v_0 = u\) and \(v_n = v\), such that the endpoints of each edge \(e_i\) are \(v_{i - 1}\) and \(v_i\). The length \(n\) is the number of edges in the sequence, counted with repeats. In a directed graph (Definition 5), each edge \(e_i\) must go from \(v_{i - 1}\) to \(v_i\).











Example 22 (A walk in the office graph) In a simple graph (Definition 4), the vertices of a walk (Definition 18) name its edges, so we write the walk as its list of vertices. In the office graph (Figure 1),
\[
a, b, c, a, b, d
\]
is a walk of length 5 from \(a\) to \(d\), along the edges \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{c, a\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}\). It uses the edge \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}\) twice. A single vertex, such as \(a\), is a walk of length 0 from \(a\) to \(a\).











Definition 19 (Trail) A trail (Wikipedia contributors 2026v) is a walk (Definition 18) whose edges \(e_1, \ldots, e_n\) are all different.











Definition 20 (Path) A path (Wikipedia contributors 2026v) is a walk (Definition 18) whose vertices \(v_0, \ldots, v_n\) are all different.











Example 23 (Walks, trails and paths) In the office graph (Figure 1):

\(a, b, c, a, b, d\) (Example 22) is not a trail (Definition 19), since it uses the edge \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}\) twice.
\(b, c, a, b, d\) is a trail, since its four edges \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{c, a\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{b, d\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are all different. It is not a path (Definition 20), since it visits \(b\) twice.
\(a, c, e, f\) is a path of length 3 from \(a\) to \(f\).

A path is always a trail: if two of its edges were the same edge, they would have the same endpoints, and a vertex would repeat.











Definition 21 (Circuit) A circuit (Wikipedia contributors 2026h) is a trail (Definition 19) of length at least 1 that starts and ends at the same vertex.











Definition 22 (Cycle) A cycle (Wikipedia contributors 2026h) is a circuit (Definition 21) \(v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n\) whose vertices \(v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_{n - 1}\) are all different. Its only repeated vertex is \(v_n = v_0\).











Remark 4 (Why cycle graphs are called that). In a cycle graph \(C_n\) (Definition 13), the walk \(v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n, v_1\) is a cycle (Definition 22) that contains every vertex, which gives the graph its name.











Example 24 (Circuits and cycles in three triangles) Figure 6 draws a simple graph (Definition 4) \(T\) made of three triangles in a row. In \(T\):

\(1, 2, 3, 1\) is a cycle (Definition 22) of length 3;
\(3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 5, 3\) is a circuit (Definition 21) of length 6, since its six edges are all different. It is not a cycle, since it visits \(5\) twice before it comes back to \(3\).

In the office graph (Figure 1), \(b, d, f, e, c, b\) is a cycle of length 5.



Figure 6: The graph \(T\): three triangles in a row.

















Remark 5 (Other names for walks). Books do not agree on these names. Some, including Kameron Decker Harris’s notes for this course, call a walk (Definition 18) a “path”, call a trail (Definition 19) a “simple path”, and call a closed walk of positive length a circuit. Others call a cycle (Definition 22) a “simple circuit”. When you read about graphs elsewhere, check which definitions the author uses.











Theorem 3 (A shortest walk is a path) Let \(u\) and \(v\) be vertices of a graph (Definition 1) or a directed graph (Definition 5). If there is a walk (Definition 18) from \(u\) to \(v\), then every walk from \(u\) to \(v\) of the smallest possible length is a path (Definition 20). In particular, there is then a path from \(u\) to \(v\).










ProofProof






Proof. The lengths of the walks from \(u\) to \(v\), each plus 1, form a nonempty set of positive integers, so that set has a smallest element (Remark: Smallest elements), and subtracting 1 from it gives the smallest length of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\). Let \(v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n\) be a walk from \(u\) to \(v\) of that smallest length \(n\).
Suppose, for contradiction (Definition: Proof by contradiction), that it is not a path. Then \(v_i = v_j\) for some \(i < j\). Leaving out the part between them gives the sequence
\[
v_0, e_1, \ldots, e_i, v_i, e_{j + 1}, v_{j + 1}, \ldots, e_n, v_n,
\]
which is still a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), since the edge \(e_{j + 1}\) joins \(v_j = v_i\) to \(v_{j + 1}\) (in a directed graph, it goes from \(v_i\) to \(v_{j + 1}\)). When \(j = n\), the sequence ends at \(v_i = v_n = v\). Its length is \(n - (j - i) < n\), which contradicts the choice of \(n\). So the walk is a path.











Theorem 4 (Counting walks with powers of the adjacency matrix) Let \(G\) be a graph (Definition 1) or a directed graph (Definition 5) with vertices \(v_1, \ldots, v_n\) and adjacency matrix \(A_G\) (Definition 17). For every integer \(r \ge 1\), the entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) of the power \(A_G^r\) (Definition: Matrix power) is the number of walks (Definition 18) of length \(r\) from \(v_i\) to \(v_j\).










ProofProof






Proof. Write \((M)_{ij}\) for the entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) of a matrix \(M\), and \(a_{ij} = (A_G)_{ij}\). We use induction (Definition: Proof by induction) on \(r\).
Base case. A walk of length 1 from \(v_i\) to \(v_j\) is a sequence \(v_i, g, v_j\), where \(g\) is an edge with endpoints \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) (from \(v_i\) to \(v_j\), in a directed graph). There is one such walk for each such edge, so there are \(a_{ij}\) of them, by Definition 17. A loop \(g\) at \(v_i\) gives one walk \(v_i, g, v_i\), and adds 1 to \(a_{ii}\).
Inductive step. Suppose that \((A_G^r)_{ik}\) is the number of walks of length \(r\) from \(v_i\) to \(v_k\), for all \(i\) and \(k\). Every walk of length \(r + 1\) from \(v_i\) to \(v_j\) is a walk of length \(r\) from \(v_i\) to some vertex \(v_k\), followed by an edge from \(v_k\) to \(v_j\) and the vertex \(v_j\). Sort these walks by the vertex \(v_k\) just before the last edge. For each \(k\), a walk is made by choosing one of the \((A_G^r)_{ik}\) walks to \(v_k\) and one of the \(a_{kj}\) edges, and different choices give different walks, so there are \((A_G^r)_{ik} \, a_{kj}\) walks with that \(v_k\). Adding over \(k\), and using the definition of the matrix product (Definition: Matrix multiplication), the number of walks of length \(r + 1\) from \(v_i\) to \(v_j\) is
\[
\sum_{k = 1}^{n} (A_G^r)_{ik} \, a_{kj} = (A_G^r A_G)_{ij} = (A_G^{r + 1})_{ij}.
\]
By induction, the statement holds for every \(r \ge 1\).

\\
1 & 3 & 1 & 0 & 2 & 1
\\
1 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 0 & 1
\\
1 & 0 & 2 & 3 & 1 & 1
\\

\\

\end{bmatrix}.

7 Connected graphs

Definition 23 (Connected graph) A graph (Definition 1) is connected (Wikipedia contributors 2026g) if there is a walk (Definition 18) from \(u\) to \(v\) for every two vertices \(u\) and \(v\).











Example 26 (Connected or not) The office graph (Example 1) is connected (Definition 23). The walks
\[
a, b \qquad a, c \qquad a, b, d \qquad a, c, e \qquad a, b, d, f
\]
go from \(a\) to each other vertex. For two vertices \(u\) and \(v\), reading the walk from \(a\) to \(u\) backward and then following the walk from \(a\) to \(v\) gives a walk from \(u\) to \(v\).
The graph \(H\) of Exercise 7 is not connected, since it has no walk from \(a\) to \(f\).
By Theorem 3, a graph is connected exactly when there is a path (Definition 20) between every two vertices.











Definition 24 (Connected component) A connected component of a graph \(G\) (Definition 1) (Wikipedia contributors 2026f) is a connected (Definition 23) subgraph (Definition 15) of \(G\) that is not a subgraph of any other connected subgraph of \(G\).











Example 27 (The components of the cut office) The graph \(H\) of Exercise 7 has two connected components (Definition 24): the subgraph with vertices \(a, b, c\) and the three edges among them, and the subgraph with vertices \(d, e, f\) and the three edges among them. Each of them is connected, and each already has every edge of \(H\) between its vertices. A connected subgraph of \(H\) that contained \(a\) and one of \(d\), \(e\), \(f\) would have a walk from \(a\) to that vertex, and Solution 7 showed that a walk from \(a\) in \(H\) stays in \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}\). The same argument from \(d\) shows that no connected subgraph contains \(d\) and one of \(a\), \(b\), \(c\).
A connected graph, such as the office graph, has one connected component: the whole graph.











Definition 25 (Strongly connected directed graph) A directed graph (Definition 5) is strongly connected (Wikipedia contributors 2026y) if there is a walk (Definition 18) from \(u\) to \(v\) for every two vertices \(u\) and \(v\), where each edge of a walk is followed from its start to its end.











Example 28 (Following the links) The directed graph of Example 5 is strongly connected (Definition 25). The walk home, about, contact, home goes from home to about and to contact and back, and the edges \((\text{home}, \text{blog})\) and \((\text{blog}, \text{home})\) join home and blog both ways. So there is a walk from every page to home, and from home to every page, and following one walk after the other goes from any page to any other.
If the contact page lost its link to home, the graph would not be strongly connected: no edge would start at contact, so there would be no walk from contact to any other page.











Definition 26 (Weakly connected directed graph) A directed graph (Definition 5) is weakly connected if the graph (Definition 1) with the same vertices and edges, in which each edge has the same two endpoints but no direction, is connected (Definition 23).











Example 29 (The steps of a software project) A project moves between four steps: plan, code, test and ship. The directed graph with these steps as vertices has the four edges
\[
(\text{plan}, \text{code}), \quad (\text{code}, \text{test}), \quad (\text{test}, \text{code}), \quad (\text{test}, \text{ship}),
\]
since after testing, the team either fixes the code or ships. It is weakly connected (Definition 26): ignoring the directions, the walk plan, code, test, ship visits every vertex, and the part of it between any two vertices, read in one direction or the other, is a walk between them. It is not strongly connected (Definition 25), since no edge starts at ship, so there is no walk from ship to any other step.

Exercise 8 (Drawing an envelope) Can you draw Figure 8 without lifting your pencil from the paper and without drawing any line twice?

Definition 27 (Euler circuit) An Euler circuit of a graph (Definition 1) (Wikipedia contributors 2026n) is a circuit (Definition 21) that contains every edge of the graph. Since a circuit is a trail, it contains each edge exactly once.











Definition 28 (Euler trail) An Euler trail of a graph (Definition 1) (Wikipedia contributors 2026n) is a trail (Definition 19) from a vertex \(u\) to a different vertex \(v\) that contains every edge of the graph.











Example 30 (An Euler circuit and an Euler trail) In the graph \(T\) of Figure 6,
\[
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 5, 3, 1
\]
is an Euler circuit (Definition 27): it is a circuit that goes from 1 to 5 along two edges of the left triangle and two edges of the middle triangle, around the whole right triangle back to 5, and back to 1 along the third edge of the middle triangle and the third edge of the left triangle, so it uses each of the nine edges once.
The walk \(v, w, x, v, y, x, z, y, w\) of Solution 8 is an Euler trail (Definition 28) from \(v\) to \(w\) of the envelope graph.











Lemma 1 (Ends of the edges of a trail) Let \(v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n\) be a trail (Definition 19) in a graph (Definition 1), and let \(w\) be a vertex. Count the ends at \(w\) of the edges \(e_1, \ldots, e_n\), as in the proof of Theorem 1.

If the trail starts and ends at the same vertex, \(v_0 = v_n\), then the count is even.
If \(v_0 \ne v_n\), then the count is odd for \(w = v_0\) and for \(w = v_n\), and even for every other \(w\).











ProofProof






Proof. The edge \(e_i\) has one end at \(v_{i - 1}\) and its other end at \(v_i\), both at the same vertex when \(e_i\) is a loop. The edges \(e_1, \ldots, e_n\) are all different, so no end is counted twice. Let \(k\) be the number of indices \(i\) with \(1 \le i \le n - 1\) and \(v_i = w\), and write \([P]\) for 1 if \(P\) is true and 0 if \(P\) is false. The ends at \(v_{i - 1}\), for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), give \(k + [v_0 = w]\) ends at \(w\), and the ends at \(v_i\), for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), give \(k + [v_n = w]\) ends at \(w\). So the count is
\[
2k + [v_0 = w] + [v_n = w].
\]
If \(v_0 = v_n\), the last two terms are equal, so the count is even. If \(v_0 \ne v_n\), the last two terms add up to 1 when \(w\) is \(v_0\) or \(v_n\), and to 0 otherwise.











Lemma 2 (A trail that cannot go on) Let \(G\) be a graph (Definition 1) in which every vertex has even degree (Definition 9). Let \(v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n\) be a trail (Definition 19) in \(G\) with \(n \ge 1\) that cannot be extended: every edge with endpoint \(v_n\) is one of \(e_1, \ldots, e_n\). Then \(v_n = v_0\), so the trail is a circuit (Definition 21).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose, for contradiction (Definition: Proof by contradiction), that \(v_n \ne v_0\). By Lemma 1, the edges of the trail have an odd number of ends at \(v_n\). The degree \(\deg(v_n)\) is the number of ends at \(v_n\) of all the edges of \(G\), and it is even. So some end at \(v_n\) belongs to an edge that is not in the trail. That edge has endpoint \(v_n\) and is not one of \(e_1, \ldots, e_n\), which contradicts the assumption that the trail cannot be extended.











Theorem 5 (Euler circuits and even degrees) Let \(G\) be a connected graph (Definition 23) with at least one edge. Then \(G\) has an Euler circuit (Definition 27) if and only if every vertex of \(G\) has even degree (Definition 9).










ProofProof






Proof. Only if. Let \(C\) be an Euler circuit, and let \(w\) be a vertex. Every edge of \(G\) is an edge of \(C\), so the ends at \(w\) of the edges of \(C\) are all the ends at \(w\), and there are \(\deg(w)\) of them. By Lemma 1, that number is even.
If. Suppose every vertex has even degree. A trail has at most \({\mathopen{}\left|E\right|\mathclose{}}\) edges, since its edges are all different. So, given an edge and one of its endpoints, there is a trail of greatest length among the trails that start at that endpoint with that edge. That trail cannot be extended, so it is a circuit, by Lemma 2. So \(G\) has at least one circuit. Let \(C\) be a circuit \(v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n\) of greatest length in \(G\). Suppose, for contradiction (Definition: Proof by contradiction), that some edge \(h\) is not in \(C\).
Some edge that is not in \(C\) has an endpoint on \(C\). Let \(y\) be an endpoint of \(h\). If \(y\) is a vertex of \(C\), take \(g = h\). Otherwise, since \(G\) is connected, there is a path (Definition 20) \(y = w_0, w_1, \ldots, w_m = v_0\), by Theorem 3. Let \(j\) be the smallest index with \(w_j\) a vertex of \(C\), so that \(j \ge 1\). Let \(g\) be the edge of the path between \(w_{j - 1}\) and \(w_j\). It is not in \(C\), since its endpoint \(w_{j - 1}\) is not a vertex of \(C\), and its endpoint \(w_j\) is a vertex of \(C\).
A circuit outside \(C\). Let \(H\) be the graph with the vertices of \(G\) and the edges of \(G\) that are not in \(C\). By Lemma 1, the edges of \(C\) have an even number of ends at each vertex, so every vertex has even degree in \(H\) too. The edge \(g\) is in \(H\) and has an endpoint \(v_k\) on \(C\). As in the first paragraph, a trail of greatest length in \(H\) that starts at \(v_k\) with the edge \(g\) is a circuit \(D\) in \(H\), from \(v_k\) to \(v_k\), by Lemma 2.
A longer circuit. Follow \(C\) from \(v_0\) to \(v_k\), then go around \(D\) back to \(v_k\), then follow the rest of \(C\) to \(v_n\). This is a walk from \(v_0\) to \(v_0\). No edge repeats in it, since \(C\) and \(D\) are trails with no common edge, so it is a circuit. Its length is the length of \(C\) plus the length of \(D\), which is greater than the length of \(C\). That contradicts the choice of \(C\). So \(C\) contains every edge, and it is an Euler circuit.











Example 31 (No walk over each bridge once) The people of Königsberg asked whether they could walk through the city, cross each bridge exactly once, and come back to where they started. In 1736, Leonhard Euler showed that they could not (Wikipedia contributors 2026x). In the graph of Example 3, such a walk is an Euler circuit (Definition 27). The graph is connected (Definition 23), since \(D\) is adjacent (Definition 6) to \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). The degrees are
\[
\deg(A) = 5, \quad \deg(B) = 3, \quad \deg(C) = 3, \quad \deg(D) = 3,
\]
all odd, so the graph has no Euler circuit, by Theorem 5.











Theorem 6 (Euler trails and odd degrees) Let \(G\) be a connected graph (Definition 23), and let \(u\) and \(v\) be different vertices of \(G\). Then \(G\) has an Euler trail (Definition 28) from \(u\) to \(v\) if and only if \(u\) and \(v\) have odd degree (Definition 9) and every other vertex has even degree.










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(G'\) be the graph \(G\) with one new edge \(h\) with endpoints \(u\) and \(v\). It may be parallel (Definition 3) to an edge of \(G\). \(G'\) is connected, and has at least one edge. The edge \(h\) adds 1 to the degrees of \(u\) and \(v\), and changes no other degree. So the condition on the degrees in \(G\) says exactly that every vertex has even degree in \(G'\).
Only if. Let \(u = v_0, e_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n = v\) be an Euler trail of \(G\). Adding \(h\) at the end gives the circuit \(v_0, e_1, \ldots, e_n, v, h, u\) in \(G'\), which contains every edge of \(G'\). So every vertex has even degree in \(G'\), by Theorem 5.
If. Every vertex has even degree in \(G'\), so \(G'\) has an Euler circuit, by Theorem 5, and \(h\) is one of its edges. A circuit can start at any of its vertices: moving the part before a vertex to the end gives a circuit with the same edges. Reading a circuit backward gives a circuit with the same edges, so we may assume that the Euler circuit crosses \(h\) from \(v\) to \(u\). So \(G'\) has an Euler circuit that starts at \(v\) with the edge \(h\), as \(v, h, u, \ldots, v\). Leaving out \(v\) and \(h\) at the start gives a trail from \(u\) to \(v\) that contains every edge of \(G\).

Remark 6 (No simple test for Hamiltonian cycles). Theorem 5 decides whether a connected graph has an Euler circuit by looking at its degrees, which takes one pass through an adjacency list. No test like that is known for Hamiltonian cycles (Definition 29). Deciding whether a graph has one is an NP-complete problem (Wikipedia contributors 2026q): no algorithm is known that decides it in a number of steps bounded by a polynomial in the number of vertices.

Definition 31 (Queue) A queue (Wikipedia contributors 2026w) is a list that a program changes in only two ways: it adds an element to the back of the list, and it removes the element at the front. Definition 32 (Breadth-first search) Let \(G\) be a graph (Definition 1) or a directed graph (Definition 5) with no parallel edges (Definition 3), given by an adjacency list (Definition 16), and let \(s\) be a vertex of \(G\). Breadth-first search (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) from \(s\) is the algorithm (Definition: Algorithm) bfs, written in the pseudocode of Remark: How to read the pseudocode in this chapter:
procedure bfs(G, s)
    mark s, and set dist[s] := 0
    Q := a queue containing only s
    while Q is not empty
        v := remove the front of Q
        for each vertex u in the list of v, in order
            if u is not marked
                mark u, and set dist[u] := dist[v] + 1
                add u to the back of Q
Here \(Q\) is a queue (Definition 31), and dist[u] is a label that the algorithm gives to \(u\) when it marks \(u\).
